The biggest downside in Brunskill’s game is his light frame and he is susceptible to being bull rushed in pass protection and does not have great experience playing offensive line in general. Brunskill has an uphill climb to be an lineman but his productivity in grades can’t be ignored as to his potential.
pff_pros: Good feet and moves well in space. Very smooth working to second level in zone-blocking scheme. Good at generating movement in run blocks. Good understanding of angles to blocks. Had excellent run-blocking grades in 2015 as a tight end before moving to right tackle in 2016 and blocks % finishing ninth in the nation with a run-blocking grade of 81.3. Eighth-highest percentage of positively graded plays among draft class tackles.
pff_cons: Lighter frame and is susceptible to bull rushes. 20 percent of his surrendered pressures came from bull rushes, above the NCAA average of 10 percent. Can get thrown off of blocks. Does not have natural position fit in the NFL. May not be able to hold up physically vs. NFL defensive lineman. Had an average pass blocking efficiency amongst tackles in all of FBS.

pff_overview: After a productive junior season, Davis returned for his senior year only to suffer an ankle injury midway 70 through the season, and then have his playing time lessened when returning due to Ronald Jones ’s emergence. Davis injured an ankle again in the Rose Bowl that forced him to miss the Shrine Bowl and most drills at the combine. He shows good speed and change of direction once he has some room to run, but he is going to need more help getting to the second level than backs. He isn’t very physical as a runner, and won’t break many tackles unless he’s making a defender miss almost completely. He shows potential as a receiver if he can get into the open field, but drops and lack of reliability in pass 10 protection will hinder his opportunities in the passing game if he doesn’t improve. Reoccurring ankle injuries and fumble rate are also things to be wary of.
pff_pros: Can make defenders miss at the second level and in open space. Fluidly shifts from one move to the next. Can stop on a dime. Great fit in a zone-blocking scheme. He wasn’t utilized heavily in the passing game, but does show potential, especially when he can get into space — if he catches the ball.
pff_cons: Has a hard time creating his own yards prior to the second level if little is provided by the offensive line. Dropped 18 percent of his catchable targets from 2014 to 2016. Ball security — fumbled eight times on 451 touches from 2014 to 2016, one of the higher rates in the draft class. Huge liability in pass protection. In 2016, he allowed 10 pressures on just 36 snaps in pass protection, easily the worst pass-blocking efficiency among the running back draft class.

pff_overview: Buchanan has a natural blocking frame especially as a pass-blocker but he lacks some mobility at tackle. Buchanan’s best asset is his pass-blocking ability as he can lose his balance in the run game. 20 The biggest concerns for Buchanan going forward will be his ability to handle the speed of defensive lineman in pass and run situations. His grades were below average in several games and that’s concerning as the level of competition he faced was not top end talent. Buchanan may fit best as a guard at the next level and this will probably be his best shot to help a team.
pff_pros: Flexibility to play tackle or guard. Natural blocker who keeps a solid base at the point of contact. Outstanding hand usage in pass protection. Throws his punch without getting off balance. Flashes nifty footwork and shows good reactions to counters in pass protection. Strong and powerful core. Shows up in run game and anchoring down in pass pro. Rarely gives ground versus bull rush. blocks % Improved his pass-protection grade in all three seasons of grading.
pff_cons: Defenders can get their hands into his chest and disengage from his block. Loses balance from time to time when he tries to play low. Below-average athlete for a tackle. Takes forever to get going on pulls/reaches. Didn’t face top end speed rushers at Miami (OH) and could struggle with them at the next level. Grades were average and below average in several games. Regularly has a hitch coming out of his stance in run game.

pff_overview: Excellent feel in the middle of the field. Throws with anticipation and knows how to throw receivers open against zone coverage. Posted the No. 2 grade on intermediate throws in 2016 but ranked only 23rd in the draft class last season. Ranked second in the draft class with a big-time throw percentage of 6.8. Throws well on the run, but will make a few ugly throws off-platform. Long throwing motion will get some publicity, but it’s not an issue when he’s playing confidently (2016). Was an issue at times last season, and there were some ugly fumbles on tape. Far too many poor decisions last season. Ranked 33rd out of 38 draft- class qualifiers at avoiding turnover-worthy throws. Tied for the 3rd-highest grade in the class on short (0-9-yard) passes. Still has work to do on the deep ball. Wasn’t great in 2016, ranked 22nd in adjusted completion percentage last season.
pff_bottom_line: There’s plenty of concern after Darnold was much riskier with the ball in 2017, but his 2016 was one of the best seasons you’ll see from a redshirt freshman. Even during his slump, the high-end plays were still present, as few college quarterbacks possess Darnold’s anticipation and accuracy in the middle of the field. He must cut back on the turnover-worthy throws that littered his tape in 2017. His throwing motion, rightly or wrongly, will likely be dissected at the next level, but overall, Darnold’s top end play is worth a first-round investment.

pff_overview: One of the best receiving backs in the nation, gained 1.9 yards per route run, led all FBS RBs with at least 40 targets. A threat to take it to the house on any carry, ranked fifth among all FBS RBs with a breakaway percentage of 56.8. Broke 35 tackles on 200 carries in 2017. Averaged 3.4 yards per carry after contact. Had an elusive rating of 65.6, good for 26th in the nation in 2017. Elusive rating declined each of the past two seasons. Pass protection has not been stellar, allowed at least eight total pressures in each of the last three seasons. Naturally gifted ball carrier with spectacular skills, his only negative is a natural desire to want to make the big play every carry. Can be reluctant to just hit the designed hole and take 2-3 yards when that is all that’s available.
pff_bottom_line: Saquon Barkley is the most gifted back in this draft class and is a threat to take it to the house on any touch of the football. His only real negative is wanting to make that happen on every carry, occasionally turning down the correct hole to try and bounce it outside and make a bigger play happen. That can lead to him leaving yardage on the table and not taking what’s there every carry, but it is offset with his playmaking ability overall. Pass protection has been suspect, but his receiving skills are elite on passing downs.

pff_overview: Top-notch velocity and ability to create downfield opportunities both off- platform and when throwing on the run. Makes spectacular plays outside the pocket and on the run. Almost looks more comfortable there. Posted the 3rd-highest grade in the draft class in the red-zone last season. Ranked 7th in the draft class in big-time throw percentage last season after posting the highest percentage in 2016. Must make better decisions. Ranked 28th in the draft class at avoiding turnover-worthy plays last season. Short-area accuracy is an issue and ranked 24th in the draft class in PFF grade on short (0-9-yard) passes. Had the 4th-highest percentage of negatively graded throws in the draft class last season.
pff_bottom_line: Allen certainly looks the part with his frame, athleticism, and cannon, but there’s plenty of projection to his game. Even in a strong 2016 season, there were questions as to how well he can play within structure and in the short game, and that was before his performance took a step back in 2017. While the tools are tantalizing, and he can make the big-time throws necessary for the NFL, he must get better at handling the easy stuff, from working in the quick game to throwing with touch and accuracy to all levels of the field.

pff_overview: Unmatched career as far as on-field production. Posted the top two individual seasons in four years of PFF grading. Has plenty of arm to make tight-window throws, even off platform. Natural playmaker capable of creating big plays both within and outside of structure. Made plenty of NFL throws throughout his career, but production was also aided by favorable Oklahoma offense. Will hold the ball too long at times, inviting late pressure. Will need to play on rhythm more consistently at the next level. Led the nation with a passer rating of 139.9 when blitzed and also led at 135.7 when not blitzed. Posted highest grade in the nation both from a clean pocket, pressured. Led the draft class with a big-time throw percentage of 7.58 last season. Tied for the 5th-lowest percentage of turnover-worthy plays in the class.
pff_bottom_line: At some point, Mayfield’s on-field production is too difficult to ignore and that’s what makes him a first-round talent. He has enough arm to make NFL throws and he’s shown the ability to make plays both within and outside of structure. While he could stand to speed up his process on certain plays, May- field’s accuracy, decision-making and natural playmaking ability make him the best quarterback in the draft, and only a few inches of height have instilled doubt in NFL decision-makers.

pff_overview: Posted the highest grade in the draft class on intermediate throws. Aggressive thrower in tight windows; works both for and against him. Instinctive passer capable of working full-field progressions. Generally throws with good balance, but capable of throwing accurately when off-platform. Has the full arsenal of throws. Can fire the seam or layer the ball over linebackers. Has a good feel for back-shoulder throws. Ranked eighth in the draft class in big-time throw percentage at 5.72. Ranked only 24th out of 38 draft-class qualifiers at avoiding turnover- worthy throws. Had the 4th-highest percentage of turnover-worthy throws in the red- zone among draft-eligible quarterbacks. Ranked only 24th in the draft class in PFF grading on deep passes.
pff_bottom_line: Seemingly destined for the first round since he stepped onto campus, Rosen put together a strong career at UCLA, though he never truly dominated like a first-round lock should have. Still, he has a good feel for getting the ball down the field and a fearless mentality works both for and against him, as he’ll create big plays while also sprinkling in a few head-scratchers. Overall, Rosen’s top-end plays add enough value that the volatility is worth a shot at the top of the first round.

pff_overview: Far and away the highest graded guard in college football this past season with a 95.1 overall grade. Graded above 90.0 in 2016 as well. Plays to the whistle snap after snap. Never met a block he didn’t want to finish with the defender on the ground. Flashes power at the line of scrimmage as well as on pull blocks. Can generate movement off the line of scrimmage on nearly any type of block. Freakish blend of athleticism and flexibility. Wins the leverage battle regularly. Natural aggression can be detriment at times when he gets overextended trying to deliver a blow. Pass sets look like instant replays. Technique is consistent snap after snap with a deadening, quick punch.
pff_bottom_line: The most dominant offensive line process in our four years of PFF College. Could legitimately play tackle at the next level, as the only reason he started at guard in the first place was because Notre Dame had future first rounders at both tackle positions (Ronnie Stanley and Mike McGlinchey).

pff_overview: Top graded overall safety in the nation as a true freshman in 2015 and again as a junior in 2017. Outstanding size and athleticism. Flies around the field and even has the quicks the hang with slot receivers, despite his size. Can fill multiple roles on defense. Can cover slot receivers or tight ends or play deep in a split-safety role. Also a classic dime linebacker. Can rush the passer in true 1-on-1 situations. Has seven sacks, six hits, and 25 hurries on only 111 career pass-rushes. Attacks downhill from quarters alignment. Finished second in the nation with 16 stops in the pass game. Tied for second in the nation with eight pass breakups last season. Athleticism allows him to gain depth in zone and size allows him to compress passing lanes. Can be a step slow to recognize routes in zone coverage.
pff_bottom_line: James is exactly what the NFL needs on the defensive side of the ball. His size and athleticism allow him to fill multiple positions along the defense, but he may be best in a Landon Collins-like split-safety role where he can work downhill, support the run, and make an impact in the short passing game. As offensive continues to trot out offensive chess pieces, players like James are the answer. A creative defensive coordinator will make the most of James’ skills and he’ll be a game-changer at the next level.

pff_overview: Elite coverage skills. Did not have an interception in 2017 but had one of the best coverage grades in the nation at 88.5. Has incredible speed and burst, and notched 74 defensive stops over the season, the second-most in the nation among all linebackers. On just 54 blitzes this season had eight sacks and 22 total pressures, showing top-level burst to finish pass-rushes. Pass-rushing productivity score of 29.6 was the No. 1 mark among inside linebackers against SEC competition this year. Ranked 6th among 145 eligible linebackers in run-stop percentage (13.0 percent). Has improved his overall grade in each of the past two seasons and been in an exceptionally good range for two years. Was at his best in big games, with impressive grades in the SEC Championship game as well as the college football playoffs.
pff_bottom_line: Roquan Smith is one of the draft’s best linebackers. A player that excels in all areas, he has the elite athleticism and coverage skills to be the perfect NFL line- backer. He has displayed special coverage skills at the college level, even if that hasn’t translated to interception numbers, and coverage linebackers in the NFL have never been more important. His athleticism, along with those coverage skills, could make him a special next-level defender, and any weaknesses in his game are all in the less-important area of run defense.

pff_overview: Allowed an NFL passer rating of 52.9 when targeted in 2017, with two interceptions and twelve pass breakups from 57 targets. Ward allowed just 35.1 percent of passes thrown his way to be caught, one of the best marks in the nation. Like all Ohio State corners, coached not to look for the ball, so tough to tell if those instincts exist, hence just two interceptions in 2017. Aggressive in man coverage and will need to dial down the contact levels at the next level, but was only flagged three times in college career. Played more man coverage than anything else for the Buckeyes, but had a good feel for zone coverage and made some nice plays on the ball. Occasionally missed tackles diving at players’ ankles, but only fell off a total of 11 tackles over two seasons. Athletically gifted corner, who has the tools to become a top cover guy at the next level. Adjustment from Ohio State’s technique a key variable.
pff_bottom_line: Denzel Ward it the latest in a line of Ohio State cornerbacks to hit the NFL draft. Like all Buckeyes cornerbacks, he has been coached to play a specific technique which will need adjustment in the NFL where contact rules are stricter, but he has the athleticism and tools to make that adjustment. He has outstanding coverage numbers and extensive experience in man coverage, but flashed a good feel for zone coverage and shouldn’t be scheme-specific at the next level. One of the best pure cover corners in this draft class.

pff_overview: Played just 13 snaps as a perimeter cornerback in 2017, the position that will hold the most value for him at the NFL level. Made 38 solo tackles in 2017, 23 of which were defensive stops, as he operated largely from the slot and around the line of scrimmage. Graded well in all facets of the game and had three-straight seasons of impressive PFF grades, culminating in an 84.8 mark this year. Wasn’t beaten for a reception longer than 31 yards in 2017. Allowed an NFL passer rating of 83.5 on 61 targets in 2017, but that same stat was just 37.8 the season before. Has been a versatile and effective player for Alabama in multiple positions, and has top-level size and athleticism Teams will need to project him as a perimeter cornerback. The traits and talent are there, but the experience is not. Can he be Jalen Ramsey?
pff_bottom_line: Minkah Fitzpatrick is a playmaker anywhere he lines up on defense, but while that versatility was a plus in college, it presents a challenge to NFL teams look- ing to take him high in the draft, because they need to identify exactly where he plays at the next level. The position that holds the highest value – perimeter corner – is the one that he has the least experience playing (just 13 snaps in 2017). He has excellent instincts, strength and on field communication, and will likely succeed somewhere in the NFL, but what position?

pff_overview: Huge linebacker at 6-foot-5 and 250-pounds, and is just 19 years old. He will be just 20 by opening day of the 2018 NFL season. Has 128 defensive stops over the past three seasons of college play, only two of which were every-down roles. Has also been a significant factor on the blitz, notching six sacks in each of the past two seasons and adding four hits and 13 hurries in 2017. Shows elite lateral movement and can shed blocks at ease when scraping to mirror the running back behind the line. Occasionally blows his run fits, attacking the wrong side of a block and allowing significant breakdown in defensive gap integrity. Immense physical talent, but even at his size can’t overwhelm blockers at the second level without improving hand use.
pff_bottom_line: Physical monster at the linebacker position with an athletic profile unmatched by any other linebacker in this draft, and at just 19 has plenty of room to grow as well. His production has been outstanding at Virginia Tech and the flaws in his game are easily rectified with some more experience and coaching at the next level. Is a huge player for the position, and may not be done growing. Needs to show he can maintain speed and skills in coverage at that size in the NFL. Pro-Bowl level potential in any scheme.

pff_overview: Rare coordination for a 340-pound man. Dancing bear-esque qualities. Even mixes in a spin move from time-to-time. An absolute unit. Dominated from first snap to the last against the run. Plays with immense power and solid leverage for his size. Tackle radius is iffy at best. More disruptor than finisher. Only 25 run- stops on the year. Was already on a very limited snap count at Washington. Played only 62 percent of their defensive snaps this past season (554 total). Already a well-developed pass-rushing repertoire. Hump was his go-to move, but also push-pulled well. Worrisome that he still ran hot and cold even on limited snap counts. Some low energy reps on film. Three games with only 1 pressure in 2017.
pff_bottom_line: The evaluation of Vea is as much about value as it is about talent. There’s no denying that he could step in and be a force at nose tackle from day one, but how much will he offer as a pass-rusher and how many snaps can he play? He’s only played over 50 percent of his team’s snaps in one season in college. It’s going to be tough to get first-round value if he can only be a two-down player in the NFL.

pff_overview: Looks the part in every regard. Size, length, strength, and athleticism are all top notch. Has graded extremely well every single year of his career. Even after making the switch from right to left tackle. Had some dominant outings. Two of his four highest graded games this season came against extremely talented fronts of USC and NC State. Formed the best double team combo in the country with left guard Quenton Nelson. Moved DTs multiple yards off ball almost every time. Inconsistent with his punch in pass protection. Had his hands swatted away far too easily at times. Carries hands low in pass sets and leaves his chest open. Will be susceptible to bull rush in NFL.
pff_bottom_line: McGlinchey is as clean as any tackle prospect in this class, but there are a handful of things on his tape that still are concerning. He has a lot more de- cisive losses than you’d like from a tackle you’re taking at the top of the draft and his traits aren’t necessarily ‘elite.’ He still figures to be a high pick who can start at either tackle position from day one.

pff_overview: Ranked 14th out of 37 draft-eligible quarterbacks at avoiding turnover- worthy plays last season. Turnover-worthy plays contain far too many instances where Jackson mis-read or didn’t see underneath linebackers. Posted the No. 3 grade in the draft class when facing pressure. Had the 9th-highest grade in the draft class on intermediate (10-19-yard) throws last season. Good zip to make tight-window throws and solid touch to get the ball down the field. Accuracy is not great. Misses too many throws and ball location needs work on a throw-for-throw basis. Had 12th-highest percentage of negatively graded plays last season. Dynamic athlete. Rushed for 4,790 yards on 556 carries (8.7 yards/ attempt) during his three-year career.
pff_bottom_line: While he’s not the cleanest passer in the class, Jackson has showed enough with his arm that he can make plays at the next level, and when paired with his incredible athleticism, there’s an offense to be built around Jackson’s game. He’ll miss his fair share of throws, but he can make up for it with enough arm to make special throws downfield. It may take a creative offensive mind, but Jackson can be an exceptional option in the designed run game while opening up bigger pass windows to ease the burden of his inconsistent accuracy.

pff_overview: Excellent speed makes him a big-play threat. Accelerates off the line and gets to second gear very quickly. Attacks off-corners in a hurry, allowing him to get on top of them for deep routes or open up the underneath route tree. Explosive route-runner who maintains his speed in and out of breaks. Dropped 23 out of 247 catchable passes in his three years at Alabama. Career drop rate of 9.3% would have ranked 193rd in the nation in 2017. Production limited in run-first Alabama scheme. Averaged 45.1 yards per catch on deep passes, sixth-best among draft- eligible receivers. Took a step back in the screen game last year, gaining only 40 yards on 10 receptions, after tying for third in the nation with 3 TDs on screens in ‘16. Age will always be a question. At 23 years old, is he just a man among boys in college football?
pff_bottom_line: Few receivers possess the downfield speed and route running that Ridley displays on a weekly basis, it’s just unfortunate that we didn’t get to see it play out in a pass-heavy offense. He gets on defensive backs in a hurry and his crisp route-running makes him a threat in the short and intermediate game. Ridley is a potential deep threat on the outside who must be accounted for by oppos- ing defenses, and outside of the age question mark and a high percentage of drops, he looks like one of the top receivers in the draft.

pff_overview: As with most defensive linemen from Alabama, very technically sound as a run defender and pass-rusher already. High swipe is his go-to pass-rushing move. Likes to hands fight with opposing offensive linemen. Tackle radius is fantastic – especially if teams see him as a nose tackle. Can make plays up and down the line of scrimmage. Heavy hands. When he wins, it’s usually on first contact where he can control the interaction from the jump. Rarely wow’d as a pass-rusher. Not a ton of clean, quick, dominant wins. Motor is nothing special. Struggled to chase down quarterbacks when moved off their spot. Blew up the national championship game, where he was the highest graded player.
pff_bottom_line: Payne is an NFL ready defensive tackle whose versatility will push him up draft boards. He is comfortable performing in any alignment imaginable between the tackles without his performance declining. At the same time though, he never truly dominated until the Georgia game. He’s not near the pass-rusher that Jonathan Allen was a season ago, but his game should still translate quick- ly to the league.

pff_overview: Allowed a passer rating of just 36.5 when targeted this season from 91 passes, the 5th-best mark in the class and best with that volume of targets. Allowed 40 receptions from 91 targets (44.0 percent), surrendering only 432 yards from the 2nd-highest target volume in the draft class. Surrendered four touchdowns on the season, but had eight interceptions and 18 pass breakups. Improved his overall grade significantly each of the past two seasons and his 96.2 overall grade is the best grade of the class. Was a ballhawk in 2017, contested plenty of receptions he didn’t pick off. Got his hands on a lot of passes. Only 17 corners in the draft class surrendered more than the four touchdowns Jackson gave up this season. Only moved to cornerback in 2015, so is extremely young at the position
pff_bottom_line: Josh Jackson’s grade in 2017 was off the charts, leading all corners not just this season, but it’s the highest grade we’ve seen from any corner in this draft class in any year of their college careers. Jackson was a wide receiver in high school and only moved to corner in 2015, playing just 297 snaps over the first two seasons of his career as depth on the Iowa bench. In 2017 he started and had a huge season, picking off eight passes and breaking up another 18. Sample size is an issue, but the potential is huge.

pff_overview: Graded well in 2017, but all too much of that grade came as a pass-rusher on the blitz where he often added to the rush rather than covered. Has outstanding speed, athleticism, agility and size. Will likely be among the best testers pre-draft when it comes to measurables. Is able to live with matchup weapons on offense as well as chase down athletic quarterbacks trying to escape the rush. Didn’t have an interception in 2017, but had two pass breakups and allowed only one touchdown. Has been excellent against the run for two straight seasons, but has yet to stand out in coverage consistently – the area of most NFL importance. Has exceptional athletic talent and is still low on experience, with just 1,126 total snaps on defense in his college career, 644 of which came this year.
pff_bottom_line: There are few – if any – linebackers in this draft class that will be able to match Rashaan Evans’ athletic and measurable profile before the draft, and he has as high a ceiling as any linebacker in the draft. He is an unfinished prospect though, and needs to develop his coverage skills – the success of which will ultimately determine his NFL value. His play against the run and ability to im- pact the pass game on the blitz should mean he has an early impact regardless, and then development will determine his ceiling.

pff_overview: Took a big leap forward in 2017 in terms of performance, going from good player to excellent, grading among the best in the country. Graded well in all facets of the game, but his biggest strength was run defense. Led all FBS inside linebackers in both run-stops (57) and run-stop percentage (15.9 percent). Flows to the football on the ground, making 46 tackles in the run game for a gain of two or fewer yards, the most in the nation at any position. Can get out of position in the run game trying to run around blocks rather than take them on. Shows solid coverage awareness but without the elite athleticism to squeeze windows and tighten throwing lanes yet.
pff_bottom_line: In his first year starting, Leighton Vander Esch catapulted himself into the elite linebacker conversation after looking solid in spot duty the two years before that. He’s an instinctive linebacker who is able to work quickly to the running back in the run game and bottle up those plays. His coverage is solid, and he shows good positioning, but may not have the elite level athleticism to make special plays in that area. Should still have room to develop given relative experience. Will likely be a solid NFL player quickly.

pff_overview: Targeted on 36 percent of his routes, 3rd-most among draft-eligible WRs and was targeted 131 times, 6th-most among draft-eligible WRs. Ranked 16th among draft-eligible receivers with 2.78 yards per route. Caught only 38.5 percent of his contested targets, but still had plenty of highlight-reel, downfield catches on film. Excellent acceleration, both in his routes and with the ball in his hands. Catches the ball and flies up field, especially on screens. Averaged 7.0 yards after the catch per reception in his career. Forced 39 missed tackles on 146 career receptions. Dropped 15 passes on 161 catchable targets in his career. Did most of his damage on the outside at Maryland, but has the skillset to produce from the slot at the next level. Shows the toughness to make plays in the middle of the field.
pff_bottom_line: Moore’s speed and quickness make him a weapon as a route runner and after the catch, where he tenaciously gets up the field as soon as he catches the ball. He has the toughness to work the middle of the field, and despite inconsis- tency at the catch point, he’s willing to go up and make plays in traffic and he came down with his fair share. Moore could do damage both outside or in the slot, but taking advantage of his after-the-catch skills should be in the cards regardless of alignment.

pff_overview: Injuries limited his playing time in 2017, but when he was on the field his coverage numbers were phenomenal on very limited targets. Allowed a passer rating of just 17.7, and picked off or broke up more passes (six) than he allowed to be caught (five). The season before he had five interceptions and nine pass breakups to put himself on the map, but also surrendered six touchdowns. Most of the issues were in the red-zone. He allowed just 46.7 percent of red-zone passes to be caught in 2016, 45.3 percent over his career. May be seen as a slot corner as much as a perimeter corner, but played just 13 snaps inside in 2017, 61 the year before. Has excellent speed and athleticism, and can tick all of the movement boxes NFL teams will want to see. Can be outmuscled by bigger receivers.
pff_bottom_line: Jaire Alexander had an excellent 2016 season when it comes to playmaking, but also surrendered six touchdowns that year. His 2017 was derailed by mul- tiple injuries, which limited him to only 314 total snaps, but he came back to play extremely well over the final three games, and his coverage numbers over that period are spectacular. Has the athletic measurables teams will want, and looks to have the skills to play inside or out at the next level. Frame and injury history may give some teams pause for concern, but the ceiling is high.

pff_overview: Truly dominated the competition at UTEP. His 95.2 overall grade in 2016 is the highest single season grade we’ve ever given to a guard. Has the anchor of an aircraft carrier. Good luck bull rushing him. Allowed all of four pressures in the past two seasons combined. Not infallible in pass protection though. Struggled with speed and when defensive tackles got into his shoulder pads at the Senior Bowl. Thickly built frame from top to bottom. Fire hydrant who out-muscled every single player he went against. Iffy locating in space. When he gets a clear line of sight and can deliver a blow, it’s scary. Slow footed. Can stop his feet in pass protection and fails to recover when taken of balance.
pff_bottom_line: Hernandez is such a fun prospect to evaluate because his strengths and weak- nesses are so well defined. He’s a certified people moverr who will be a weapon on double teams from day one. Hernandez isn’t the most fleet of foot, however, and would be best suited in a gap scheme that asks him to fire off the ball.

pff_overview: First step is fantastic. Got plenty of college guards completely off balance with how quickly he got on top of them. Flexibility of a man much smaller than his listed 290-plus pounds. Can dip and rip on guards. Tweener who may ultimately be best suited playing outside the tackles rather than inside. Power in his strike is nothing special. Not the kind of defensive tackle who can stand offensive linemen up on contact. Block awareness was poor in the run game. Would get washed completely out of plays from not seeing where block was coming from. Weapon on stunts with his ability to crash the B-gap.
pff_bottom_line: Bryan has the kind of first step that GMs will fall in love with – especially in a light defensive line class. It’s concerning though that Florida let Bryan explode off the line of scrimmage consistently and he still wasn’t anything special production-wise. He’s a project in a number of ways, but his flashes suggest he could someday put it all together.

pff_overview: Size, length, and build of an NFL tackle. Good enough athlete to get out and move in the run game. Not scheme limited. Plays high and isn’t strong enough to make up for it. Can get rocked into the backfield. Very wide feet in pass protection. Feet can stop on contact and he struggles to recover. Solid hand usage in the running game. Consistent with his placement. Good awareness of stunts and blitzes in pass protection.
pff_bottom_line: Miller looks the part of an NFL tackle, but his strength and athleticism don’t get evaluators particularly excited. He took a big step forward this past season and was one of the most effective pass protectors in college football. He’ll need to add a good deal of strength to be a plus pass protector at the NFL level.

pff_overview: A powerful runner, Guice broke 36 tackles on the ground on 216 carries in 2017. Averaged 4.1 yards per carry after contact in both 2015 and 2016, but was almost a full yard lower in 2017 (3.2). Was thrown at a total of 40 times over the past three seasons, caught 31 passes and dropped three of the incompletions. Had 12 runs of 15 or more yards in 2017, giving him a breakaway percentage of just 29.4, almost 20 points lower than the class leaders. Finished with an overall grade of 85.0 or higher in each of the past two seasons. Shows good patience, ability to cut and accelerate into holes at the line of scrimmage and generate yards at the second level. Has prototypical size and measurables, and has graded well in limited use as a receiver. Seen as one of the top backs in this class.
pff_bottom_line: Derrius Guice is the latest back to come out of LSU, following in the footsteps of Leonard Fournette a season ago. Guice has prototypical size, speed and measurables and has been very productive over his college career. He ticks all of the boxes in terms of his patience and vision to hit the right hole but can occasionally fail to wow with his big play ability. He wasn’t a huge part of the passing game at LSU but graded well on those snaps when he was used and should have the ability to expand that at the NFL level.

pff_overview: Undersized tackle who likely profiles to the interior in the NFL. Still got the job done in pass protection despite his height. Only allowed five pressures all season long and 26 in 2,609 snaps for his career. Dominated the week at the Senior Bowl. Was highest graded player in 1-on-1s and he only lost two reps. Extremely consistent. Plays under control snap after snap. Very polished already. Could step in and start from day one. Plays with solid natural leverage. May not be the strongest, but still generates movement.
pff_bottom_line: Wynn is one of the most talented offensive line prospects in this draft. He’ll have to make the transition from tackle to guard or center, but the track record of players successfully making that switch is so vast that it’s not even a point of concern. He’s an incredibly clean prospect otherwise and should be taken highly as a result.

pff_overview: Gets in and out of breaks better than most receivers his size. Could still improve his route-running at the top of his breaks. Has enough quicks to get off press. Solid straight-line playing speed. Uses his body well in contested situations. Big catch radius, though he could have done a better job on a few off-target throws in 2017. Forced 26 missed tackles on 143 catches over the last two seasons. Red-zone and back-shoulder weapon at the next level. Caught 574 yards on deep (20-plus yard) passes in 2016, 13th-best in the nation. Deep pass catch percentage dropped from 45.7 percent in 2016 to 33.3 percent last season.
pff_bottom_line: While Sutton’s size is the first thing that comes to mind, he moves well for a bigger receiver and he can be more than just a red-zone weapon. His downfield production took a step back last season, but he’s shown he’s capable of using his body to win down the field and his large catch radius gives quarterbacks a bigger margin for error. Sutton has the size and body control to excel as a possession receiver, but he’ll surprise with his work after the catch and more consistent work down the field could make him one of the better all-around receivers in the class.

pff_overview: Elite athlete for tackle position. Can execute any block asked of him. Has been a dominant college tackle from the first day he stepped on the field. Allowed all of four hurries his sophomore season in 2016. Took a bit of a step back in 2017 and played only 332 snaps through injuries. Very few true pass sets in Texas’ offense. Still a work in progress in that regard. Well-proportioned for his size. Carries 300-plus pounds with ease. Strong frame throughout. Hand placement in the run game is fantastic. Gets hands inside play after play. Doesn’t get enough depth consistently in his pass sets.
pff_bottom_line: Williams has multiple seasons of production as one of the top tackles in college football. If he would have been able to come out in the draft a season ago, he’d likely go higher than he will now after disappointing this past season. Still, Williams has high-level traits and grading that make him a day one pros- pect.

pff_overview: Very productive center. Hails from an Iowa offense whose concepts closely mirror that of NFL offenses. Consistently under control. Patient almost to a fault at times. Great feel for zone blocking scheme. Not much of a people mover. Taken into the backfield more than you’d like to see from a college center. Play strength overall can be issue, as he struggled with bull rush at times. Locating linebackers was an adventure for him at times. Once he gets moving in space, he really struggled to change directions. Biggest pass pro issue was recovering to the looper on stunts. Feet and reaction time both slow. Allowed 10 pressures this past season.
pff_bottom_line: Iowa head coach Kirk Ferentz called Daniels the most NFL ready center he’s ever coached. That’s high praise with the linemen Iowa has put out and the grades back it up. He’s been one of college football’s best centers each of the past two seasons. Daniels is far from a perfect prospect, but he’s close enough to step in and contribute on an NFL field next season.

pff_overview: Allowed an NFL passer rating of just 35.5 when targeted in 2017, surrendered only 273 yards in coverage all season. Did not allow a single touchdown in coverage all year, and had four interceptions and eight pass breakups. Was not beaten for a pass longer than 21 yards all season. Has just 1,049 snaps of playing time, 884 of which came this past season. Is under 6-foot tall but shows good strength and does not look like a player that will need to move inside to the slot. Played just 23 snaps in the slot in 2017, with 737 of his snaps at left cornerback. Looks to have blazing speed, which will help mitigate some of his relative lack of size, has helped him add value as a return man. Averaged 31.9 yards per kick return and 16.6 per punt return, scoring three times overall and grading well.
pff_bottom_line: Mike Hughes is an exceptionally talented corner who hits the NFL after one elite season at UCF. He played in 2015 for North Carolina before being suspend- ed for violating team rules. He attended community college in 2016 before transferring to UCF and starring at left corner. His grade was excellent and coverage numbers fantastic, but his play is still a little raw and there may be more development to come. Will have value early as a return man in the NFL, but may take a season or two to fulfil his potential as a perimeter corner.

pff_overview: Incredibly explosive off the ball. When he fires off as pass-rusher there’s a noticeable difference between him and others in this class. Almost always wins leverage battle. Plays very low even for an undersized DT. Led all DT/NTs with 49 total pressures. Superb motor. Always fighting even when initially stoned as pass-rusher. Will chase from backside of runs and screens. Small strike zone for opposing offensive linemen. Can rarely get him locked up cleanly Holding up to double teams difficult at his size. Played 237 snaps at NT in 2017, but almost has to be 3-tech only in NFL. Awareness can be an issue. Will attack blocks head down and lose ball carriers Balance is iffy at times. Has some ugly reps when he gets off balance and can get swallowed by Offensive linemen.
pff_bottom_line: Hurst is the cream of this defensive tackle crop. There isn’t another interior player that can come close to his production as a pass-rusher in college and everything on tape suggests it will translate to the NFL. His size will give teams pause, but at no point in his college career was it ever a serious issue against the run – he still ranked 14th nationally in run-stop percentage. Hurst is a con- sistently dominant force whose only real question marks have little to do with his on-field performance.

pff_overview: Did not drop a pass on 43 catchable passes last season. Only dropped three of 103 catchable targets in his career. Good catch radius and body control. Went 7-for-11 on contested targets (63.6 percent). Has the speed to stretch the seam and the quicks to make defenders miss after the catch. Forced 14 missed tackles on 100 receptions in his career. Averaged 7.0 YAC/reception in his three years. Shows toughness running after the catch. Not afraid of contact. Run blocking is still a work in progress. Misses his target far too often when on the move in the run game. Can fly to the second level in the run game and has a few highlight-reel blocks to his name.
pff_bottom_line: Putting his age aside, Hurst’s athleticism stood out on tape, as he has the speed to work the middle of the field and the quickness and toughness to make plays in the short game. He has potential to create mismatches in the slot or out wide, and he has plenty of experience in a ‘move’ tight end role in South Carolina’s offense. He still has plenty of work to do in the run game, but he’s serviceable in more of an H-back role. Hurst is right up there with the top pass-catchers in this draft.

pff_overview: Consistently dominant on-field performance when healthy over the last two seasons. PFF’s highest graded center in 2016 & 2017. Some of the best hands of any offensive linemen in this class. Placement and strength are both consistently elite. Not going to be mistaken for Jason Kelce anytime soon, but is more than a capable athlete to play in any offensive scheme. Great feel for timing on combo blocks. Sprung a ton of big runs by climbing to pick off a linebacker at exact right time. Allowed all of 15 total pressures over the past two seasons. Feet can be slow to recover and could struggle with quicker linebackers and nose tackles at next level. Thing of beauty watching him fire off the ball 1-on-1 into a nose tackle. Play strength is top notch.
pff_bottom_line: Ragnow checks almost all the boxes one could want from a center other than his health (senior year ended with high-ankle injury). He’s a three-year starter with dominant tape that has experience at both guard (2015) and center (2016 and 2017). The Arkansas center has also done it against top competition in the SEC and never once looked overmatched.

pff_overview: Forced 12 missed tackles after the catch, tied for the first in the nation. Averaged 8.2 yards after the catch per reception. Mismatch weapon in the passing game and South Dakota State got him the ball in a variety of ways. Has the speed to be a vertical threat and the quickness to get off press and win on short routes. Body control allows him to make spectacular catches. Dropped five passes on 76 catchable targets last season. Had 206 run-blocking snaps from a traditional tight end position last season. Not powerful at the point of attack in the run game. Gets to the second level and can locate targets both from tight end or slot alignment.
pff_bottom_line: Goedert should challenge to be the top tight end off the board as he has a fantastic combination of size and athleticism. He moves like a wide receiver despite weighing 260 pounds and he’ll be able to create mismatches at the next level from all over the formation. Goedert looked like a serviceable run-block- er at the FCS level, though he rarely had an opportunity to take on NFL-caliber defensive ends. He’ll make his mark as in the pass game in the NFL, and his size and body control should make him a premier red-zone weapon.

pff_overview: Posted three straight years with 90.0-plus overall grades Excellent feel, accuracy and timing when throwing outside the numbers. Had the 2nd-highest percentage of positively graded throws in the draft class last season. Posted the highest grade in the draft class on third down and ranked second with a passer rating of 112.2. Posted the No. 2 grade in the nation both from a clean pocket and when pressured. Ranked 5th in the draft class with an adjusted completion percentage of 67.6 percent on intermediate throws. Velocity comes and goes. Will zip some passes while others don’t come out of his hands cleanly. Was a productive deep-ball thrower at Oklahoma State, and had his fair share of highlight-reel throws, but also left too many on the short side. Ranked 16th in the draft class at avoiding turnover-worthy plays.
pff_bottom_line: Rudolph did a fantastic job running Oklahoma State’s offense, but there are plenty of question marks given his NFL-caliber receivers and opposing Big 12 defenses. However, he’s showed the ability to zip the ball outside the numbers while continuing to improve his work in the middle of the field. He could stand to throw a cleaner ball on a down-to-down basis, but Rudolph’s on-field production is too difficult to ignore and he should be in the first-round mix.

pff_overview: A tall corner who has the kind of physical dimensions that NFL teams are looking for, Oliver has impressive radius to challenge for the ball. Allowed just 43.6 percent of passes thrown his way to be caught after allowing just 43.1 percent the season before. Has just three interceptions over the past two seasons, but has 17 pass breakups to go along with those picks. Can struggle to control his larger frame and gets out of control when at full speed – leads to being shaken at times by shiftier receivers. Has allowed catches longer than 40 yards in every season of his college career, including one of 52 yards in 2017. Isn’t assertive as a run defender, choosing too often to just occupy the right space rather than attacking to finish the play. Follows in the footsteps of former teammate Ahkello Witherspoon, who had similar style and skills and flashed ability as a rookie for the 49ers.
pff_bottom_line: Isaiah Oliver has the body type that NFL teams covet in 2017, with the size, speed and length to be able to play man coverage on the outside and challenge for any deep ball. That body type does cause him problems at times when throttling down and changing directions at speed, but his talent is evident. Will remind many of his former teammate Ahkello Witherspoon, who was drafted a year ago in the third round and flashed plenty of ability as a rookie in San Francisco. May not be a star right away, but has huge potential.

pff_overview: Hauled in four touchdowns out of the slot, third-most among FBS tight ends. Uses his long frame to attack the ball. Good body control to adjust to off- target throws. Caught 75 percent of contested targets (9-for-12), best in the nation among tight ends. Long strides allow him to glide down the field. Inconsistent getting in and out of horizontal routes, but will flash some wiggle at the top of routes. Ranked 31st in the nation with 1.51 yards per route in 2017. Dropped 14 of 146 catchable targets in his career. Had one of the best weeks of practice among tight ends at the Senior Bowl.
pff_bottom_line: Gesicki’s length stands out as he can get up the seam and he uses his frame to make off-target and contested catches. He can be a weapon in the middle of the field, but like many of the tight ends in this class, he’ll have to be used in the right role in the run game. He struggles as an in-line blocker, but was capable enough when asked to block on the move. Gesicki is a mid-tier tight end in this class and he can work well with an aggressive quarterback willing to give him opportunities to win in tight windows.

pff_overview: Has played all three interior positions at some point in his career at Ohio State. LG as freshman/sophomore. RG as junior. C as senior. Nastiness that offensive line coaches love. Is out for blood on every snap. Very active hands. Even when he doesn’t get initial placement perfect, he’s quick to reset and regain control. Overextends in pass protection for his punch. Lots of quick losses in pass protection as a result. Speed gives him problems. Aggressiveness gets him in trouble in run game as well. Always looking for the kill shot. Power is superb for the position. Can line up a target and take them yards downfield.
pff_bottom_line: Price is the rare four-year starter at a major college program and that itself is enough to get evaluators attention. He’s far from a perfect prospect, though, as he’s had inconsistencies on tape still this past season that you’d have hoped would be cleaned up by now. He alternates ugly blocks with dominant ones that NFL coaches will think they can harness every snap.

pff_overview: Averaged 2.51 yards per route from the slot, 7th-best in the draft class. Dropped 18 of 251 catchable targets in his career. Forced 35 missed tackles on 233 career catches. Good straight-line speed. Works hard to get on top of defensive backs on vertical routes and it creates big-play opportunities. Creates big plays more with speed than quicks. Accelerates out of his routes allowing him to separate at the top of the stem. Adds punt return value with six career returns for touchdowns. Lined up on the outside on 21 times in 2017 Can be used in jet sweep game
pff_bottom_line: Kirk may not be as good as some of the hype, but he’s an explosive playmaker with an excellent combination of speed and quickness. He’s does most of his damage with his straight-line speed and he can stretch the field from the slot in a vertical offense. He adds special teams value as well as the ability to make plays on gadget plays. Kirk is yet another playmaking slot receiver in this draft class.

pff_overview: Part of a backfield partnership with Nick Chubb throughout his career, Michel has only 592 carries across four seasons. Has averaged 3.3 yards per carry after contact in his college career, and broke 127 tackles on those 592 carries. Hasn’t featured much in the passing game, with just 80 targets sent his way over four seasons, caught 63 of them (78.8). Gained 3.8 yards per carry after contact in 2017, best average of his career. Broke 36 tackles from 157 carries. Has good speed and burst and the ability to cut and change angles quickly, but is more of a straight-line runner than nifty in space. Had 16 runs of 15-plus yards in 2017, gaining 903 yards on those big plays for a breakaway percentage of 52.2. Allowed just two hurries on 52 pass-blocking snaps in 2017 and gave up just one sack in his college career.
pff_bottom_line: Sony Michel is an impressive physical specimen with a big body and good straight-line speed. He shows quick cuts and the ability to get up field in a hur- ry, turning modest holes into big gains. He is ideally suited to a zone blocking offense, whether that be inside or outside zone, but doesn’t have the same short-area quickness and moves of some other backs. Was a bigger factor in the passing game than teammate Nick Chubb, and graded well in that facet over his career. Has relatively few miles on the clock given college workload.

pff_overview: High points the ball in the air. Went up and snagged interceptions when given the opportunity. Uses size and length well at the catch point. Played challenging role at Stanford, playing man coverage against difficult slot receivers. Stays in-phase when covering down the field, but struggles on underneath routes against shiftier slot receivers. Attacks and defeats screen blocks. Plays with good leverage in the short pass game. Has too many plays where he’s late to react to route combinations when in zone coverage. Too many ugly downfield plays and catch-point mishaps. Physical player in the run game. Will attack blockers and finish plays with authority.
pff_bottom_line: While the flash plays will keep teams intrigued, Reid has a few areas to clean up in his game. His athleticism shows up on the field, from pure movement skills to high-pointing interceptions, but he’ll also get lost down the field and give up too many big plays against the run. Reid played a challenging role cov- ering slot receivers, something he should likely only do on occasion at the next level. He has the skills to play in the box or on the back end, but must clean up some of the big plays he surrendered in college.

pff_overview: Struggles with shifty slots and horizontal routes in man coverage. Good size and physicality to cover tight ends and bigger receivers. Has some ugly plays in the open field at free safety. Will miss tackles in the open field. Has 22 missed tackles on 166 career attempts. Times blitzes extremely well. Excellent feel for zone coverage. Played all over the field at Alabama. Has potential as a dime linebacker at next level. Reads and breaks quickly on screens. Plays under control in the run game and finishes with power. Run-stop percentage of 6.7 when lined up in the box ranked 10th in the draft class.
pff_bottom_line: Harrison does his best work closer to the line of scrimmage, where he can cov- er bigger receivers and finish plays against the run. He has an excellent feel for the game, from understanding zone coverage to timing blitzes, though he has his limitations when playing deep safety. Harrison can fill multiple roles for a defense and a coordinator playing to his strengths should get a very productive player.

pff_overview: As large a human being as you’ll see on a football field. Brown engulfs smaller edge defenders. Impressive length that he knows how to use to his advantage. Makes defenders run a long loop to the quarterback. Strength that you can’t teach. Almost never ceded ground to a bull rush and wasn’t getting taken into the backfield on runs. Slow footed. Simply can’t mirror at a high-level because of his weight. Looks like he’s running in mud on pulls. Inconsistent with technique from snap to snap. Possibly scheme limited with his movement ability. Not a guy you want playing in space too often.
pff_bottom_line: Brown’s highest levels makes you think he’s a future All-Pro, but his lowest ones give you pause about him matching up with NFL-caliber athletes. In the right scheme though, it will be easy to fall in love with Brown and his sheer physical prowess. You hope he can lean out in an NFL training facility and get some quickness back in his game.

pff_overview: Highest graded back in the nation, not just the draft class, in 2017, with a rushing grade of 93.1 and an overall grade of 92.4. No kind of factor in the passing game at USC. Saw just 14 targets in 2017, catching 13 of them, dropping the 14th. Saw just 40 targets over past three seasons, 18 fewer than Saquon Barkley saw in 2017 alone. Against Power 5 conference opponents, he had the 18 rushes of 15-plus yards (T-5th among all FBS RBs). Averaged 3.5 yards per carry after contact in 2017, gained 743 yards after being first hit, broke 50 tackles on 212 carries. Extremely reliable, he hits the right hole and takes what’s there the vast majority of the time. Has been a spectacular runner, but receiving is a question mark after barely featuring in the passing game at USC.
pff_bottom_line: Ronald Jones has been a phenomenal ball carrier throughout his college career. He displays excellent vision, speed, moves and reliability – maximizing the available yardage on every play. His ability to play in the passing game is more of an unknown, as he saw very few targets, but he did perform solidly as a pass protector and caught the ball well when it did come his way. Was the highest graded running back not just of the draft class but in the nation in 2017. Should make an immediate impact in the NFL.

pff_overview: Has played extensively over the past two seasons, but took a huge leap forward in 2017, improving his grade each of the past two years. Allowed a passer rating of 80.1 in 2017, thanks largely to snagging just one interception, giving him just four in the past three years. Stands 5-foot-11 but is listed at just 175 pounds, and that lack of bulk shows up at times if players get their hands on him. Has played in the slot, with 270 snaps inside in 2017, which need to be his alignment in the NFL. Moves exceptionally well whether outside or in the slot and can change direction in an instant, and has elite straight-line speed. Doesn’t have an exceptional feel for zone and understanding how to adjust his positioning. May be best suited to a man-coverage scheme.
pff_bottom_line: Donte Jackson has one of the most exciting athletic profiles in the draft, with elite speed and short area quickness. He is a slight build, but stands 5-foot-11 and could potentially play either outside or in the slot, giving NFL defenses the option of having him as a second or third corner early and kicking him inside to the slot in nickel packages. Hasn’t made as many plays on the ball as his athleticism should have dictated, but his potential is intriguing and he could become an excellent man cover corner at the next level.

pff_overview: Primarily a nose tackle at Stanford (455 snaps last season), but unlikely to hold up there in the NFL. Very disciplined against the run. Often played head up nose tackle and did well to keep his two-way go versus the center. Much more developed as a run defender than pass-rusher at this point. Didn’t have an above average pass-rushing grade until this season. That being said, was asked to be a run first player much of the time in Stanford’s scheme. Fantastic awareness in the run game. Eyes always tracking running back. Led all defensive tackles this past season with 46 run-stops. Nothing special athletically. Wins almost exclusively with strength and technique. Showed the ability to take over games against Oregon State and USC, with two of the highest graded games this season.
pff_bottom_line: Phillips doesn’t have the sort of raw, physical traits that turns heads, but he does have an impressive track record of performance that’s seen him improve every single year of his career. In a defensive line class lacking high-end talent, Phillips could move up boards because of how capable he is of contributing right away as a run defender.

pff_overview: Big, tall CB who also elevates and challenges at the catch point extremely well. If he’s in the vicinity, will make offenses work for the catch. Allowed just 49.1 percent of passes thrown his way to be caught in 2017, gave up just 361 receiving yards all year. Surrendered a passer rating of 76.1 thanks largely to picking off just one pass all season. He did have six pass breakups to go along with that pick, giving him 20 over the past three seasons. Had eight games in 2017 in which he allowed fewer than 20 receiving yards, including six of fewer than ten. Struggled down the stretch, with multiple bad games to the season, including the SEC Championship against Georgia. Missed just two tackles in 2017, missed 12 the year before.
pff_bottom_line: A tall, long corner with excellent size and physicality, Carlton Davis is what NFL teams are looking for right now. He has impressive strength to get disrupt receivers in press coverage and ride them down field, and has translated that into strong play in the run game. He challenges at the catch point very well, making receptions hard work, but doesn’t pick many passes off. Had six pen- alties in 2017, and all were pass interference. Needs to dial back the contact at the next level, and can struggle in off-coverage.

pff_overview: Maintains speed in and out of breaks. Allows him to get on cornerbacks quickly and run away from them at the top of the route. Ranked eighth in the nation with 3.25 yards per route against Power-5. Led the nation with 815 yards on deep passes in 2017 and ranked second with eight touchdowns on deep passes. Caught all 10 of his slant targets for 192 yards and three touchdowns. Ranked fourth in the nation with 343 yards in contested situations and tied for third with three touchdowns. Top receiver during Senior Bowl practice week. Dominated both the 1-on-1s, particularly against press coverage, and the team drills. Other than posts and slants, did most of his work outside the numbers. Can he be a middle-of-the-field option? Production certainly padded in Big 12, where he was given plenty of 1-on- 1 situations with room to work. Has continued to improve his ability to win at the catch point.
pff_bottom_line: Washington has been one of the nation’s most efficient deep receivers over the last three years as he showed the ability to run away from cornerbacks and he’s continued to improve his game in contested situations. His speed plays well on the field, especially his ability to maintain it in and out of his cuts, and he answered questions about facing press coverage with a dominant Senior Bowl. Washington should be in the mix to be one of the top WRs off the board.

pff_overview: Three straight years of excellent production at Memphis. Ranked 15th in the nation in yards per route in 2016 (3.22) and ranked ninth in 2017 (3.47). Has the speed to run by defenders when given a free release. Has the quickness and route-running ability to win from the slot. Ranked sixth in yards per route from the slot at 3.43. Nifty after the catch. Forced 19 missed tackles on 96 catches last season and forced an impressive 18 misses on only 47 catches in 2015. Averaged 6.9 yards after the catch per reception in his three years. Led the nation with 288 yards on screen passes. Showed impressive skills on contested targets and tied for the national lead with six touchdowns in such situations. Drops have been an issue as he has 21 on his 212 catchable targets the past two years.
pff_bottom_line: Miller is one of the few receivers in the class capable of winning both on the outside and in the slot. He has excellent quickness and route-running ability, allowing him to get open and make defenders miss after the catch, but he’s also capable of making tight-window, highlight-reel catches. Much like Sterling Shepard of the New York Giants, Miller may find most of his NFL production in the slot, but he his speed and quickness could also be a weapon on the outside.

pff_overview: Missed 22 of 197 career tackle attempts, 16 of which came in 2017. Some ugly plays on tape, particularly in the open field. Good feel for quarters coverage. Can hang with receivers down the field and closes with authority on underneath routes. Made a few top-notch plays on the ball from quarters looks. Attacks downhill in the run game. Sifts through the trash to fill his gap. Good physicality in the run game. Not afraid to take on blocks. Generally has a good feel for crack blocks in the run game. Few opportunities to play true single-high safety and likely fits best in two-high safety looks.
pff_bottom_line: While most safeties have trouble sticking with receivers when isolated in 1-on- 1s, Bates had some of his best plays in those challenging situations, making him a good fit for a quarters-heavy scheme. He’s aggressive and physical in the run game, though he must cut down on the missed tackles and the big plays that he allowed in 2017. Bates has the size and movement skills to develop into a solid player in a two-high system.

pff_overview: Back to his best in 2017 after injury had threatened to derail his career, Chubb averaged 3.8 yards per carry after contact, his best college mark. 2017 was the first season of his career in which he didn’t fumble the ball. 0 fumbles from 227 touches from scrimmage. Was thrown the ball just 37 times in the past four seasons, 20 of which came in 2014. Caught only 13 passes over the past three years. Had an elusive rating of 95.2, the fourth-best mark in the draft class. Broke 44 tackles from 178 carries and one tackle on two receptions. Had 18 runs of 15-plus yards in 2017. Has been touted as a top running back prospect for years, but injury threatened to torpedo his value. 2017 was an important big bounce-back season. Never played more than 50 percent of Georgia’s snaps on offense and his largest single-season workload was 237 touches in 2014.
pff_bottom_line: A top high school recruit (top-50 overall), Nick Chubb was dominant as a fresh- man before a major knee injury ended his sophomore season and threatened to derail his career. He was clearly not the same player in 2016 so this past season was an important bounce-back year, showing the NFL that he hadn’t PASS BLOCK EFFICIENCY lost the ability to dominate on the ground. Has solid power, cutting ability and speed and despite the injury was never overloaded with work in college. Chubb % NOT TACKLED ON seems to have fallen out of favor with many, but could be a steal in this class.

pff_overview: Four-year starter at left tackle for Nevada. Only allowed 23 total pressures on his last two seasons. Keeps hands tight in both the run game and in pass protection – regularly hitting his strike zone. Can get antsy trying to deliver a deadening punch in pass pro. That aggressiveness can be used against him at times. Plays to the whistle. Often times saw him carrying linebackers offscreen that didn’t want any part of him. Gets good depth out of his pass sets and cuts down angles quickly on edge rushers. Active with his hands. Has the size and athleticism to play multiple positions along the offensive line.
pff_bottom_line: Corbett is a touch undersized for an NFL tackle, but has all the traits neces- sary to hold up there. He’s far more technically sound than most small school offensive linemen and even with the huge jump in competition he could start sooner rather than later.

pff_overview: Multiple seasons of elite grades at both right and left tackle. Thick, strong tackle who owns a power advantage against almost every defensive lineman he faced. Run blocks with a mean streak. When his hand placement is on point he buries defensive linemen. Feet are slow and mirroring ability suffers as a result. Made a living off his strength and ability to snatch defenders in pass pro. Rarely took true pass sets at Oregon. Keeps hands wide and gets grabby when he did. At his best when he can play straight ahead. Could be scheme limited in the NFL. Not great in space.
pff_bottom_line: Crosby isn’t going to win any beauty contests with his play style, but he got the job done at a high level at Oregon. It’s encouraging that he showed well in pass protection 1-on-1s at the Senior Bowl, with a 67 percent win rate, considering his pass sets at Oregon were underdeveloped. His quickness could even see teams value him as a guard at the next level.

pff_overview: Forced 80 missed tackles on the ground last season, No. 1 in the draft class. Had the 3rd-most rushes of 15-plus yds (30), and 2nd-most yards gained on those rushes (1135) among all FBS RBs. Has the ability to take it to the house in an instant. Ranked 7th among all FBS RBs with a 55.8 breakaway percentage. Caught 18-of-24 passes thrown his way in 2017, but dropped only one of the incompletions. Struggled to pass protect in 2017, allowed two sacks and seven additional hurries on 66 pass-blocking snaps. Was little better the year before. Dominated at the Senior Bowl with 64 yards on nine carries and a 73- yard receiving touchdown in the game. Was solid in practices. Competition in college will be a factor in his evaluation, but stepped it up at the Senior Bowl and has tape that wows.
pff_bottom_line: Rashaad Penny is a powerful back who also has the quickness and speed to make big plays from anywhere on the field. He broke 80 tackles on the ground from his 276 carries, gaining more than 1,200 rushing yards after contact. Pen- ny shows excellent vision, balance and burst when carrying the football, but his work in the passing game is more of a projection. He has struggled in pass protection and hasn’t been extensively used as a receiver, so he may be limited to running downs early in his NFL career.

pff_overview: Speed. Ran 4.34 at the NFL Combine and it shows up on the field. Second gear allows him to separate down the field. Ranked 6th in the nation with 572 yards on deep passes in 2017. Caught six deep passes for 237 yards in 2016. Shows good ball skills at the catch point and caught 67 percent of his contested catches, 2nd-best in the nation among wide receivers. Only dropped five out of 76 catchable passes in his career. Adjusts well to off-target throws. Can be a big-play weapon when running the vertical route tree. Struggles to use leverage to set up cornerbacks. Only forced three missed tackles on 71 career receptions. Struggled in 1-on-1s during Senior Bowl practice.
pff_bottom_line: While Chark’s speed makes him a legit deep threat, it’s his length and ball skills make him a downfield weapon even if it’s not based on speed alone. He’s not the most polished route runner and he may never be a high-volume op- tion, but he adds an outside vertical presence as one of the best deep receivers in the draft.

pff_overview: Excellent athlete, both before and after the catch. Good quickness for his size, allows him to separate and make defenders miss in space. Did a much better job of adjusting to off-target throws this season. Little experience as an in-line blocker and it shows with some ugly reps on tape. Can be used as a mismatch weapon all over the offense, either outside, in the slot, or in an H-back role. Ranked 5th among FBS tight ends with 2.63 yards per route. Led all FBS tight ends with 10 deep receptions and 318 deep receiving yards. Ran 81.4 percent of his routes from the slot, 3rd-highest among tight ends.
pff_bottom_line: Andrews was essentially a slot receiver at Oklahoma and he can fill multiple roles at the next level due to his athleticism and ball skills. Like most receiving tight ends in the class, he has work to do in the run game, but he’s capable of lining up in the slot, out wide, or in an H-back role and creating mismatches for opposing defenses. Usage will be key, as Andrews works to improve as an in-line blocker, but he has the receiving skills to make an immediate impact.

pff_overview: Plays angry. Feet never stop churning and plays consistently to the whistle. Has a constant forward lean. Gets off-balance on contact too often because of it. Has a hitch in his giddy-up when coming out of his stance on pulls. Looks unnatural in space. Choppy with his feet and slower to locate than you’d like. Strong as an ox. Regularly moves the line of scrimmage even on 1-on-1 blocks. Late reacting in pass pro on blitzes and stunts.
pff_bottom_line: Smith is a home run hitter type of guard who will alternate dominant reps with whiffs. You can’t teach his strength though, and he’s going to be drafted highly because of it. He’s far from a perfect prospect, but he’s an easy projection with how advanced he is as a run blocker already.

pff_overview: Fantastic athlete for the position. Moves about as well as any tackle in this class. Mirrors extremely well. Can get out of his stance quickly and maintain favorable relationship with edge rushers. Punch in pass pro does him no favors. Weak and easily slapped away by defenders. Was awful in Senior Bowl 1-on-1s. Only won 27 percent of his reps throughout the week. Play strength is nothing special. Not a people mover. Likely zone scheme limited. Oversets at times and is susceptible to inside counters.
pff_bottom_line: After a dominant 2016 season where he allowed all of four pressures all year, O’Neill took a step back in 2017. His Senior Bowl performance is incredibly worrisome, as he was dominated by the better competition. He’ll need to add strength to have a chance of starting early in the league.

pff_overview: Has the build and athleticism of an NFL linebacker and ticks all of the boxes from a measurables standpoint. Substantially better when he is coming forward than when he is forced to drop away from the line of scrimmage and play moving backwards. Took a big leap forward in production in 2017, both in terms of raw numbers and overall grade. Almost doubled tackles and defensive stops. Was only thrown at 24 times in coverage and just 55 times over his three- year college career. Didn’t allow a touchdown across three seasons. Missed at least ten tackles in every season of his college career, including a career-high 15 in 2017, albeit on significantly more attempts. Was previously one of the top high school recruits in the country and the best linebacker recruit. Had five sacks and 26 total pressures from 135 pass-rushing snaps in 2017. He has had five sacks in back to back seasons.
pff_bottom_line: One of the top high school recruits in the country, Malik Jefferson never quite realised that potential at Texas and only in 2017 did we begin to see why he was so sought after. He looks the part of an NFL linebacker from a size and speed standpoint, and when attacking the line of scrimmage can be a star. Things get a little more uncomfortable when he has to play in space and drop away from the line in coverage. If he is limited to a two-down role despite that athleticism he will be worth nothing more than a mid-round pick.

pff_overview: Quick setup and release. Average arm. Throws a few risky passes into tight coverage. Quick decision-maker. Excellent feel for throwing in the middle of the field. Completed 40-of-52 passes (76.9 percent) at the intermediate (10-19 yard) level in between the numbers. Had an outstanding week at the Senior Bowl. Posted the top grade among QBs in 1-on-1 drills and graded well in both team drills and the game itself. Showed off excellent red-zone accuracy during Senior Bowl practice, regularly making tight window throws, including excellent touch on fades. Must improve deep ball. Ranked only 101st in the nation in adjusted completion percentage on the deep ball at 34.9 last season.
pff_bottom_line: Lauletta vaulted toward the top of the class behind a strong week at the Senior Bowl, but it was really just confirmation of what he showed on film at Rich- mond. His middle-of-the-field feel gives him a chance to succeed, though he must improve his downfield accuracy in order to take the next step. Lauletta’s short and intermediate accuracy make him a worthwhile mid-round selection and we’ve seen quarterbacks improve their deep ball in the NFL, making him strong in the right areas for a transition to the next level.

pff_overview: Well built, strong tackle with two-years of starting experience coming off a breakout season in 2017. Only allowed 11 total pressures this past season. Adept independent hand usage in pass protection. Long arms that he knows how to use. Great depth out of his kick slide for a big man. Didn’t take a ton of true pass sets, but already looks well developed in that regard. Doesn’t play with consistent leverage. Won’t always sink hips on contact in run game instead opting to lurch into blocks. Gets off-balance easily and doesn’t always play under control.
pff_bottom_line: Jones has all the tools to play tackle at the next level, but he’s not a finished product yet. His pass sets are a thing of beauty and he should only improve with more experience in an NFL passing game. He rarely flashed dominant potential, but you don’t need to be a dominant run blocker to be a high-level tackle in today’s NFL.

pff_overview: Broke 50 tackles on 285 carries in 2017, averaged 2.9 yards per carry after contact and gained 826 yards after the first hit. Has an ability to glide as a runner to the hole and then shift gears through the gap in a way reminiscent of Arian Foster. Had 16 runs of 150-plus yards, giving him a breakaway percentage of 33.8, 23rd in the draft class. Overall grade improved dramatically each season of his career, resulting in the 87.8 we saw this past season. Struggled in Auburn’s championship game and bowl game, being held to just 118 total yards on 35 total carries by Georgia and UCF combined. Didn’t allow a sack from 89 pass-blocking snaps for a pass-blocking efficiency score of 95.8, a top-25 mark in the draft class. Runs hard and can drive forward on contact, but too often goes down on the first hit and doesn’t generate what you expect from his size.
pff_bottom_line: Kerryon Johnson has improved his grade every season and enters the draft after an impressive year in which he had the sixth-best grade in the class. He’s a tall, upright runner with good speed and the ability to make big plays, but too often hits the dirt from the first tackle attempt and can’t make moves in short PASS BLOCK EFFICIENCY spaces to avoid defenders. Has an interesting style of gliding to the hole and then accelerating quickly through it that proves very effective, and has shown % NOT TACKLED ON he can carry a big workload and be a factor on all three downs.

pff_overview: Caught 34.8 percent of his deep targets in 2017, tied for 151st in the nation. Dropped six passes on 98 catchable attempts in his career. Moves well for a big receiver. Gets in and out of his breaks well on vertical routes. Gets to top speed quickly and can get on cornerbacks in a hurry. Shows good footwork when getting off press but can improve his hand usage. Large catch radius shows up on off-target throws. Disappointing results in contested situations, especially given his size. Caught only 37.5 percent of his contested targets in 2017. Plays like more of a speed receiver despite his 6-foot-5 frame. Could stand to be more physical in all aspects on the game.
pff_bottom_line: With surprising speed and quickness for his near 6-foot-5 frame, St. Brown has the ability to win at all levels while providing a capable deep threat.
