He can stand to be more physical, tapping into his size both at the line of scrimmage and down the field, and if he improves in that area, he could develop into one of the best receivers in this draft class.

pff_overview: Dropped only three of his 64 catchable targets, good for a drop rate of 4.69 that ranked 13th in the nation in 2017. Smooth route runner. Sharp in and out of his cuts. Uses hands to separate at the top of routes. Nifty footwork to get off press coverage. Sure-handed. Dropped only seven passes on 169 catchable targets during his four-year career. Outstanding punt returner. Set NCAA career mark with nine touchdown returns for touchdowns. Athleticism doesn’t always show up down to down on the field.
pff_bottom_line: Pettis has a good feel for the game, whether getting off press, separating at the top of routes, or finding holes in zones. He adds punt return value af- ter a record-breaking career at Washington, and he fits in as a dependable, sure-handed option who can work on the outside or in the slot. He may never develop into a big-play threat down the field, but Pettis is a solid complementa- ry option to a receiving corps that has other vertical threats.

pff_overview: Powerful big man who flashes some of the most impressive reps of the entire class. Rare coordination for a man his size. Balance is a serious issue. Ends up on the ground far too often on seemingly innocuous blocks. Gets playmaking happy at times and can easily get caught out of position. A redshirt sophomore with two seasons of outstanding grading for his age. Has the size of a nose tackle, but the play style of a 3-technique. Could be best served to drop weight in NFL. Shows the ability to separate off blocks consistently and finish plays.
pff_bottom_line: Everyone wants the mythical nose tackle that can also rush the passer and Settle certainly fits that billing. As intriguing as his high-end is, his low-end is equally concerning. He’s terribly unrefined at this point and for all the hype around his athleticism, his disappointing performance at the combine sug- gests he might not have the perceived ‘upside’ some think.

pff_overview: Initial punch is completely deadening when it lands. Long arms with the strength to stop defenders in their tracks. Slow feet that struggle mirroring any sort of quickness. Allowed 18 pressures in 247 pass-blocking snaps. Allowed two sacks, a hit, and three hurries in a dreadful performance against Mississippi this season. Struggles sustaining blocks. Even when he gets initial engage, he loses control of far too many blocks. Attacks blocks high in the run game and doesn’t play with leverage as well as you’d like. Had some dominant blocks leading out in front of screens.
pff_bottom_line: Rankin improved from 2016 to 2017, but still graded out as a below-average college tackle this past season. He’s likely not athletic enough to hold up on the outside in the NFL and is ultimately better suited for guard or center. Even there he’s a project though, as his hands aren’t good enough to draft highly there.

pff_overview: Penetrating defensive end. At his best when he’s allowed to fire off into the backfield. Extremely inconsistent. Would disappear for games at a time. Four games this year without a single pressure. Highest grade, far and away the best performer in Senior Bowl 1-on-1s. Won 73 percent of his reps there. Not much of an anchor against double teams. Lower body strength leaves something to be desired. Versatility to play any alignment between the tackles. Took 84 snaps as a nose tackle last season. Hit and miss with his leverage. Doesn’t fire off particularly low at the snap and can get forklifted by offensive linemen. Creative pass-rusher who times his move well. Killed a ton of guards this year with a spin move.
pff_bottom_line: Hill will be limited by his athleticism at the next level, but can still be a push- the-pocket type of nose tackle. The problem is, he won’t be a run-stuffing nose tackle anytime soon and some teams aren’t ready to make that trade off. His performance at the Senior Bowl practices was hard to ignore and will attract teams looking for some pass-rush from the nose tackle position.

pff_overview: Looks the part from a size and length perspective. Moves like an athlete when he’s out in space. Slow out of stance and chasing from backside on zone plays. Lackadaisical punch in pass protection. Long arms, but doesn’t yet know how to use them to his advantage. Lacks a mean streak. Possesses rare physical traits, but almost never saw him impose his will on defenders. Feet get all over the place in pass protection. Gets himself in bad situations too often. Strong upper body that can toss and ragdoll defensive linemen. Three-year starter with experience at both tackle spots.
pff_bottom_line: Okorafor is nothing more than a project at this point. He’s not ready to step on an NFL field day one, but could be a few years down the line if he puts it all to- gether. Only earned an average 76.4 grade this past season against MAC com- petition. His game will need to be built from the ground up at the next level.

pff_overview: Havoc creator. McIntosh wants to disrupt every single play by fighting his way into the backfield in some way, shape, or form. Legit range in the run game. Can work his way from the backside to the front side and still finish on the ball carrier. Slightly built to translate to the NFL game. Looks more like a defensive end at this point than a 3-tech. Plays higher than you’d like against both run and pass. Form against double teams is non-existent much of the time. Plays neither blocker and can get owned. Led to him getting his butt kicked to his lowest grade all year in the bowl game against Wisconsin. High motor type player who’s will to make plays is inspiring. Not always the most technically sound pass-rusher, but fights snap after snap.
pff_bottom_line: McIntosh is an athletic 3-technique, defensive end tweener that profiles to attacking 1-gap defenses. He’s not so overtly athletic though to where you’d fall in love with him at the top of the draft. Still, McIntosh is one of the few interior players in this class who offers legitimate pass-rushing tools that will translate to the NFL.

pff_overview: Freeman’s 2015 season is tied for the best single-season overall grade any back in this draft class has on their résumé (92.4). Struggled as Oregon’s prowess on offense declined over the past couple of seasons, but was dominant in 2015. Broke 51 tackles on 243 carries in 2017, gained an average of 3.4 yards after contact and notched 823 yards after the first hit. Caught 80 of the 89 passes thrown his way over his college career, breaking 23 tackles after the catch on those 80 catches. Allowed a sack and four hurries this season in pass protection from just 49 snaps blocking. Has excellent balance and vision and usually hits the right hole at the right time, maximizing the blocking that unfolds in front of him. Doesn’t immediately play like a player of 230-plus pounds, and has a lot of miles on the clock, which will concern some teams.
pff_bottom_line: Oregon’s Royce Freeman has had spectacular play at times in college, but his best season came back in 2015, and he hasn’t looked the same since, though he was markedly better in 2017. Though a big back, he doesn’t always play like it, which is both a good and bad thing depending on the play. His college career shows he can be special in the right situation, but also that he can struggle to overcome suboptimal blocking and won’t offset a bad offensive line. Workload may be a worry for some teams, but he could easily have a big early impact.

pff_overview: A solid linebacker with three-straight seasons of impressive PFF grades, graded well in all facets of the game in 2017. Did not allow a touchdown across 55 targets this season, the largest number of targets among all linebackers in the class. Had two interceptions and seven pass breakups, the latter mark led the draft class by 3. 61 defensive stops over the season, 6th among all linebackers in the draft class. Shows some good straight-line speed, but looks a little more suspect in short area quickness and change of direction. Is inconsistent with block shedding, and doesn’t have the size or power to stack and shed at the next level. Needs to improve how he attacks blocks.
pff_bottom_line: An all-around linebacker who has graded well in all areas at Iowa, Josey Jewell has some interesting numbers and tape that will make NFL teams take a long look despite some measurables concerns. He was a solid coverage player and made a lot of plays on the ball to go along with a relentless collection of defen- sive stops. Can run with speed in a straight line, but will need to prove he can move with NFL-level quickness and deal with second-level blocks. Has three- down talent and the kind of instincts that may mitigate measurable concerns.

pff_overview: Three straight seasons of solid grading in limited snaps before taking a huge leap forward in 2017 with a full-time role for Clemson Graded well in all facets of the game and had impressive grades at the most crucial times, including the college football playoffs. Allowed two touchdown catches on 47 targets, but also had two interceptions and a pass breakup, allowed an average of just 7.8 yards per reception. Both of his interceptions in 2017 were returned for touchdowns. Missed only five tackles all year, including three in one game against Virginia Tech. Had 198 snaps on special teams, including play in all phases of special teams. Made 39 career tackles on special teams, including six this final year. Just an average athlete for his size, despite coverage ability.
pff_bottom_line: Coverage linebackers have never been more important in the NFL and that’s Dorian O’Daniel’s speciality, even if he has also graded well in other aspects of the game. He is undersized without the typical boost in speed and athleticism that usually brings, which makes his projection to the next level tough, but he has been a monster on special teams for Clemson, which will give any NFL team comfort while they work out what he can do for them to contribute on defense. NFL future may be as a matchup coverage player.

pff_overview: Graded solidly in 2017, but was dramatically better the season before for the Buckeyes, earning an overall grade of 87.7 as a sophomore. Was at his best in 2017 during the Big-10 Championship game and the team’s bowl game against USC. Allowed three touchdowns in coverage in each of his past two seasons of play, notched just two interceptions and two pass breakups over that span. Has speed to burn and can be extremely effective coming forward towards the line of scrimmage Has the skills to mirror receivers and stick with them in coverage, but needs to improve challenging at the catch point. Is significantly more lost in zone coverage, and will need to improve that at the next level to be a three-down player.
pff_bottom_line: Jerome Baker has the athletic profile of a top pick in this draft, and at least one season of play that suggested he can live up to that potential. Took a step back in 2017, which is always a concern, but has the skills to attack at speed against the run and cover backs and tight ends in man coverage. Will need to develop his game as a zone defender to avoid being a scheme-specific player in the NFL.

pff_overview: A phenomenal looking athlete, saw just 1,014 snaps in his college career after being a star high school recruit. Has been a better run defender than pass-rusher at Alabama, notching a dozen defensive stops in each of the last two years. Had back-to-back dominant games against Colorado State and Vanderbilt in 2017, imposing himself as a run defender. Was almost anonymous in the National Title game against Georgia, notched just a single hit on the quarterback from 56 snaps. Graded well during practices at the Senior Bowl, particularly on inside moves or the bullrush. A player whose draft stock is based almost entirely on potential rather than production.
pff_bottom_line: Hand was once the No. 1 overall high school recruit in the country, but since that point has played very sparingly at Alabama – never more than 43.7 percent of the possible defensive snaps – and has only flashed the elite potential he does possess. Dominated individual games but has never had an extended stretch of excellent play and has been particularly anonymous as a pass-rusher. NFL teams will likely boost him up their boards based on prototypical measurables, but he needs to find consistent play at the next level to be anything more than a rotational body.

pff_overview: Stout frame that’s difficult to out-leverage and generate movement on 1-on-1 and Nnadi knows how to play low. At the same time, Nnadi struggled to consistently move the line of scrimmage the other way in the run game. Impressive mobility for a nose tackle. Centers had a hard time reaching him from a shade. Limited pass-rushing skill-set. Registered all of 19 pressures this season and was shut out in seven different games. Struggled cleanly separating from offensive linemen in the run game. Lack of length could be an issue. Consistently productive. Only one truly poorly graded game in the past three seasons.
pff_bottom_line: Nnadi might look like a pass-rushing 3-technique, but his best position at the next level is likely nose tackle. He simply doesn’t offer enough as a pass-rusher to warrant early consideration, but it’s hard to overlook three straight seasons grading above 82.0 for us. He never quite took the next step after a strong sophomore campaign though, and even took a step backwards as a pass-rusher this year.

pff_overview: Allowed two touchdowns over the season from 68 targets, surrendering 520 receiving yards at an average of 11.5 per reception. Had two interceptions and only four additional pass breakups, yielded a passer rating of 91.5. Has impressive movement skills in off coverage for a corner of his size, and has had solid games against tough competition. Has improved his overall grade in each of the past two seasons, ending with an 84.4 overall grade in 2017. Playing time also increased in each of the past two seasons, and for his three-year college career has been on the field for 2,135 snaps. Will have to buck the recent trend of Stanford defensive backs that have struggled at the next level. Had six games in 2017 with fewer than 20 receiving yards surrendered, including the Pac-12 championship and bowl game.
pff_bottom_line: Quenton Meeks is working against a recent history of Stanford defensive backs that have struggled at the NFL level, but he does have the physical stature that teams covet. Moves well in space for a player of his size, but can struggle to be as physical as he should be. Has been solid, not spectacular in coverage over the past couple of seasons, but does give up occasional big plays and will need to rely on more potential than proven production.

pff_overview: Allowed just one touchdown on 57 targets in 2017 and three scores across the last two years of play on 121 targets. Had just one interception over the past two seasons, broke up 11 passes. Didn’t allow more than five receptions in a single game all season. Moves well and has solid athleticism, has an impressive track background, and that shows immediately on tape. Is not a big player, and needs that athleticism to match up to bigger receivers and win with movement rather than physicality. No major weaknesses to his play, but strengths are limited also, may struggle to find the traits that elevate him to the NFL level. Solid tackler, missed just four total tackles in his college career.
pff_bottom_line: Another Alabama defensive back hitting the draft this season, Anthony Averett has been solid if unspectacular for the Tide during his college playing time. He has fluid athleticism and speed, and can stick with receivers in man coverage, but struggles to play the ball and as a result has just one interception across 121 targets. Does everything pretty well but nothing to an elite level, and may struggle to translate that to a higher level of competition against bigger, stronger and faster athletes.

pff_overview: Ranked 15th in yards per route in 2017 (3.18) and second in 2016 (4.34). Gained 250 yards on screen passes in 2017, 3rd-most among FBS WRs. Faced press coverage on 64 of his targets in 2017, most among FBS WRs. Caught 30 of those 64 targets for 568 yards (8.8 yards/target). Smooth route runner and uses his hands well both against press and at the catch point. Good acceleration allows him to eat up cushion on cornerbacks. Good feel for making defenders miss in the open field and forced 38 misses on his 179 catches the last two seasons. Caught only 31.3 percent of his deep targets last season (171st in nation) after catching 38.5 percent in 2016. Dropped only 12 of 191 catchable targets over the last two seasons. Had a strong week at the Senior Bowl, grading well during team drills and in the game itself.
pff_bottom_line: In a wide receiver class that lacks true top-10 overall talent, Gallup may be the best all-around option. He has the speed to make plays down the field and his feel for route-running and making defenders miss after the catch make him a threat at the short and intermediate levels. Gallup’s two-year production is as good as it gets in the class and when combined with his physical tools, he should be one of the top wide receivers off the board.

pff_overview: Bulldozer in the run game. Had some of the most impressive blocks in the country this year. Destroyed some defenders. A little tight in the hips. Really shows up when asked to change directions. Ducks his head into blocks far more than you’d like. Can be impatient in pass pro. When he gets his hands inside a defender’s shoulder pads it’s game over. He’s not letting go. As powerful a guard as you’ll see in a compact frame. Was running with defensive tackles at times. Can get a narrow base in pass protection that causes balance issues.
pff_bottom_line: Teller has been one of the highest graded guards in the country for four straight seasons now, but it’s concerning that he took a slight step backwards as a senior instead of taking his game to the elite-level. The level of play he’s sustained throughout his career though is hard to ignore, and he’s got all the tools to succeed in the NFL.

pff_overview: Feel for developing blocks and finding the maximum space in rushing lanes is exceptional. Throws himself around with reckless abandon, scoring multiple touchdowns because he’s willing to take flight. Very powerful for his size. Averaged 3.8 yards per carry after contact in 2017, consistently worked extra yardage after the hit. Two drops in 2017 from 33 targets, and they were both concentration drops trying to run before he had caught the ball. Can cut at speed and fire through space when he sees it open up, negating some of his lack of bulk. Outstanding speed and athleticism, needs to become more dynamic and confident as a receiver to be a real impact player at the next level.
pff_bottom_line: Hines came along at exactly the right time, hot on the heels of the success of Alvin Kamara in New Orleans. He has that kind of potential but needs to become a more consistent receiver. He is a much smaller player than Kamara, but he runs hard, aggressively, and with excellent vision and feel for blocks, aspects that neutralize much of the size concerns, and he has the speed to be a home-run threat on any play. Hines runs with a reckless abandon that may expose him to injury, but it has been a major strength thus far.

pff_overview: Faced 5th-most targets against press coverage in 2017. Caught 54.8 percent. Caught only 23.5 percent of his deep targets in 2017 after catching 43.8 percent in 2016. Has big-play potential. Knows how to separate down the field to create chunk plays. Far too many drops during his three-year career. Finished with 13 drops on 140 catchable targets during his career (9.3 percent). Caught only 40 percent of his contested targets last season. Forced 26 missed tackles on 130 career catches. Not great at catching passes in traffic over the middle.
pff_bottom_line: Losing Deshaun Watson hurt Cain’s downfield production in 2017, but he has shown a second gear and the feel for creating late separation in order to be a deep threat. He still has work to do in order to cut down on his drops, but he’s also shown the ability to make spectacular, downfield catches. He does his best work on the vertical route tree and may never be a dependable middle-of-the- field option, but he can make his mark on the outside in a vertical scheme.

pff_overview: Led all FBS receivers with a deep catch rate of 73.3 percent in 2017. Gained 845 yards from the slot last season, 8th-most among FBS WRs. Attacks the ball in the air. Caught 61 percent of contested targets, 22nd- best in the nation. Savvy route runner. Varies the speed of his routes and knows how to set up defenders. Uses his hands well down the field to create late separation. Understands timing of route concepts and how to work off other WRs. Excellent week of practice of the Senior Bowl, where he ranked third among wide receivers in 1-on-1 PFF grading. Dropped 25 passes on 253 catchable passes in his career. Played 3,149 snaps in his four years at Penn State (787 per season).
pff_bottom_line: Hamilton had a productive career at Penn State, with a slight lull in his num- bers in 2015 and 2016. He’s a nuanced route-runner who developed into a big-play threat from the slot for Penn State, a role he could fill at the next level, perhaps in the mold of Atlanta Falcons wide receiver Mohamed Sanu. He may top out as a No. 3 option, but he can be productive in that role given his feel for the game and ability to make plays at the catch point.

pff_overview: A transfer from Hawaii, was one of the best graded cornerbacks in the nation in 2017. Only one season of exceptional play despite lower competition in previous years, flashed excellent games at Hawaii. Did not have an interception across three seasons of play but had 29 pass breakups over that span. Improved his completion percentage surrendered every year, down to just 37.7 in 2017. Remained occasionally susceptible to the big play, gave up at least three touchdowns every season. Plays the run with good technique and aggressiveness and can be a complete corner at the next level. Can be occasionally overpowered by big, strong receivers.
pff_bottom_line: Judging from 2017 tape alone, Nelson is one of the best corners in this draft. It’s a little concerning that his previous years weren’t as stellar, particularly against lesser competition at Hawaii, but that is his situation. He didn’t have an interception in three seasons but had 29 pass breakups and showed the abil- ity to make plays on the ball. Does get beat for a big play occasionally and may have a Malcolm Butler-type of high-variance play.

pff_overview: Had his left hand amputated as a child, so has played his entire football career without his left hand. Missed just 10 tackles across 900 snaps in 2017, and 26 over his career, fewer than some linebackers in this class did in 2017 alone. At his best as an edge rusher, where he generated pressure once every 5.8 rushes in his career, slightly better than Myles Garrett’s rate. Graded well as a pass-rusher at the Senior Bowl, but also played as an off the ball linebacker and was solid. Dominated Auburn in their bowl game, notching 10 total pressures and seven defensive stops. Had four games in 2017 with seven or more total pressures. Posted 20 bench reps at the combine using a prosthetic hand, and his 4.38 40-time was the fastest time by a linebacker in over a decade.
pff_bottom_line: Griffin is one of the best stories in the entire draft. He was born with a defect in his left SNAPS/INSIDE hand, had it amputated at the age of four, and has played his entire football career with no left hand, but he still dominates. His biggest drawback is not a missing hand, but the fact that his best trait is pass-rushing, and he has a defensive back’s body (6-foot-1, 227-pounds at the combine). He has been exceptionally productive in college and will find a way to make an impact in the NFL. His ideal role may be two-down off the ball linebacker and then situational third-down pass-rusher.

pff_overview: Efficient, quick release. Touch thrower. Arm strength is a question mark, especially outside the numbers. Will get through reads and throws efficiently in the short game. Had the 2nd-highest percentage of turnover-worthy throws on intermediate (10-19-yards) attempts. Ranked 33rd in the draft class in PFF grade on intermediate throws. Inflated stats coming out of Washington State passing scheme and rarely faced heavy pressure. When he did face pressure last year, was sacked on 25.5 percent of his drop backs, 4th-highest in the draft class. Ranked 33rd in the draft class in big-time throw percentage last season. Ranked 27th in the draft class at avoiding turnover-worthy plays. Was better in previous seasons. Can he get back to previous form?
pff_bottom_line: Last season did not go as planned for Falk, who took a step back while battling through injury. Even at his best, his arm strength is a question mark, as he struggles to consistently drive the ball outside the numbers on out-breaking routes. He has good touch and feel for in the short game, but arm strength and athleticism issues raise enough questions that he can create enough big plays at the next level.

pff_overview: Flies to the ball on underneath routes. Will sometimes be a step slow to react to routes in his zone. Can get caught with his eyes in the backfield on play action. Missed 13 tackles on 116 attempts in his two years at Southern Miss. Moves well. Can hang with receivers when isolated 1-on-1. Reads the quarterback and breaks quickly on the ball. Finished with seven pass breakups last season, tied for 7th in the nation among safeties. Good length allows him to make plays in underneath zones. Keeps his leverage when playing contain in the run game. Can get moved at the point of attack against bigger tight ends.
pff_bottom_line: Moore had a breakout 2017 season that saw him making plays on the ball from a variety of alignments. He can hang with receivers when isolated and he has the movement skills to make plays on the back end of the defense. Against the run, he’s not a hammer, but he plays under control and knows how to prevent big plays on the edge. Moore is one of the underrated safeties in this class and he has a potential fit in multiple schemes.

pff_overview: Three years of solid grading, but his best season actually came in 2015, an 89.2 grade that marginally edges 2017’s mark of 87.9. Didn’t have an interception in 2017, but did have eight pass breakups and allowed fewer than 50 percent of passes thrown his way to be caught. Has played multiple spots for North Carolina and demonstrated a varied skillset. NFL future could be as a slot/safety/matchup weapon. Had two sacks, three hits and two hurries from just 22 pass-rushing snaps on the blitz. Graded well in all facets of the game in 2017, and had excellent coverage grades in each of the past three seasons. May struggle with long speed to play perimeter corner in the NFL.
pff_bottom_line: Less of a true perimeter cornerback and more of a defensive back whose ver- satility should lend itself to a hybrid role in an NFL defense, M.J. Stewart has three excellent seasons of play at North Carolina. Stewart also played at the Senior Bowl and graded well during the week, but any NFL team will need to have a plan in terms of how to use him at the next level. He is a classic tweener player, but at a time where that role has in itself become a position in some defenses. Could make an early impact as a matchup weapon on defense.

pff_overview: A jack of all trades at BYU, Warner has played in several different alignments, including defending the slot for 41.7 percent of his 2017 snaps. Had 112 snaps on special teams across a variety of different units and graded well in each season on special teams. Always productive against the run, had impressive coverage grades until 2017 where that form dipped and he allowed a passer rating of 101.3 Something of a tweener, or at least a player whose NFL position has yet to be defined. Has shown the skill set that would fit either at linebacker or strong safety, with the ability to be a matchup weapon on defense. Had three pass breakups in 2017 to go along with his lone interception on 45 targets. Missed double-digit tackles in each of the past three seasons, with 10 in 2017 on 84 solo attempts.
pff_bottom_line: Warner is an intriguing player who lined up all over the defense at BYU. The NFL will have to decide where best he fits in a pro defensive scheme, but he has shown the production and versatility to excel in a league where coverage matchup weapons have never been more coveted. He has the athleticism to play safety and the size to be a linebacker, and could find himself becoming a key part of some team’s passing defense over the next few seasons.

pff_overview: Played in just four games as a junior before an ankle injury shut him down for the year, but was spectacular before getting hurt. Is short (5-foot-9), but stocky, and does not look out of place running between the tackles against much larger players. Average yards per carry increased every season of his college career, and he had runs of 80-plus yards in his last two seasons. Has quickness and speed to burn, and can immediately turn a blocked point of attack into a bounce out gain. Was more of a factor in the passing game than some other backs in this class, with 60 targets over his first two seasons. Has just one game of 20 or more carries in his career, and durability will be a concern given his size. Broke 71 tackles on 394 college carries throughout his career.
pff_bottom_line: Mark Walton’s tape in 2017 was spectacular, but it lasted just four games before an ankle injury shut him down. Pre-draft measurements will be important, as his listed weights right now span a 17-pound range from 188 to 205. He has a squat and stocky build, but under 200 pounds will have many in the NFL PASS BLOCK EFFICIENCY limiting him to a third-down back or role player. Shows the ability to play on all three downs and make plays on the ground or as a receiver. In a strong run- % NOT TACKLED ON ning back class could be pushed down the draft by bigger-bodied players.

pff_overview: A versatile player who has shown the ability to run the ball, catch it and return kicks well, but never put it all together in the same season. Ballage’s measurables are impressive and he is a physical specimen, so will likely see his hype rise post-combine workouts. Was exceptional during the week of practice as a receiver at the Senior Bowl, winning consistently in all practice scenarios. Coming off his lowest grade of the past three seasons, but was used confusingly at Arizona St., often as a wildcat QB (70 times over 2016-7). Only averaged 2.7 yards per carry after contact over his college career, lower than a player of his size and talent should. Broke only 15 tackles from 167 carries in 2017, and has never broken more than 16 in a season. May be a better receiver than ball carrier, but displays intriguing skills in all areas.
pff_bottom_line: Kalen Ballage is a player of intriguing potential and versatility, whose stock is likely to rise in the lead up to the draft. He is an impressive athlete in a big body, and has the ability to perform well on the ground, catching the ball in the pass game and returning kicks. He was extremely impressive as a receiver during the week of Senior Bowl practices and will likely blow up at the com- bine during workouts, but teams will need to reconcile that with relatively pedestrian college production.

pff_overview: Experience playing low zone as curl/flat defender. Made a few spectacular plays in this role. Attacks wide receivers in the screen game. High points the ball. Finished with three interceptions and four pass breakups on 87 career targets. Moves well and stays on top of routes down the field. Not the smoothest back pedal in the world, something that may need to be re-done if used in a deep safety role. Missed 17 tackles on 163 career attempts. Technically lined up as a slot corner for the majority of the time in West Virginia’s scheme and tied for fourth among draftable cornerbacks with a run-stop percentage of 4.9. Plays the run well from an overhang position. Posted top grade against the run among all cornerbacks in 2017.
pff_bottom_line: White has two excellent years of production for West Virginia in their hybrid safety/ slot cornerback role. He has an excellent feel for playing underneath coverage and he was the nation’s top graded run defender among cornerbacks in 2017. White could fill a similar role at the next level as a cover-3 strong safety, capable of working downhill in the run game and playing traditional curl/flat responsibilities. He moves well enough to play deep safety in two-high looks, though he’ll need to tighten up his technique and backpedal in order to make the transition.

pff_overview: Big corner, but doesn’t play like it consistently, often losing out for physicality while also struggling against quick movement. Allowed two touchdowns in 2017 from 66 targets, allowed 53.0 percent of passes thrown his way to be caught. Gave up an NFL passer rating of 70.4, picked off two passes and broke up another four. Played at the Senior Bowl and in the game itself, allowed no receptions from three targets. Didn’t allow a reception in the bowl game against Iowa, and was not targeted in the game. Has played special teams extensively, with 146 special teams snaps over the season across multiple special teams phases. Will help him play early.
pff_bottom_line: Another corner that fits the height and length profile that NFL teams are looking for, Isaac Yiadom’s quickest route to playing time in the NFL may be on special teams because he has extensive experience and playing time there while many other corner prospects do not. He flashes the plays that speak to big potential but can be exposed in almost all facets of the game and struggled badly against Notre Dame, particularly in space.

pff_overview: Four-year starter who bounced back and forth between left tackle and center throughout his career. Coming off the best season of his career in 2017, where he allowed a total of 17 pressures at left tackle. Got torn apart by Nick Bosa and Ohio State this past season. Exposed weak punch in pass protection. Hails from pro-style running game at Michigan that asked him to execute numerous different blocks. Ducks into blocks with wide hands. Struggles to maintain a clean engage as a result. Nothing special strength wise. Not a line of scrimmage mover by any means.
pff_bottom_line: Likely best suited to be a center in the NFL, Cole could play guard and maybe even tackle in a pinch as well. That versatility will be coveted, but not enough to warrant a high draft pick. He may not be a super exciting prospect, but he’s fairly clean and has a huge body of work to evaluate off of.

pff_overview: Long frame and catch radius that he uses well at the catch point. Tied for 6th in the nation with a 66.7 percent catch rate in contested situations. Tied for 8th in the nation with a catch percentage of 64.0 when facing press coverage. Not an explosive athlete. Struggles to consistently separate. Most of his big plays will come in contested situations. Only played 1,066 snaps in his three years at Florida State. Red-zone and back-shoulder weapon.
pff_bottom_line: Like other taller receivers, Tate has a strong highlight reel of off-target and contested catches, and that should make him a valuable red-zone threat at the next level. He’s not an explosive or shifty athlete, so he may never become a high-volume option in the passing game, but he’s willing to make plays over the middle in traffic. Tate has the skills to be a complementary possession target capable of winning in the back-shoulder game, over the middle and in the red-zone.

pff_overview: An imposing physical specimen, Scarbrough is 6-foot-2 and 235 pounds and will remind some of former Alabama teammate Derrick Henry. Scarbrough has had just 267 career carries at Alabama, 29 fewer than Henry had in 2015 alone, grading solidly but not spectacularly. Has averaged 3.9 yards per carry after contact over his career, but that dropped to just 2.9 in 2017. Has never carried the ball 20 or more times in a game, so his capability as a workhorse back is in question in a way it wasn’t for Henry. Caught 17 of the 20 passes thrown his way in 2017, breaking five tackles after the catch, but dropping two of the incompletions. Pass blocking has been suspect, allowed a sack, hit and two hurries from 43 pass-blocking snaps in 2017. Has dealt with numerous injuries in his short career, which doesn’t bode well for a player reliant on physicality and size.
pff_bottom_line: Bo Scarbrough may bear a passing resemblance to former teammate Derrick Henry, but while Henry’s durability and production wasn’t in question, Scar- brough has never held up to that kind of workload. He is an old school power back who can be dangerous at full speed and in the open field, but has little value in the passing game and isn’t capable of generating much yardage on his own without the aid of blocking to let him get rumbling. There is talent there, but he may be a more impressive physique than football player.

pff_overview: Caught 70.84 percent of his deep targets, second-best in the nation. Led all FBS receivers with nine touchdowns on deep passes. 55.4 percent of receptions went for a first down or a touchdown, second- best among draft-eligible receivers. Averaged 9.0 yards per attempt when facing press coverage, tied for 32nd in the nation among wide receivers with at least 20 targets. Long strides get on cornerbacks in a hurry. Good feel for defenders in the open field. Enhances his big-play ability. Forced 32 missed tackles on 175 career receptions. Dropped 16 passes on 191 catchable attempts. Shows toughness and body control when catching the ball in traffic. Caught 54.5 percent of contested targets and tied for 13th in the nation with four touchdowns.
pff_bottom_line: After two solid seasons, Smith broke out as a big-play threat in 2017, averaging 19.2 yards per catch and hauling in 14 touchdowns. He has good size and body control and he uses his long strides to gain ground and separate from corner- backs down the field. He has the toughness to make plays over the middle of the field and the speed to succeed as a vertical slot option, much like he did at UCF, while also adding value when lined up on the outside.

pff_overview: Had eight interceptions in 2016, but none in the rest of his college career. Tightened up his coverage overall in 2017 despite failing to register the interceptions. Wasn’t beaten for a catch longer than 34 yards all year. Allowed just 47.1 percent of passes thrown his way to be caught over his college career, but gave up 11 touchdowns on 140 targets. Long and physical, but struggles badly in space if he can’t get his hands on the receiver and use his hands to re-route. Has flashed ball skills, but only in one season, and is more of an obstacle to receptions than a genuine ballhawking threat to an offense. Needs the right defensive scheme to protect his deficiencies and take advantage of his (literal) strength.
pff_bottom_line: A big cornerback with excellent size (6-foot-2) and length, Tarvarus McFadden has the ability to make impressive plays if he can turn his assignment into a physical encounter with a receiver. If he is asked to play in space or allows separation against speed he is in significant trouble and can be exposed badly. Surrendered 11 touchdowns over the past two seasons of play and gave up almost 13 yards per reception. Needs the right schematic fit to take advantage of his physicality and limit his exposure against speed.

pff_overview: Played both inside and outside linebacker for Memphis, with 533 of his 884 snaps outside in 2017. Pass-rush has been consistently his best trait, and he notched 57 total pressures in 2017, though was shut out in the NFLPA Bowl. Run defense has also been solid and his run-stop percentage ranked inside the top 20 in the nation in 2017. 50 defensive stops were also good enough to rank top 20 in the nation among all linebackers. Coverage has been his weakness, with poor grades in all but one season. He allowed 11.3 yards per catch over his college career, including 14.4 in 2017, his most extensive playing time in coverage.
pff_bottom_line: Avery needs to be tied down to a position at the NFL level, after he played both inside linebacker and outside, edge rushing linebacker for Memphis. His strength has been pass-rushing to date, with solid run defense, while coverage has been a weakness, so he may naturally project to the edge. His immediate route to NFL playing time may be special teams while teams work out how best to deploy him on defense.

pff_overview: College career consisted of just 791 snaps, 483 of which came in 2017. Graded well in 2017, but almost all of it came in the opening three games. Failed to sustain anything like that performance over the long haul. In those opening three games, he gained 244 yards after first contact from just 56 carries (4.4 yards per attempt) and broke 20 tackles. 2017 was his only year with a significant receiving role, and he caught 82.2 percent of targets, broke 14 tackles after the catch. Eight of his 14 broken tackles came in those first three games. An undersized-but-determined and violent runner, Kelly has little mileage on the clock and can be a three-down factor at the next level.
pff_bottom_line: Kelly was sparingly used at Tennessee and enters the NFL as a dynamic weapon in all facets of the game and has very little wear and tear. His grades have been impressive but very inconsistent, showing potential rather than reliable pro- duction. He has a lot of weight on a short frame but doesn’t have the powerful legs that that usually translates to. He represents an interesting and versatile option for a team looking for a complementary back who could have success early.

pff_overview: Ranked 34th out of 38 qualifiers in PFF grade when facing pressure last season. Maneuvers the pocket well to find room to throw, but struggles to evade rushers. Sacked on 23.0 percent of his pressured drop backs last season, 5th-highest in the class. Willing to make difficult throws under pressure. Posted 11th-highest PFF grade in the draft class on third-/fourth-down situations. Posted 7th-lowest percentage of turnover-worthy plays in the draft class last season. Many of his poor throws are thrown just a tick late and off rhythm. Posted 6th-highest grade in the draft class on deep (20-plus yard) throws. Throws with zip and touch to at the intermediate level.
pff_bottom_line: The 2017 season didn’t start out great for White, who adjusted to a new of- fense, but he improved down the stretch. His 2016 season saw him break out and attack down the field, so the big-play potential is there. White has the arm to win at all levels of the field, but he must be more consistent with his timing and there’s a concern that he can’t make plays outside of structure like other quarterbacks in the draft class. Still, he’s worth a mid-round look as a develop- mental option who has put much more good than bad on tape.

pff_overview: Experienced. Played 3,088 snaps in four years at Texas A&M Missed 55 tackles on 357 career attempts. Missed at least 11 tackles in every season. Active player who makes plays all over the field. Tied for seventh in the nation with 32 stops in 2017. Improved every year of his career. Has potential in the slot. Allowed a passer rating of only 54.3 there in 2016 and lined up in the slot on 286 snaps over the last two seasons. Moves well laterally, but can get stuck in the mud at the top of routes. Drives well on the ball from off and quarters looks. Aggressiveness at the catch point works both for and against him. Will make plays on the ball, but also whiffs and gives up big plays. Had 10 interceptions and nine pass breakups on 144 career targets.
pff_bottom_line: Watts is experienced player who can fill multiple roles on a defense. He han- dles 1-on-1 situations well for a safety and his movement skills give him slot flexibility at the next level. He’s aggressive and willing to make plays on the ball, but he’s also been burned when he gets there a step slow. Watts must do a better job of tackling after missing 55 in his career, but there’s more good than bad to his game and he’ll offer positional flexibility to his future team.

pff_overview: Caught 39.5 percent of contested catch opportunities and 2017 and led the nation with 43 attempts. Will make impressive plays in tight situations but should be able to use his long frame more consistently. Long-strider with buildup speed. Not particularly quick off the line of scrimmage. Will need to rely on using his body, as he does not consistently separate against man coverage. Uses his hands well to get off press coverage. Not a dynamic threat after the catch. Forced only 17 missed tackles on 243 career receptions. Dropped 30 passes on 273 career targets in his career.
pff_bottom_line: Like many receivers in the 6-foot-5 range, Lazard can be a contributor in the possession game, though he may never be a consistent downfield or after-the- catch threat. He uses his big body to win in contested situations, but he could stand to improve his ability to make plays on off-target throws. While Lazard may never separate well enough to become a high-volume receiver; he has a role as a potential big-bodied mismatch option.

pff_overview: Violent hands and first strike. Has the ability to ragdoll and toss aside opposing offensive linemen like it’s nothing. Balance is an issue. Gets top heavy and has trouble staying on his feet when changing directions. Double teams were a problem. Had reps where he got taken out of the play completely. Injuries plagued him throughout his college career. Only played 1,079 snaps his entire college career. Checks boxes from a size and athleticism perspective. Ideal 3-4 defensive end toolbox to take on guards and tackles. Rangy versus the run. Can win quickly and close on the opposite side of the line of scrimmage. Not a power player. Wants to win with quicks and isn’t quick enough to win consistently that way as pass-rusher.
pff_bottom_line: Thompson is a bull in a china shop at this point in his development. His game is unrefined and even awkward looking at times, but it still got the job done. His injuries are a concern, as is his mediocre pass-rushing prowess (only 13 total pressures this year). Thompson is an intriguing player after the top of the crop is gone on the interior.

pff_overview: Slightly built defensive tackle with little college production to speak of. Would disappear for whole games at a time. 7 sacks in college career. Plays with terrific leverage. Able to consistently move the line of scrimmage when going 1-on-1. Asked to play run first from a frog stance most snaps. Scheme not well suited to his strengths. Getting off of blocks is a major issue. Seemingly attached to offensive linemen far too often. Almost awkward looking in his movements. Nothing looks terribly natural about his play style. Pass-rushing toolbox is incredibly limited at this point. Only 35 pressures all last season. Never truly dominated.
pff_bottom_line: Brown flashed a number of reps that make him an intriguing evaluation, but they were so few and far between that you’re left wanting more. He’s graded out right around average all four seasons in college and isn’t so athletic that makes one think there’s underlying potential he hasn’t reached.

pff_overview: Long, lean tackle with requisite build to hold up on the edge in the NFL. Explosive at the point of contact. Regularly rocks back edge players and widens point of attack. Tight splits of the offensive linemen at N.C. State often masked some of his agility deficiencies. Waist bending is a serious concern with him. Often out over his toes and easily gets off-balance. Gets good depth and mirrors well in his pass sets. Feet never stop moving. Patient in pass protection. Doesn’t go searching for the first punch and lets the defender come to him.
pff_bottom_line: Richardson has been suspended multiple times throughout his college career and his off-field will need thorough vetting. He offers much more than most day two and day three tackles, though. He could stand to add some strength to his frame but has all the tools to be a starting tackle in time.

pff_overview: Squatty defensive tackle with thick build throughout. Limited length but shouldn’t be a huge issue at nose tackle. Ability to slide into any alignment between the tackles and not be out of place. Usage of leverage is fantastic. Comes naturally at his height, but he still fires off low. Bench presses centers with his hands above his eyes. Technique versus the run is a plus. Surprisingly not much of a pocket pusher. Got it done more with his hands and athleticism as a pass-rusher but will be limited in that regard at NFL level. Plays with a reckless streak as a pass-rusher. Relishes his chance to take shots at opposing quarterbacks.
pff_bottom_line: Athleticism in a nose tackle is rare, but Senat possesses it. That in and of itself will put him on NFL radars. Add to it the way he plays with leverage and his overall hand usage and you have a mid-round prospect that could make an impact early in his NFL career.

pff_overview: Fantastic athlete for the position. Quick off the snap and reaches shades with ease. Play strength is lacking. Struggled to take even college defensive tackles off the line of scrimmage. Loses control of blocks at the line of scrimmage too easily. Hands struggle to latch on consistently. Got dominated in the week of practices leading up to the Senior Bowl. Lowest graded offensive lineman in the 1-on-1s. Athleticism doesn’t translate to quick feet in pass protection. Had issues recovering and passing off stunts. Three-year starter with experience at guard as well as center.
pff_bottom_line: Quessenberry is a perfect fit for teams that like to get their centers out on the move. Whether that be a team that is outside zone heavy or pulls their center to the edge – the UCLA product can do either. He also has some positional flex- ibility and could hold up at guard. His strength limitations are obvious though and it’s concerning how overpowered he was in the Senior Bowl 1-on-1s.

pff_overview: Attacks downhill in the run game. Classic box safety. Finishes plays with good power. Ranked 6th in the draft class with a run-stop percentage of 7.7 when lined up within eight yards of the line of scrimmage. Run-stop percentage of 8.3 when lined up in the box ranked 5th in the nation in 2016. Limited range at free safety. Can hold his own in split safety looks. Not a great coverage player, but handles curl/flat responsibilities well. Missed 39 tackles on 335 career tackles attempts. Has the size to match up 1-on-1 with tight ends.
pff_bottom_line: Allen fits the box-safety mold, as he works well in the run game and does his best coverage work in underneath zones. He had a better showing from split-safety looks last season, and he could see some snaps there at the next level, but he’s most at home closer to the line of scrimmage. Allen fits best as a true strong safety in a cover-3 heavy scheme, where he can limit his snaps at free safety and have an impact against the run and in the short passing game.

pff_overview: Averaged 5.2 yards per carry after contact, the highest figure in the draft class by almost a full yard. Broke 44 tackles on the ground and another one as a receiver to give him an elusive rating of 116.5, the second-best figure in the draft class. Improved his grade in each of the past two seasons as playing time increased. Played 62.1 percent of Notre Dame’s snaps in 2017. Is extremely hard to stop moving. Had five games in 2017 alone with 100- plus yards after contact. Has good long speed, but can take time to hit that top end and needs some open room. Was asked to pass block 71 times in 2017, surrendering one sack and four hurries across those snaps. Broke at least one tackle in every game this season until the bowl game.
pff_bottom_line: Josh Adams is a big, bruising back that has been excellent for Notre Dame at getting into open space and making big plays. He has runs of at least 74 yards in every season of his college career, and when he gets into open space he can be tough to catch with excellent long speed. He doesn’t have the best short area burst and quickness, but shows the ability to read cutback lanes and find daylight. May be less successful at the NFL level where that short area quick- ness is more of a premium.

pff_overview: A tall, long corner who has some impressive tape and measurables, but also maturity concerns and was suspended late in the 2017 season. Didn’t allow a touchdown in 2017, but was beaten badly on a few plays that could easily have resulted in them. Had two interceptions and five pass breakups, allowed a passer rating of just 48.1 on 57 targets. Had solid grades against the run in his two biggest seasons of playing time, posting 18 defensive stops this past season. Struggles to live with receivers at the breaking point in the route and can allow significant separation even on deep passes, or grabs to prevent it. Played with an unconventional alignment at Texas on off-coverage zone plays that will likely be reworked at the next level. Had big games against top competition, surrendering just 18 yards to Oklahoma’s James Washington on three targets.
pff_bottom_line: Holton Hill is another cornerback that fits the profile that NFL teams are look- ing for with exceptional size and length, but he is a significantly more flawed prospect than some other others in the class that tick those boxes. Hill also has significant maturity concerns and had the best season of his college career cur- tailed by suspension incurred by violating team rules. Has size and length, but can struggle at the breaking point in routes and needs work to realize his true potential. Likely to be a boom-or-bust candidate later in the draft.

pff_overview: Uses his size well to win on slants and downfield routes. Ranked ninth in the nation with 320 yards in contested situations. Caught 55.0 percent of deep targets, tied for 16th-best among FBS WRs. Ranked fourth among draft-eligible receivers with a WR rating of 135.5. Shows some quicks when getting off press coverage and it showed in the numbers. Against press coverage, caught 15-of-20 attempts for 250 yards and three touchdowns, good for the second-best passer rating in the class at 156.3. Dropped only 11 out of 137 catchable targets in his career. Doesn’t make many defenders miss in space. Forced only 11 missed tackles on 126 career catches.
pff_bottom_line: Ateman is an intriguing talent, as he can use his size both in the possession game and down the field, but he may be limited when it comes to creating sep- aration along the entire route tree. He handles press well and he can likely be a weapon in the red-zone, but don’t expect him to make defenders miss after the catch. Ateman has a complementary role in the NFL, especially if playing with a quarterback who is willing to let him make plays in contested situations.

pff_overview: Very good and productive run defender, averaged over 50 defensive stops in each of the past three seasons. Has been a productive pass-rusher on the blitz, but typically through persistence and strength more than dynamic pass-rushing. Coverage is a major issue, and was a problem in 2017, he allowed 81.6 percent of passes thrown his way to be caught. Kiser allowed a passer rating of 116.4 when targeted over his career, allowed seven touchdowns with just one interception. Likely a two-down thumper at linebacker at the next level in a league where passing has never been more important. Had 114 snaps of special teams play across multiple roles, which could be his biggest asset at the next level.
pff_bottom_line: Kiser has been exceptionally productive across his career at Virginia, but is a limited player and a one dimensional athlete heading into a league that covets the other dimension more. Kiser can be a two-down thumper against the run, and may have to excel on special teams, but his coverage is a major weakness and will keep him off the field on third downs.

pff_overview: One of the smallest corners in the 2018 draft class, stands just 5-foot-9 and weighs 188 pounds. Had one of the best grades in the nation, allowed just 356 yards on the season from 64 targets. Has two seasons of excellent grading, and has graded well against the run in both seasons despite small stature. Didn’t allow a reception longer than 30 yards in 2017, and surrendered a passer rating of 55.5 when targeted. Played almost exclusively at RCB, with 741 of his 785 snaps at that position. At his size will almost certainly need to play in the slot in the NFL, but saw just 13 snaps inside in 2017. Worst game in 2017 came against Texas Tech where he allowed 101 yards on 12 targets, with 98 of those yards coming against Dylan Cantrell.
pff_bottom_line: D.J. Reed is the prototypical small cornerback which means he faces an uphill battle heading into an NFL that has never been more interested in size and measurables. He is a feisty corner that does play with more physicality than his size suggests, but there are barely a hand full of corners that have even been given a shot on the perimeter at his size in the past decade. Reed’s tape is outstanding, but his NFL future lies in either defying those odds or moving to the slot, where has not played extensively in college.

pff_overview: Had his best PFF grade in 2017, and had an impressive run of play from the Wake Forrest game onwards. A tall and rangy linebacker, nonetheless looks a little short of true explosive play and top end speed. Has had a tumultuous college career spanning five years since being one of the top recruits in the nation. Missed 15 tackles in 2017 after missing 11 the season before, as he can tend to hit rather than wrap up in the tackle. Plays too high and can struggle to move fluidly in tight quarters and in short areas. Had one interception and three pass breakups in 2017 from 27 targets, allowed just 6.8 yards per reception and 130 yards all year.
pff_bottom_line: One of the top recruits in the country, Matthew Thomas had a five-year career at Florida State due to a number of reasons that derailed his career. 2017 was by far his best season and his most productive for the Seminoles. He is a tall player with good length, but does look to lack true explosive burst and the ability to live with high-end athletes. His best hope of sticking in the NFL may be special teams.

pff_overview: Solid route runner, can make plays at the intermediate level. Good catch radius. Doesn’t have great athleticism but knows how to use his body and work the middle of the field. Plays right on the border of leveraging defenders and pushing off. Tied for 4th among draft-eligible tight ends with 1.87 yards per route in Caught 45.5 percent of contested targets. Dropped 12 of 147 catchable targets in his career. Provides little after the catch with only four career missed tackles on 135 catches and 3.8 YAC/reception. Continues to improves as a run blocker and can handle first contact. Gives his running back a chance.
pff_bottom_line: Fumagalli knows how the work the middle of the field, using his body and catch radius to move the chains. He’s not a dynamic athlete, and it shows in his subpar after-the-catch stats, but he can be a useful option in the pass game at the short and intermediate level. He’s improved every year as a run blocker and he’s capable of at least holding up against stronger defensive players while also showing the ability to lock onto moving targets.

pff_overview: Caught 55.0 percent of deep targets, tied for 16th-best among FBS receivers. Moves well for his size. Gains ground on corners off the line of scrimmage. Excellent catch radius. Attacks the ball in the air. Routinely makes off- target catches. Rounds his routes down the field. Varies the speed of his routes in order to create separation. Good feel for defenders and a tough runner after the catch. Forced 10 missed tackles on only 46 catches last season. Dropped six of his 52 catchable targets in his career. Only one strong year of production at Georgia.
pff_bottom_line: Another big target in this draft class, Wims has good straight-line speed and some nuance to his route running, though he doesn’t always get in and out of his breaks cleanly. He has a number of highlight-reel catches on tape, as he uses his long frame and body control to routinely make off-target catches. If paired with an aggressive quarterback, Wims can be productive in contested situations and perhaps a bit more if he can clean up some of his route running.

pff_overview: Experience in a pro-style scheme at LSU playing both guard and center. Three straight seasons of quality grades playing against top quality competition. Very consistent with his technique already. Almost robotic in the way he goes about his business. Plays very much under control. Rarely overextends himself or ends up on the ground. Lacking high-level physical traits. The dominant blocks are few and far between. Well-timed punch in pass protection. Hardly any whiffs on tape. Only eight pressures allowed this past season.
pff_bottom_line: Clapp was and extremely solid if unspectacular player for LSU over the past three seasons. He has the ability to play both guard and center while maintain- ing a high level of play. The only thing he’s lacking is the ‘wow’ factor at this point because he checks a ton of other boxes to be a starting interior offensive lineman in the NFL.

pff_overview: Had four straight solid years of PFF grading, with his best season coming back in 2015 as a sophomore for Western Michigan. That sophomore season was his first season playing cornerback in college, and he had been a freshman wide out the year before. Allowed a passer rating of 75.1 in 2017, with three interceptions and 10 pass breakups from 50 targets. Has given up big plays, with receptions of at least 50 yards in each of his three seasons, and 13 touchdowns over 206 targets. Allowed fewer than 50 percent of passes thrown his way to be caught over his college career (49.5) despite playing WR in his freshman season. Has excellent speed and ball skills, but is undersized and weak both against the run and in coverage. Likely moves to the slot at the next level.
pff_bottom_line: Darius Phillips is an interesting story and prospect. He had four impressive seasons at Western Michigan, but one of them was at WR as a freshman before moving to the defensive side of the ball and playing extremely well for three seasons. Has performed well against top competition and adds value as a re- turn man. His athleticism and ball skills are excellent, but his size and strength are a concern, and will likely restrict him to the slot at the next level. Gives up big plays to go along with those big plays of his own in coverage.

pff_overview: Allowed an NFL passer rating of just 41.0 when targeted in 2017, and 32.5 the season before. Allowed just two touchdowns over those two seasons. Had only one game in 2017 in which he surrendered more than three receptions. Showed impressive ball skills with 10 interceptions and 13 pass breakups over the past two years. Was an obvious star in the Tulane secondary, often isolated on an island, but played a lot of off-coverage. Plays the ball very well both in the air and attacking the catch point or the receiver’s arms to prevent the reception. Was beaten for only one catch over 40 yards over the past two seasons and didn’t give up a catch over 30 all 2016.
pff_bottom_line: Nickerson is one of the most interesting cornerback prospects in this draft. Far from many people’s radars, Nickerson has three good years of PFF grading and was exceptional in 2017. He has athleticism, enough size and length for the NFL, and plays the ball as well as any cornerback in this class. He’s aggres- sive for his size, has a light frame that could use some extra weight to combat NFL-level athletes, but he is one of the most attractive mid-round options.

pff_overview: Had one of the best coverage grades in the nation in 2017, an 88.7 that ranked one spot above Roquan Smith. Has had back to back excellent seasons in coverage, but matched that coverage performance with his run defense in 2017. Shows a great feel for the game against the run and the pass, particularly in zone, but has clear athletic limitations. Didn’t allow a touchdown in either of his last two seasons of play and had seven interceptions over that span. Allowed a passer rating of just 49.9 when targeted in 2017, one of the best marks in the draft class and the best mark of anybody with 20-plus targets. Allowed just 62 yards in coverage from 26 targets in 2017. Has excellent technique against the run or the pass, but can lose balance and control against superior athletes.
pff_bottom_line: Skai Moore missed the entire 2016 season with a herniated disc in his neck that required surgery. That is the kind of injury that will raise plenty of medical red flags, and to go along with that he is both undersized and under-athletic. He has, though, been incredibly productive over multiple seasons in the SEC and shows clearly excellent instincts and play. Moore has plenty of negatives to overcome, but his tape suggests he deserves a look in the NFL and could yet surprise those that would write him off.

pff_overview: One of the best track records in pass protection of any tackle in the class grade-wise. The pass sets at Washington State aren’t the same as he’ll be taking in the NFL. Will have to be completely reworked. Good feet and mirror. Rarely got himself into bad situations. Athleticism overall is poor. Showed up a lot in the screen game where he struggled to locate. Plays high far too often and can get bowled over because of it. Very susceptible to the bull rush. Projection in the run game. Barely utilized at Washington State and concepts/technique weren’t what he’ll be running in NFL.
pff_bottom_line: Madison has already shown to be proficient in pass protection throughout his career, but there’s a lot of question marks about whether it will translate to the NFL level. His strength and overall athleticism are below-average for NFL tackles and he projects better as a guard.

pff_overview: Had exceptional coverage numbers in his final season at Alabama, his first with significant playing time. Didn’t allow a touchdown all season from 68 receptions. Allowed a passer rating of just 43.3 including the college playoffs. Gave up a catch on just 44.1 percent of passes thrown his way over the season. Wasn’t beaten for a catch longer than 30 yards all year. Had a couple of ugly games in 2017, including against Auburn, where he missed two tackles and gave up 62 yards from four catches. Played at the Senior Bowl, where he struggled throughout the week of practice before allowing one catch for 31 yards on two targets in the game. Tall and long, but light build and can be bullied at times. Has beaten long odds to get to this position.
pff_bottom_line: A former walk on at Alabama, Wallace has gone from flag football to starting for the Crimson Tide in a national title game in three seasons. Just one year of extensive playing time, Wallace posted impressive grades and had 11 pass breakups in 2017. He’s tall and has excellent movement skills, but very slight and can be bullied. Graded well this season, but struggled during practice at the Senior Bowl all week, and may struggle unless he can develop with more experience.

pff_overview: Great natural leverage. Comes out of stance low and under control. Below average athlete. Really shows when asked to get out and pull the edge and locate. Noticeable hitch in his pull. Experience at both guard (2016) and center (2017), but size profiles best to center in the NFL. Short-arms and struggles to maintain engage with longer defensive tackles. Issue in both run and pass game. Rarely takes opposition off the line of scrimmage. Wins mostly via control rather than brute force. Never looked overmatched by an opponent at the college level. No poorly graded games over last two seasons.
pff_bottom_line: Allen has been one of the best offensive linemen in college football each of the past two seasons, but he doesn’t check a ton of NFL boxes physically. Allen is an undersized center who doesn’t quite have the athleticism to make up for the lack of strength. As technically sound as he is, Allen is still a solid option later in the draft.

pff_overview: Good combination of speed and quickness that shows up on the field. Ranked second in the nation with 1,088 receiving yards from the slot. Caught 66.7 percent of his deep targets, fourth-best in the nation. Ranked second in the draft class with a WR Rating of 139.7. Ranked eighth in the nation with 542 yards on deep passes despite tying for 114th with only 18 deep targets. Averaged 8.5 yards after the catch per reception and forced 39 missed tackles on his 160 catches over the last three years. Dropped 17 passes on 177 catchable targets in his career. Has value on ‘gadget’ plays at the next level, though only given eight career rushing attempts. Caught only three of 15 contested catch opportunities.
pff_bottom_line: There’s a role for Coutee in the slot at the next level, where he’ll be more than just a quick receiver capable of winning in the underneath game. His speed and body control make him a vertical threat, and a creative team may be able to maximize his value on jet sweeps and other ‘space’ plays. His lack of size can be an issue on the outside, but Coutee’s speed and quickness make him a weapon at the next level.

pff_overview: Caught 57.9 percent of contested targets, 29th-best in the nation. Adjusts well to off-target throws. Uses his frame well down the field. Caught 43.5 percent of his deep targets last season, tied for 75th in the nation. Ran limited route tree in Missouri offense. Long strides and solid straight-line speed. Gets on cornerbacks in a hurry. Solid showing after the catching in 2017, forcing 14 missed tackles on 66 catches and averaging 6.5 yards after the catch per reception. Dropped 24-of-173 catchable targets in his career. Had a good showing during the week of practice at the Senior Bowl. Ranked fourth among receivers in PFF 1-on-1 grading.
pff_bottom_line: Like many receivers coming out of the ‘Baylor’ system that Missouri runs, Moore will have to adjust the NFL’s more intricate route tree. He has good straight-line speed, allowing him to gain ground into the secondary and he has a knack for using his body to secure downfield throws. He has some work to do in the short and intermediate game, but Moore could have value as a potential deep threat while he develops the rest of his game.

pff_overview: Caught 54.2 percent of contested targets (13-for-24). Caught 50.0 percent of his deep targets last season, tied for 31st in the nation. Dropped 19 passes on 131 career catchable targets. Ranked 334th out of 369 qualifiers in drop rate in 2017. Adjusts well to off-target throws and back-shoulder fades. Solid after the catch. Forced 22 missed tackles on only 112 career receptions. Good route runner. Can do damage in the slot, as he runs horizontal routes well when given a two-way go. Knows how to leverage defenders in 1-on-1 coverage, both at the intermediate level and down the field.
pff_bottom_line: Lasley has the skillset to do damage both in the slot and on the outside, but he must do a better job of catching the ball in order to make an impact at the next level. His tape is filled with strong routes in which he wins all over the field, but also far too many easy drops. Lasley could be one of the bigger boom-or- bust prospects in this draft class.

pff_overview: Four strong years of grading, though 2017 represented the lowest grade of his four-year career. Can turn defenders when on the move on front side of zone runs. Loses on first contact too often in the run game. Experience in a zone-heavy scheme and can make all of the necessary blocks in an outside-zone heavy system. Late to recognize blitzing linebackers. Looks for work when uncovered in pass protection. Has solid tape at right tackle, playing 172 snaps there in 2016 and 433 snaps in 2015. Experienced. Has played 3,162 career snaps. Allowed only 36 pressures on 1,313 career snaps in pass protection.
pff_bottom_line: Gossett had an excellent career at Appalachian State, capping it off with a solid week at the Senior Bowl. His experience in a zone-blocking scheme should translate well at the next level, and his size, length and experience at right tackle give him some versatility. Gossett makes difficult run blocks look easy, but he must improve his consistency on the “easy” stuff in order to maximize his value. He’s worth a look in the middle of the draft.

pff_overview: Posted a WR rating of 150.3 in the middle of the field, second-best among FBS receivers with at least 35 targets. Led all FBS receivers with 4.58 yards per route against Power-5 conferences. Has good quicks after the catch and forced 22 missed tackles on 140 catches over the last two years. Dropped only 10 of 150 catchable targets over last two seasons. Adjusts well to off-target throws. Has the route-running ability to do damage in the slot. May not be much of a deep threat at the next level and caught only 38.7 percent of his deep targets last season, 112th in the nation. Ranked second in the nation with 383 yards in contested situations.
pff_bottom_line: Wilson has two solid years of production under his belt at Boise State, where he showed the skills to win on the outside or in the slot at the next level. He may not have the speed to be a true deep threat, but he did show well in contested situations. There are plenty of spectacular and off-target catches littered throughout his tape. Wilson is yet another complementary piece from this draft class, and his ability to line up in multiple roles should only help his cause.

pff_overview: Loose arm creates easy velocity at all levels. Gets the ball down the field with ease. Posted the 4th-highest grade in the draft class in the red-zone. Ranked 36th out of 37 draft QBs in PFF grade when facing pressure. Ranked 30th out of 37 draft-eligible QBs at avoiding turnover-worthy plays last season. Ranked 35th in the draft class in adjusted completion percentage on deep (20-plus yard) throws (32.9 percent). Posted the 9th-highest percentage of negatively graded throws in the draft class last season. Throws well on the move, but he’s a backyard player outside the pocket. Can drop it in a bucket or zip it into a tight window, but also forces too many passes late in the down. Too many poor fumbles when trying to do too much outside the pocket. Tape is littered with well-placed bucket throws.
pff_bottom_line: Benkert is another tools-first prospect who has to clean up the finer points of his game. He’ll make a few jaw-dropping throws down the field, either drop- ping them in a bucket or while on the move, but for every great throw there’s another poor decision in there as well. He’s a developmental prospect who must improve his accuracy and decision-making in order to succeed at the next level.

pff_overview: Built like an ox. Short for the position but carries 300-plus pounds with ease. Consistently a line of scrimmage mover when going 1-on-1. Takes on blocks with little plan of attack. All too often puts his head down and drives. Nothing as a pass-rusher. Hand usage needs a lot of work. Only 22 total pressures this past season. Often the 0-tech in Texas’ defense. Looked out of place and was far less effective when he didn’t get to simply fire into the center ever snap. Still light as far as nose tackles go and struggled to hold up to double teams.
pff_bottom_line: Ford has a lot of knocks against him. He’s an undersized nose tackle that offers nothing as a pass-rusher. It’s a role that’s simply being phased out of many NFL defenses and will limit him to aggressive, one-gapping teams only. His multi- ple seasons of grading are difficult to overlook though, and he has the build to put on some more weight in time.

pff_overview: Ranked 19th among safeties with a run-stop percentage of 6.2 and led the draft class with 29 run-stops last season. Recorded 50 tackles when lined up within eight yards of the line of scrimmage, 2nd-most among safeties last season. Struggles to shed blocks, but sifts through the trash well to find the ball. Very experienced. Played 3,497 snaps during his four-year career at Virginia. Missed 43 tackles on and incredible 502 tackle attempts (one every 11.7 attempts) during his career. Has nine interceptions and eight pass breakups on 136 career targets. Breaks well on out routes from quarters alignment. That aggressiveness has been used against him on double-moves. Very few snaps as a pure center fielder.
pff_bottom_line: Blanding fits the mold of a two-high safety, as he’s capable when playing quarters, but also has enough range on the back end of cover-2. He’s at his best working downhill in the running game, where he knows how to find the ball and he’s a sure tackler. We haven’t seen a whole lot from him as a single-high safety, and he could stand to improve at the catch point, but a split-safety role or one that puts him in the box a portion of the time appears to be the best fit for Blanding.

pff_overview: Good arm, can zip the ball into tight windows and get the ball down the field when off-platform. Had the 9th-highest percentage of positively graded throws last season. Had the 5th-best grade in the draft class on intermediate throws last season. Must improve his touch in the short game. Ranked only 31st in the draft class on deep passes last season. Falls off too many throws and gets himself into trouble. Ranked 24th in the draft class in PFF grade under pressure in 2017. Trusts his arm too much in the middle of the field. Led to his ranking 27th in the draft class at avoiding turnover-worthy throws last season.
pff_bottom_line: Ferguson has good size and solid velocity, but he got away with far too many ill-advised passes last season despite throwing only nine interceptions. The tools are worth a look, as he’s capable of driving the ball down the field, but he trusts himself too much when throwing into tight windows and he must improve in the short game, where he posted the No. 20 grade in the draft class last season.

pff_overview: Lynchpin to one of the best offensive lines in football over the past couple of seasons. Technician with his hand placement. Great independent hand usage in run and pass game. Only allowed 10 total pressures in his college career (2,220 total snaps). Core strength isn’t great. Can get flat-backed fairly easily by defensive tackles 1-on-1. Plodder. Likely scheme limited at the next level with his lack of athleticism. Can get knocked off balance far too easily. Seemed to be always on the verge of falling on his face.
pff_bottom_line: Bozeman is going to have an uphill climb to ever become an NFL starter with his athleticism.
