He got the job done for multiple seasons in the SEC though and it didn’t seem to a huge hindrance there. Bozeman has the size to play either guard or center and that versatility will be looked favorably upon in the

pff_overview: Dropped only two of his 75 catchable targets, good for a drop rate of 2.67 that ranked fourth in the nation in 2017. Dropped only four of 156 catchable targets in his career. Averaged 2.98 yards per route, tied for 22nd in the nation. Targeted only 15 times when facing press coverage and caught only 45.7 percent of those targets. Tape is filled with highlight-reel catches as he often lays out to haul in receptions. Forced 26 missed tackles on 152 career receptions, averaging 5.8 yards after the catch per reception. Lacks great vertical speed, but can separate down the field on vertical routes. Struggles getting off press against physical corners.
pff_bottom_line: Burnett has some wiggle to his game as a route-runner that lends itself to the slot or a ‘Z’ receiver role on the outside. He lacks the size and physicality to handle press coverage and he’s not great in contested situations, but he’s shown the ability to make diving catches on off-target throws. Burnett projects as a sure-handed slot receiver who has his limitations on the outside.

pff_overview: A very talented and productive linebacker whose injury history is now extensive and concerning. Has played just 737 defensive snaps over the past three seasons, and 388 over the past two. Injuries kept him sidelined during 2017. Notched 30 defensive stops in just 388 snaps in 2016, played 88.2 percent of the team’s snaps before going down injured. Was a factor as a pass-rusher on the blitz, racked up 28 total pressures and nine sacks in two seasons. Dominated against Ohio State in his penultimate college game, with a sack, hit and hurry as well as seven defensive stops. Coverage experience is limited, but he showed well in that small sample size. Did not surrender a touchdown across 25 targets.
pff_bottom_line: Cichy is a talented linebacker with impressive play on tape, but now has a concerning injury history and hasn’t seen the field since mid-way through the 2016 season. His college career is less than 800 snaps old, a comparable num- ber to former Florida linebacker Alex Anzalone, who was drafted in the third round a year ago by the Saints. Cichy may not quite match Anzalone athleti- cally, but his instincts and tape are better. If teams are happy he isn’t a medical concern, he could be a solid mid-round addition that excels early.

pff_overview: Led all FBS wide receivers with 4.66 yards per route run from the slot. Had the lowest drop rate in the nation among receivers with at least 100 targets in 2017, dropping only two of 116 catchable passes (1.72 percent). Caught 60.0 percent of his deep targets, tied for eighth among FBS wide receivers. Lacks top-end speed and athleticism Shows toughness both at the catch point and after the catch. Efficient footwork allows him to create separation, especially when given a two-way go in the slot. Solid catch radius and body control. Caught 57.1 percent of contested catch opportunities. Good feel for getting open against zone.
pff_bottom_line: Quinn doesn’t possess the speed to be a deep threat on the outside, but he’s a good ‘feel’ player who can find a home in the possession game at the next level. He has some subtlety to his short-area route running and he has a good feel for getting open against zones and feeling defenders after the catch. While he’s not a dynamic athlete, it would not surprise to see Quinn’s route running, dependable hands, and feel for the game lead to a productive career.

pff_overview: Experienced. Played 3,191 career snaps at Northwestern over four years. Missed 41 tackles on 358 career attempts. Cut his misses down to career- low seven in 2017. Shows good quickness at the top of routes. Tied for the national lead with eight pass breakups in 2017. Finished career with seven interceptions and 18 pass breakups on 163 targets. Can be a step slow recognizing route concepts in underneath zones. Made plays on the ball from two-high safety looks. Plays with good balance and control in the run game. Limited when isolated as single-high free safety.
pff_bottom_line: Igwebuike is yet another safety with starter potential who fits best in more of a two-high system. He can make plays on the ball from deep-half looks and he works downhill with control and a feel for leverage. Igwebuike has enough quickness to hold his own in 1-on-1 situations, either when covering from the slot or matching up from a quarters look. He’s worth a shot in the middle rounds.

pff_overview: Unorthodox motion, but quick release. Despite quick release, does not create great power with his throwing motion. Will flutter too many passes, hurting his ability to complete passes into tight windows. Ranked 5th in the draft class in big-time throw percentage at 6.2 last season. Ranked 19th in the draft class at avoiding turnover-worthy plays at 3.82 percent. Had the 6th-highest percentage of negatively graded throws in the class. Sticks with his pre-snap read more often than not. Will throw with anticipation on “stick” throws outside the numbers. Posted the 12th-highest grade in the draft class on deep passes last season.
pff_bottom_line: There’s some boom-or-bust to Litton’s game, as he can make special downfield throws into tight windows, but there’s also far too many poor decisions and missed throws on his film. He put together three solid years of production at Marshall, but never took the necessary next step to improve his accuracy and decision-making. Litton is still worth a look late in the draft, but the negatives must be ironed out in order to tap into his potential.

pff_overview: One of the smallest corners in the entire draft, Maddox is just 5-foot-9 and 180 pounds, and that inherently limits his NFL market. Way more physical than his size would suggest, has big-time athleticism to try and claw back size disparity. Had 30 pass breakups over the past four seasons. Tended to be boom-or-bust, shutting down receivers entirely, or losing consistently in games. Will automatically be seen as a slot at the next level, but saw just 34 snaps inside in 2017, and six in 2016. Adds versatility on the blitz. Had six sacks over the last two seasons, closes and finishes well.
pff_bottom_line: Maddox is a player that is easy to root for. One of the most undersized players in the draft, he plays with an aggressive, feisty streak, but will be behind the eight ball to make an impact in the NFL. He has impressive athleticism and plays the ball well when he can see it coming but can struggle in man coverage with his back to the play. Blitz skills adds a string to his bow as a slot weapon, but that transition will be an unknown to negotiate.

pff_overview: Another player that was markedly better in 2016 than he was this last season, Worley took a major step back in coverage. Allowed a passer rating of 111.7 in 2017 having allowed one more than 50 points lower the season before (59.1). Was beaten for more than two yards per reception more in 2017 than the season before and allowed 78.1 percent of targets to be caught. Sure tackler with just four misses in 2017 from 70 attempts and only 16 misses in the last four years of play. Can read the play and flow to the run well, but struggles to deal with blockers or when in space in coverage. Likely a two-down player at the next level. Has special teams experience, with 55 snaps across multiple units in 2017 and 117 snaps
pff_bottom_line: In terms of on field production, Chris Worley’s NFL ceiling is pretty low, and likely capped to being a two-down linebacker and core special teamer at best. Special teams is an area that he does have extensive experience in, however, with 172 special teams snaps over the past two seasons and four special teams tackles. He struggles to contend with blockers in the run game and has been exposed in coverage, so he will have to hope to impress with his intangibles and special teams work.

pff_overview: Has graded well over the past two seasons of play for Alabama, but has now had back-to-back knee injuries that will hurt his draft stock. Grade and production took a major step backward in 2017 after his knee injury and he looked noticeably slower and less explosive. Has been limited to just 1,165 snaps on defense over his college career, which is less than some NFL linebackers played in 2017 alone. Smart linebacker who communicated consistently within the Alabama defense and was rarely out of place with his run fits. Is a little undersized, but previously offset that with speed and athleticism. Will need to get back to 100 percent to be as effective in the Is capable of both running around blockers at the second level or attacking them head on with good leverage and a violent hit.
pff_bottom_line: A reliable and versatile linebacker, Shaun Dion Hamilton is always in the right place on the field, but injuries have begun to threaten his NFL prospects and durability will be the biggest red flag he has to negotiate pre-draft. He has seen his season ended two years in a row by knee injuries, and was markedly less explosive an athlete in 2017 after the first of them. He may not be able to work out for teams before the draft due to a knee fracture, but could become a late- round steal if he can get back to 100 percent health.

pff_overview: Excellent range from deep safety. Multiple highlight-reel interceptions from single-high alignment. Changes direction extremely well. Lateral agility allows him to handle two-way go from quarters alignment. Could cover slot receivers. Allowed a passer rating of just 72.0 when covering the slot last season. Uses his agility to sidestep crack blocks in the run game. Not physical in the run game, but willing to mix it up. Missed 16 tackles on 143 career attempts. Run-stop percentage of 2.3 when lined up in the box ranked 86th in the draft class.
pff_bottom_line: Webb brings some versatility to the defense, but in a different way from other safeties. He may be the best pure single-high safety in the draft, as he moves efficiently and can make plays at the catch point, but his lateral agility also lends itself to covering slot receivers. He may never be great playing downhill or in the box, but as a free safety and chess piece against shifty slot receivers, Webb adds plenty of value.

pff_overview: Caught 55.9 percent of his deep targets, 14th-best in the nation. Ranked 7th in the nation with 326 yards in contested situations. Long frame and catch radius combines with excellent body control to create tape littered with incredible catches. Struggled during week of Senior Bowl practice, winning only 27 percent of 1-on-1 reps. Dropped 10 of 180 catchable targets in his two-year career. Provides little after the catch. Forced only six missed tackles on 99 career catches. Averaged only 2.8 yards after the catch per reception in career.
pff_bottom_line: Scott has plenty of outstanding plays on his tape, but he struggles to consis- tently create separation. His struggles were highlighted during the week at the Senior Bowl, but there’s still a role for Scott at the next level if paired with a quarterback willing to give him tight-window opportunities. His size, frame, and body control make him a viable red-zone threat, but his every-down value is a question mark.

pff_overview: Right tackle with the size to stay there at the NFL level. Four-year starter at right tackle who was one of the best pass protectors in country as junior and senior. Allowed 16 pressures in 2017. Plodder. Mirror ability is subpar and got out-quicked by even average college athletes on the edge. Proficient gaining depth and playing angles in pass protection. Smooth in and out of stance. Not an overly powerful tackle. Showed in run game, where he never graded too far above average. Locating linebackers in space looked like a chore. Athleticism leaves a lot to be desired. Rarely latches into defender’s shoulder pads and locks out. More often than not just leans on guys in run game.
pff_bottom_line: Crabtree may very well be capped out as far as his capabilities go. He lacks the requisite quickness to match NFL caliber athletes on the edge. Some of that could be alleviated by a move to guard, but his overall poor leverage makes that unlikely to be a much better fit.

pff_overview: A capable all-around back at Oregon State, Nall was a good receiver as well as ball carrier for the Beavers. Averaged 4.0 yards per carry after contact over his career. Led the nation in elusive rating in 2016, broke 54 tackles on 167 touches for a mark of 160.9. That rating fell off dramatically in 2017, as he was 45th in the draft class with a mark of just 45.7. Shows good vision, understanding of run concepts and the ability to find soft shoulders and space in tight quarters. Has nifty agility and athleticism but lacks immediate burst and acceleration to break angles and generate big plays.
pff_bottom_line: Nall was an impressively productive player in 2016 and gained almost 1,000 yards on just 147 carries and broke 47 tackles along the way. He saw more touches the following year but was significantly less dynamic with the ball in his hands. He does a lot of the little things well, but just lacks the eye-popping athleticism that tends to separate running backs at the next level. Given his size, may find himself being moved to fullback or H-back where his versatility will become an asset.

pff_overview: Three-year starter who graded out better every successive season of his college career. Waist bender. Gets himself in a lot of bad situations because of that and is easily knocked off balance. Strong hands that won’t let go once he’s locked on. Easily his biggest strength. Plays with hands low and wide. Very inconsistent with his punch and technique. Needs to add a good deal of strength to play in the NFL and it’s unclear if he’ll ever get there. Feet can be a nightmare in times in pass pro. All over the place.
pff_bottom_line: McDermott’s development has been encouraging, but he’s still some ways away from being an NFL tackle. He has the size of one, but not the strength or athlet- icism. He’ll have an uphill climb to ever start in the league and may ultimately be a guard.

pff_overview: Former walk on for a UAB team that were briefly disbanded, Williams had one of the best grades in the nation in 2017. Allowed a passer rating of just 38.9 when targeted in 2017, almost the same passer rating as just throwing the ball at the dirt every play. Allowed just 31.9 percent of passes thrown his way to be caught, one of the lowest marks in the nation from 69 targets. Surrendered four touchdowns, but picked off five passes and had 13 more pass breakups. Is a smaller corner, and doesn’t have blazing speed, so his future at the next level may be inside. Played just 46 snaps in the slot in 2017. 18 defensive stops was a top-15 mark in the draft class, earning him solid grades against the run despite small stature.
pff_bottom_line: A small-school corner who is also small in stature, everything is working against Darious Williams except his 2017 tape. He was exceptional at making plays on the ball and also coming up strong in the run game. His timed speed will be important if he wants to play outside at the next level, and strength of competition is a concern, though against Florida he was thrown at seven times and did not allow a catch and broke up two passes. An intriguing name to watch who may have to move to the slot in the NFL.

pff_overview: Has the zip to fire the ball into tight windows. Throws off balance far too often. Ranked 36th out of 37 draft-eligible quarterbacks at avoiding turnover- worthy plays last season. Had the No. 35 PFF grade on third and fourth down. Throws far too many ill-advised passes. Had the 2nd-highest percentage of turnover-worthy plays in the draft class. Posted the 10th-highest percentage of negatively graded throws in the draft class last season. Had his struggles at the Senior Bowl, with the lowest PFF grade during 1-on-1 and team drills.
pff_bottom_line: Lee catches the attention of scouts with good size and a solid arm, but there’s a lot of work to be done on the field. He fires far too many passes into coverage and his accuracy comes and goes. While the top-end plays are NFL caliber, Lee’s accuracy and decision-making are huge question marks and he’s a project at this stage in his development.

pff_overview: Knows how to leverage cornerbacks in order to create separation in short and intermediate game. Had nine drops on 158 catchable passes in his career. Forced 21 missed tackles on 149 career receptions. Averaged only 4.6 YAC/reception in his career. Good acceleration with the ball in his hands and coming out of his breaks. Attacks the ball in the air. Caught 44.4 percent of his contested targets and tied for the 8th-most contested targets in the nation with 36. Caught only 20.0 percent of his deep targets, tied for 260th in the nation.
pff_bottom_line: While Cantrell’s size and athleticism make him an intriguing receiver, his tape suggests he’s more of a possession receiver. He has some nuance to his route running and he uses his frame and strong hands to win at the catch point. Cantrell may never develop into a downfield threat, he has potential to work as a possession type while trying to tap into his athleticism and acceleration after the catch.

pff_overview: Grade was solid in 2017, but was fantastic the season before at 91.2, where he graded well in all facets and was phenomenal against the run. Misses too many tackles, with 11 in each of the past two seasons including more than one that led directly to touchdowns in 2017. Reads the play well, but can look a little stiff and unathletic as he makes his way to the ball. Has a tendency to be shifted too easily upon contact, particularly laterally – gets moved out of the lane he is filling with minor impact. Was suspended for violating team rules in 2017, which along with his big decline in play will be a concern for his prospects. Surrenders to a block too easily, allowing himself to be absorbed into contact rather than shedding the block.
pff_bottom_line: A season ago Stacy Thomas posted one of the best single-season grades we have seen from anybody in this draft class. He is 6-foot-1 and 240 pounds, but his 2017 tape was a significant blow to his NFL chances. It wasn’t bad, but it was significantly less impressive and highlighted far more of his shortcomings as a player. Could resuscitate his prospects if he can test well pre-draft, but otherwise has a lot working against him.

pff_overview: Extremely solid tackler despite slight frame, with just nine misses in his college career, and only three in 2017. Allowed an absurdly low passer rating of just 26.8 when targeted in 2017, surrendered only 12 catches all season. Those 12 catches though went for 237 yards and exposed him for losing out at the catch point, particularly to bigger receivers. Occasionally gets lost flicking his eyes between receiver and quarterback on the play, is quick to recover position. Has taken occasional snaps in the slot and at free safety and looked comfortable in either spot in addition to his perimeter snaps. Special teams grades are strong, and that will give him a road to quick playing time.
pff_bottom_line: Stroman is another lightweight corner in a draft that seems full of them, but his coverage numbers in 2017 are staggering. He allowed just 12 receptions all season, but they did include some significant big plays. His natural athleticism and understanding of angles will help him get on the field, and a refinement to his technique with the ball in the air could see him become a very good player in the NFL.

pff_overview: Ranked 2nd in the draft class with an adjusted completion percentage of 72.6 on intermediate (10-19 yard) throws. Ranked 10th in the draft class with a big-time throw percentage of 5.47. Forces too many throws. Ranked only 21st in the draft class at avoiding turnover-worthy plays at 3.91 percent. Ranked 3rd in the class with an adjusted completion percentage of 51.9 percent on deep passes and ranked 9th in deep passing grade. Good timing and feel for throwing the skinny post. Shows good touch to layer the ball over underneath zone defenders. Will stand in and take a hit in the pocket. Ranked 9th in the draft class in grade while under pressure last season. Has enough mobility to escape the pocket and make plays outside of structure.
pff_bottom_line: Woodside has two strong years of production under his belt and he’s worth a look in the late rounds. He can throw with touch and accuracy in the middle of the field and he has a number of pretty deep passes on film while also showing the willingness to hang in the pocket and make tough throws. That toughness gets the best of him sometimes and he has some poor decisions late in the down and under pressure, but Woodside has the tools to be a solid backup at the next level.

pff_overview: Dropped only two of his 73 catchable passes in 2017. Only dropped 10 passes on 245 catchable targets in his four-year career. Caught only 34.8 percent of contested targets. Caught 43.5 percent of his deep targets last season, tied for 75th in the nation. Many of his downfield plays were manufactured by scheme. Inconsistent getting off press coverage. Will flash good footwork, but still gets tied up with cornerbacks far too often. Lacks great straight-line speed. Forced 40 missed tackles on 235 career catches.
pff_bottom_line: There’s not much that stands out as special to Phillips’ game. He’s not a burner, inconsistent at getting off press coverage, and below-average in contested situations. However, he did improve every year at Virginia Tech and he’s sure-handed, and there are enough intriguing plays on tape to warrant a look in the late rounds. Right now, Phillips is more in line with a backup receiver capable of producing in the possession game.

pff_overview: Runs a good hitch-and-go. Accelerates out of his break and regularly created downfield separation. Rounds his breaks at the top of horizontal routes. Caught only 25.9 percent of his deep targets in 2017, well below his 47.4 percent mark in 2016 (30th in nation). Will go up and make impressive catches in tight coverage, but also allows far too many to get into his body and be broken up. Caught only 28 percent of his contested catch opportunities (7-for-25). Dropped 12 of his 88 catchable targets in his career. Averaged 7.5 YAC/reception in his career, including a 10.5 mark in 2016. Shows the willingness and toughness to make catches over the middle of the field.
pff_bottom_line: Weah’s career contains high-level flashes, but it lacks consistency. He can be a vertical threat with his size and straight-line speed, though he doesn’t create separation on the entire route tree. He shows the toughness to win in the con- tested game and over the middle, but there are still too many plays in which he lets the defenders get back into the play. Weah’s size and big play ability make him an intriguing developmental receiver.

pff_overview: Ranked 3rd among draft-eligible tight ends with 1.93 yards per route. Caught seven deep passes in 2017, tied for 4th among FBS tight ends. Good speed and quickness as a route runner. Has the speed to stretch the seam. Caught only 3-of-10 contested targets. Works hard in the run game. Can sustain second-level blocks. Can locate and lock onto targets as a run blocker. Had an excellent showing during the week of Senior Bowl practice. Dropped 10 of 93 catchable targets in his career. Gets to top speed quickly after the catch. Averaged 6.4 YAC/reception during his four-year career.
pff_bottom_line: Akins is one of the more athletic tight ends in the draft, as he has the speed to stretch the field and do damage after the catch. He also shows the quickness to separate at the short and intermediate levels, making him a viable pass threat. Like most college tight ends, blocking is not a strength, but he’s not afraid to mix it up and he can do damage on linebackers at the second level. Akins has potential to be one of the better pass-catchers in the class.

pff_overview: Has the size and length that NFL teams are chasing, standing 6-foot-2, but is light and lanky in build. Inconsistent play at South Carolina, having some elite shutdown games and others where he struggled. Allowed a passer rating of 72.1 when thrown at in 2017, allowing 51.8 percent of the passes thrown his way to be caught. Was not beaten for a reception longer than 38 yards, but surrendered three toucdowns. Played at the Senior Bowl, where he struggled badly during the week of practice and gave up a 63-yard reception in the game itself. Allowed 70-plus yards in a single game four times in 2017, including back to back games to begin the season.
pff_bottom_line: A long cornerback with ideal NFL height and length, JaMarcus King is never- theless a little underweight and has struggled for extended periods overall. At the Senior Bowl he was badly exploited in coverage during the week of prac- tices, being beaten routinely in 1-on-1 drills before giving up a big play in the game itself. Can look a little lost within the defense at times and not always sure of what he is doing, but the measurable profile could get him looked at a little longer than if he were a few inches shorter.

pff_overview: Undersized college tackle who will likely have to move inside at the next level. False steps in pass protection often. Will need to be completely revamped. Relies on his athleticism at the moment. Slow out of his stance consistently. Will get stood up consistently by NFL edge defenders if he doesn’t fix – especially inside. Thick build through his lower half. Has the frame that could add weight and strength fairly easily. Great lower body drive in the run game. Feet never stop moving. Looks like an athlete out in space. Can locate linebackers at the second level well.
pff_bottom_line: Allen is very much a late-round project at this point. Technically he is nowhere near ready to play in the league, but his athleticism and production are in- triguing. He’s so far away at the moment that his best bet may be to develop on a practice squad.

pff_overview: Improved his PFF coverage grade in each season of his college career Had two very ugly games in 2017, but otherwise his season was consistently very good. Allowed 15 touchdowns over the past three seasons, including four in Can be a horrendous tackler in open space when closing towards a ball- carrier, sliding off contact easily. Missed three tackles in a single game multiple times in 2017 alone. Had 14 pass breakups in 2017, four more than his previous two years combined.
pff_bottom_line: Springs has some impressive coverage tape, particularly this past season at Oregon, but there are concerns too. He misses too many tackles in space, and when he misses they tend to be complete whiffs, to go along with the occa- sional rough day in coverage. There is talent there, and he answered questions about his speed at Oregon’s pro-day, but he may be a candidate to move inside to the slot in the NFL, and needs to improve his consistency.

pff_overview: Four seasons of solid grades at Southern Miss, Smith has graded well in all facets of the game, though some more consistently than others. Rushing grade has been his most consistent strength, but at 5-foot-9 and under 200 pounds, his NFL future is likely tied more to the pass game. Shows the ability to make people miss in a phonebooth, breaking 188 tackles in his college career on 829 carries. Averaged 3.1 yards per carry after contact over his college career, and had runs of over 75 yards in each of the last three seasons. Flashed talent at the Senior Bowl and did not drop a pass in 1-on-1 drills during the week of practice. Did not allow a sack across 88 pass-blocking snaps. His pass-blocking efficiency score of 96.6 was 15th in the draft class. Strength of competition will be an issue in projecting Smith, hot on the heels of former teammate WR Mike Thomas struggling in the NFL.
pff_bottom_line: Ito Smith has been a fun player to watch in college and has always been capable of making spectacular plays. He is a relatively small back, but he has quickness and the natural ability to make people miss in tight spaces. His acceleration and burst are good, but top speed may be an issue. At his size and ability, he could quickly become a weapon on third downs, but receiving has been the less consistent aspect of his college play. Strength of competition will be a concern for some, but he more than held his own during the Senior Bowl.

pff_overview: Stands just 5-foot-7 and weighs around 200 pounds, so is a very undersized back, but one with special numbers in places. Broke 51 total tackles on 199 touches from scrimmage in 2017, earning an elusive rating of 99.1, the third-best in the draft class. Averaged 3.9 yards per carry after contact despite small size. Had 17 runs of 15-plus yards from only 178 attempts. Playing time and workload more than doubled in 2017, causing his grade to go through the roof. Had the 3rd-best overall grade in the class (89.5). Pass protected 98 times in 2017. Has extensive experience blocking against the blitz, but has not excelled in that area. Had mixed results against SEC competition in 2017, gaining over 100 yards against Mississippi State but just 17 against South Carolina.
pff_bottom_line: Boston Scott is one of the most interesting prospects in the entire 2017 draft. He is short and undersized, but has made special plays and had the third-best overall grade in the draft class among all backs in 2017. His workload and playing time increased in each of the past two seasons after being a walk-on at Louisiana Tech, causing an explosion in production this year. Scott has excep- tional quickness and the ability to make plays on the ground and as a receiver, but will likely need to find a role in the NFL given his size.

pff_overview: Can get turned around when isolated 1-on-1. Overcommits to the outside. Can get stuck in the mud vs. two-way go. Stays on top of routes well from free safety role. Tracks the ball well. Tied for 14th in the nation with six pass breakups last season. Left a few interceptions on the table last season. Excellent at reading the quarterback and reacting accordingly. Only one strong year of production at Wisconsin. Played 1,186 career snaps. Good movement skills. Takes good routes to the quarterback on blitzes, has some wiggle after the catch on interceptions. Missed only seven tackles on 76 career attempts. Not a heavy hitter in the run game, but plays balanced and under control.
pff_bottom_line: While Jamerson moves well, he struggles when isolated against more nuanced route runners. He made a number of fine plays from deep safety last season and he has potential in both split and single-high looks. Quarters teams may not want him isolated on receivers and tight ends all that often, but he does his best work with his eyes on the quarterback and breaking on the ball.

pff_overview: Hard nosed downhill thumper at linebacker who was PFF’s top graded linebacker in the draft class in 2017 thanks to his run defense. Had 53 defensive stops this season, with 79 solo tackles and 35 assists. Played at the Senior Bowl and struggled in coverage during 1-on-1 drills. Saw just one rep in pass-rush drills but won that rep. Had a relatively anonymous outing in the game itself, posting an average grade and just one tackle from 30 snaps for the North team. Struggles to change direction in space and may be athletically short of the NFL standard to convert his college production to the next level. Shows the ability to play strong in tight spaces, shucking off blocks and forcing cuts from running backs behind the line.
pff_bottom_line: Ja’Whaun Bentley had an exceptional PFF grade this season, which came almost entirely in the run game where he was a consistent hammer. He is no- ticeably stiff in his movements and will struggle to play in space against more fluid athletes, but when he has the opportunity to operate in tight quarters he can deliver hits and work through contact to find the ball carrier and impact the run game. Struggled at the Senior Bowl in coverage and was anonymous in the game, suggesting that a step up in competition and athlete may cause problems.

pff_overview: Throws with good touch down the field. Ranked No. 4 in the draft class in PFF grade on deep passes last season. Had the No. 11 grade in the draft class on intermediate throws. Doesn’t have great zip, but can throw with timing and accuracy outside the numbers. Had the 3rd-lowest percentage of turnover-worthy plays in the draft class. Many of his turnover-worthy throws came on ill-advised throws to underneath linebackers. Willing to stand in there and take a hit under pressure and that works both for and against him. Had the 25th-highest PFF grade when facing pressure last season. Ranked only 32nd in the draft-class in positively graded throws, but had the 2nd-lowest percentage of negatively graded throws.
pff_bottom_line: Silvers doesn’t wow with physical tools, but he’s an efficient quarterback ca- pable of winning with timing and accuracy. He landed on the game-manager spectrum, even in college, so that likely limits what he can do at the next level. He makes up for average arm strength with quick decision-making and timing, and there may be a backup role waiting for him at the next level.

pff_overview: A big, bruising back, Richard plays with good strength and fight in his runs to get through traffic. Broke 27 tackles on 185 carries in 2017, averaged 2.9 yards per carry after contact and gained 537 of his 977 rushing yards after getting hit. Saw 100 targets over his college career, but that number went down in each of the past two seasons, as did his playing time. Had six drops in 2015 on 45 targets, but hasn’t dropped a pass since as his involvement has been dialled back. Allowed three sacks over the past two seasons as a pass protector, failing to take advantage of his size and strength. Running can lack sophistication at times, and he can be very quick to just lower his head and try to run over defenders rather than find space.
pff_bottom_line: Demario Richard is a big, stocky back with an incredibly solid build who attempts to win at the point of attack with blunt force trauma. He runs with good physicality and effort but lacks nuance to his play and doesn’t have the athletic gifts to scare defenders. He has experience in the passing game, but drops and poor pass protection saw that scaled back during his college career, so it is unlikely to be a strength in the NFL, leaving him as a two-down role player with good but not spectacular production.

pff_overview: Tracks the ball well in the air. Adjusts to throws. Physical at the catch point. Uses his hands to separate at the top of routes. Shows good toughness catching the ball over the middle of the field. Caught 50 percent of his contested catch opportunities (15-for-30). Good vision and feel after the catch. Averaged 5.1 YAC/reception in this three years. Attacks the ball in the air. Dropped 11 passes on 128 catchable career targets. Caught only 39.3 of his deep targets in 2017, tied for 109th in the nation.
pff_bottom_line: Grayson has only one year of strong production and grading, but he did a fine job last year showing physicality with the ball in the air and after the catch. He doesn’t have the speed to challenge cornerbacks down the field but could develop into a useful possession receiver with his ability to catch the ball in traffic and adjust to back-shoulder throws.

beast_summary: A one-year starter at Oklahoma, Murray had a rough start to his college football career at Texas A&M and all signs pointed to him playing professional baseball, but he put together a special 2018 season for the Sooners. He became the first FBS player to average at least 300 passing yards (311.5) and 60 rushing yards (71.5) per game for a full season, joining Clemson’s Deshaun Watson as the only players to ever record at least 4,000 passing yards and 1,000 rushing yards in a season. In the Sooners zone-read scheme, Murray was primarily in shotgun/pistol and benefited from the best offensive line in college football. There is no question that he is a pass-first quarterback, but his speed creates problems for the defense and he is ideally suited for an offense willing to incorporate a high percentage of sprints, boots and option plays. Regardless if throwing on the move or with an established base, Murray has an organic feel for using ball speeds to put the pass on his target, showing above-average velocity and accuracy. With only one season of production (in a conference with below-average defensive talent), he is still developing mentally with his reads/timing and his lack of size will always be a concern. Overall, Murray, who is incredibly unique with a skill-set unlike anything currently in the NFL, has the arm talent and playmaking instincts that translate to any level, projecting as an NFL starter.
beast_strengths: Boasts a whip of an arm with the velocity to deliver lasers…quick release, using various arm angles…naturally accurate, regardless if throwing with a firm base or off-platform…throws a catchable ball and his passes arrive with touch…on-target deep ball, dropping the ball over coverage and in the bucket…dynamic athlete with instant speed…sudden feet in the pocket to elude rushers…patient behind the line of scrimmage with innate instincts to sense pressure, falling back on his athleticism only when necessary…confident competitor and small window throws don’t intimidate him…incredibly productive 2018 season, leading the nation in total yards (school record 5,362), points responsible (342), yards per completion (16.8) and yards per pass attempt (FBS record 11.6).
beast_weaknesses: Undersized – short and lacks ideal bulk on his frame…stares down receivers and needs to be quicker eliminating things mid-read…inefficient progressions disrupt route timing…doesn’t always locate all 11 defenders…ball placement is above-average, but there is room for improvement (throwing to the correct shoulder, away from trouble, etc.)…holds the ball like a briefcase when scrambling and ball security needs improvement…unproven bouncing back from physical hits and durability concerns will always be there due to his size and lack of body armor…needs to prove that he has the maturity for the NFL – suspended the opening drive vs. Baylor (September 2018) for being late to practice…baseball will always be a fallback option for him…only one season of high-level production.

beast_summary: A two-year starter at Ohio State, Bosa rushed off the left and right edges in the Buckeyes’ four-man front where he was coached by revered defensive line coach Larry Johnson. After an All-American sophomore season, he entered the 2018 season as the No. 1 draft-eligible player in college football, but underwent surgery in September for his groin and abdominal injury (he was expected to recover by early December, but elected to leave the team and work toward the NFL). Durability is the main concern for his NFL projection, but when on the field, Bosa uses proper biomechanics to maximize his body force and convert speed-to-power as a rusher. The opportunity to watch and learn from his Pro Bowl older brother accelerated his development, both showing the same appreciation for the art of the pass rush. Overall, Bosa is a carbon copy of Joey Bosa with his blend of athleticism and violent hands, gaining ground and defeating blocks in a variety of ways to make an impact rushing the passer and stopping the run.
beast_strengths: Launches low and balanced out of his stance…gains considerable ground with first step, immediately putting blockers on their heels…enough bend to run the hoop…coordinated weight transfer with his loose hips and lateral quicks…diverse, well-timed hand tactics…aggressive rush attack, but more importantly there is nuance to his hand sequence…outstanding play violence to work his way through bodies…heavy hands to stack and set the edge vs. power…matured, limber body type…tough-minded and has no trouble doing the dirty work…close-knit football bloodlines and an NFL locker room will be a natural fit for his personality…productive when on the field with 29.0 tackles for loss and 17.5 sacks in 30 career games.
beast_weaknesses: Prefers to use forward lean mid-rush, occasionally ending up on the ground…lacks sudden redirection skills outside of his pass rush and can be a tick late reacting to backfield misdirection…doesn’t have the core strength to bully in the run game and tight ends can catch him off-guard, putting him on his back…troubling injury history as he tried to push through groin and abdomen issues during the first three games of 2018 before re-aggravating those injuries vs. TCU (September 2018), requiring season-ending bilateral abdominal surgery; he suffered a “slight ACL tear” in his right knee (November 2015) as a senior in high school and required surgery, which prematurely ended his high school career; the injury history of his father and older brother will be weighed differently by each club.

beast_summary: A one-year starter at Alabama, Williams was a defensive end in 2017, but with DaRon Payne leaving for the NFL, he identified nose guard as his best chance to get on the field, adding 25 pounds and emerging as a dominant player in 2018. He finished the season top-10 in the FBS and second in the SEC with 19.5 tackles for loss and didn’t have an “off” game. With his snap quickness and handwork, Williams has a natural feel for defeating blocks and his teammate Jonah Williams hit the nail on the head when he described facing Williams as trying to block a “300-pound bar of soap.” He is a power-packed player from head-to-toe, competing with the violence, hustle and awareness to be an elite run defender. Overall, Williams was not only blessed with a complete skill-set (explosive, strong and intelligent), but he also has the rare ability to use all his gifts in unison, projecting as an immediate NFL starter with All-Pro potential.
beast_strengths: Explosive get-off to immediately reset the line of scrimmage…controlled, cat-like quickness to win off the snap, redirect or close in short-areas…lateral agility and clean weight transfer as a pass rusher…uses a variety of swipes, rips and club moves to break the rhythm of blockers…naturally powerful and creates surge with his upper body…produces knockback and steers blockers where he wants…uniquely skilled at keeping blockers off him, using hand tactics and length…holds the point-of-attack and doesn’t get moved…understands gap leverage and how to exploit it…comfortable two-gapping and handling double-teams…above-average ball awareness…sees through blocks and reacts to the ball, not the blocking scheme…accountable and “exemplifies all the things I talk about” on and off the field, according to Alabama head coach Nick Saban…works his tail off and owns a genuine love for the game…All-American 2018 season. [136]
beast_weaknesses: Doughy body type and would benefit from added bulk…only average arm length…occasionally finds himself out of control mid-rush, leading to missed tackles…only one season of production at the college level.

beast_summary: A three-year starter at Kentucky, Allen was a hybrid outside linebacker in the Wildcats’ 3-4 base, lining up off the edge (boundary and field) and over inside receivers in the slot. After his junior year, he was considered a potential top-100 draft pick, but he returned for his senior season and improved physically and technically, which resulted in one of the best individual seasons in Kentucky history – the 2018 hire of outside linebackers coach (now defensive coordinator) Brad White, who spent the previous six seasons with the Indianapolis Colts, also aided Allen’s development. Although not an overpowering power rusher, Allen showed improved play strength and added to his pass rush tool box on his senior tape, consistently forcing the quarterback to speed up his process. As a cover defender, he has the smooth hips and play speed to cover a lot of ground, but needs to improve his ball awareness to be more reliable in man coverage. Overall, Allen transformed himself from a versatile athlete into a polished pass rusher who fits best in a 3-4 scheme where he can make plays upfield or when dropping in space, projecting as an immediate NFL starter with Pro Bowl potential. [113]
beast_strengths: Excellent first step to win the corner with a simple speed rush…expanded his pass rush repertoire each season at Kentucky…long-armed frame with a large wingspan and developed muscle tone (added 50-plus pounds since arriving at Kentucky, including 20 pounds between his junior and senior seasons)…forces holding penalties with his ability to work through the shoulder of blockers…plays with closing burst to close the gap in pursuit…loose athlete in space…stays stride- for-stride with backs and tight ends in coverage…intelligent, alert player to see plays develop pre-snap…voted a team captain in 2018…performance doesn’t fall off late in games (13 of his 17 sacks in 2018 came in the second half)…holds the school records for sacks in a single season (17.0) and career (31.5) – his career sack total ranks ninth-best in SEC history, just a half sack behind Reggie White (32)…he is tied with Danny Trevathan for the school record in career forced fumbles (11).
beast_weaknesses: Not heavy-handed at the point of attack…late to disengage from offensive linemen once locked up…pass rush moves tend to be predictable based on situation…plays loose, but lacks twitch when quickly changing direction…needs to improve his contain responsibilities vs. the run…better cover athleticism than cover instincts, especially with his back to the ball.

beast_summary: A three-year starter at Houston, Oliver was one of college football’s most disruptive players over the last three years, spending most of his time at nose tackle for the Cougars. With his football flexibility and natural biomechanics, he has rare athletic ability for the position with the backfield vision to recognize play designs and disrupt from different angles. Oliver still requires time to develop his body, mind and technique at the next level. He will struggle with long-armed blockers who get to his frame and control his chest, but his energy and motor are both elite. Overall, Oliver won’t be a natural fit for every NFL scheme, but he is an ideal one-gap penetrator due to his athleticism, instincts and relentless nature, projecting best when he is lined up closest to the football.
beast_strengths: Fluid body control to wriggle off blocks…excellent foot quickness and change of direction skills…shot out of a cannon with his first step…forces holding penalties due to his gap quickness…creates knockback with his speed-to-power skills…ball awareness to track through blocks…uses natural leverage to stay underneath the pads of blockers…better than expected play strength as a run defender…highly aggressive motor and effort never wanes, chasing down plays near the sidelines…dominated from the moment he stepped onto campus and leaves as a three-time All-American, collecting 54.0 tackles for loss over 33 career starts.
beast_weaknesses: Lacks desired frame and length…needs to continue and develop his body and stay in the 280-285 pound range (weighed 274 for most of his final season at Houston)…relied more on motor than brute power to overwhelm blockers in college…not a bull rusher…undeveloped approach with his hands…below- average counter measures once locked up…faced inferior competition in the AAC…several immature moments in college, including an on-field altercation with head coach Major Applewhite regarding a coat issue on the sideline — Oliver has a “young attitude” and has “growing up to do,” according to an NFL scout…missed five games as a junior with a right knee bruise (November 2018) and was limited at the combine with a strained hamstring (February 2019).

beast_summary: A two-year starter at LSU, White played the “Rover” linebacker position in Dave Aranda’s 3-4 base scheme, lining up both inside and outside the tackles and playing on special teams coverages. He was the unquestioned leader of the defense and looked like an excited air traffic controller pre-snap, identifying keys and communicating with his teammates. A see-ball, get-ball type, White is raw instinctually and flies around like a mad man, which is his best and most concerning quality. Everything he does is full speed, which leads to violent hits, but also breakdown issues, falling off tackle attempts. Overall, White’s tape doesn’t show the same level of instincts or discipline as current Bears LB Roquan Smith, but his play speed and relentless nature are off-the-charts, projecting as an NFL starter similar to Jarrad Davis (drafted No. 21 overall to the Detroit Lions in the 2017 NFL Draft).
beast_strengths: Unlocks his speed and chases down ballcarriers…active motor expands his range and allows him to cover every inch of the field…plays with short-area explosion to redirect and slither through gaps near the line of scrimmage…loves to scrape-and-bang in the trenches…hungry tackler, starving for contact…competes with a violent edge and looks to tune up his target…shows timing and a closing burst as a blitzer…alpha type mentality and named a 2018 team captain (LSU DC Dave Aranda: “People listen to him and respect him...his passion shows both on and off the field”)…durable and started all but one game the last two seasons (didn’t start the 2018 Alabama game because he missed the first half due to a targeting ejection the week prior)…consistently productive, leading the SEC in tackles each of the last two seasons.
beast_weaknesses: Flies around the field without coming to balance, making tackles tougher than they need to be…loses his footing and takes false steps due to his crazed movements…undeveloped anticipation and needs to quicken his reads…needs to more efficiently use his hands to stay clean…needs to better identify targets in zone and develop a better feel for coverage…showed maturation at LSU and character isn’t considered a red flag, but was charged with two misdemeanors his senior year in high school — charged with “carnal knowledge” of a 14-year-old girl when he was 17 years old (November 2015); charged with “flight from an officer” (December 2015) after he received a speeding ticket and didn’t immediately pull over.

beast_summary: A one-year starter at Ohio State, Haskins was a questionable fit in the Buckeyes’ shotgun, option-heavy offense, but that didn’t slow his production. During his prolific 2018 season, he broke 28 school records and set seven Big Ten records, including single-season passing yards (4,831), touchdown passes (50) and total offensive yards (4,939). Haskins makes playing quarterback look easy because he is so naturally gifted, but his inexperience also shows. While he showed improvements climbing the pocket, maneuvering vs. pressure isn’t yet a strength to his game with inconsistent results throwing off-script. He has a plus arm to grip- and-rip, but he tends to telegraph throws, believing too much in his arm to compensate. His placement and touch have room for improvement, but his passing accuracy is a strength (off-target throws usually tied to messy footwork). Overall, Haskins’ pocket rhythm and lower body mechanics are the biggest concerns for his next level transition, but he showed promising improvement and his special arm has the potential to carve up pro defenses, projecting as an NFL starter with Pro Bowl upside.
beast_strengths: Special arm talent…long-levered, but has an efficient load-and-fire release with the ball exploding off his hand…unforced velocity to drive the ball to every inch of the field…throws receivers open with a natural feel for accuracy…large-framed, sturdy passer…sees the entire field and stands tall in the pocket to allow routes to develop…comfortable making high-to-low reads, resetting his eyes on the move…productive on throws 20-plus yards (45.6 percent completions, 14 touchdowns, one interception)…plays poised and confident, showing improved reaction to pressure as the season progressed…at his best in high-pressure situations, completing 71.4 percent of passes with 12.3 yards per attempt, four touchdown passes and zero interceptions in one-score situations in the fourth quarter…not a nimble athlete, but coordinated with his pocket movements…able to fire strikes on the move without sacrificing placement…remarkable production in 2018, becoming only the sixth FBS player to throw for 50 touchdowns in a single-season – his 54 career touchdown passes ranks fourth-best in Ohio State history.
beast_weaknesses: Outstanding fastball, but needs improved touch on layered throws to put the ball between levels of the defense…busy lower body, often throwing with a wide base or flat feet…bad habit of abandoning his base instead of stepping into the rush…pocket presence showed steady improvement, but he is still on the ground level…long, lean lower body, which works against him when attempting to evade pocket pressure…not a graceful scrambler and lacks creative mobility…guilty of staring down targets, forecasting throws to defenders with his big body and eyes…timing as a passer lacks sophistication, dumping it off too quickly or holding the ball too long…doesn’t break tackles and not a powerful finisher like his size suggests (more likely to brace for contact than lower his pads into contact)…only one season of starting experience.

beast_summary: A three-year starter at Florida, Taylor won the starting right tackle job as a true freshman and was a staple there for the Gators’ offense, also seeing snaps at left tackle. While he can be occasionally stressed by outside speed, he is controlled in his pass sets with enough foot quickness to be a human shield. Taylor tends to allow rushers into his frame due to undeveloped hand use, but he has the stout frame to survive as a body-to-body blocker. He generates power from his core in the run game and has a high ceiling as a point-of-attack bully. Overall, Taylor is not a technically sound blocker right now, but his contact balance and competitive finish are why he is one of the best run blockers in this class and one of the most promising in pass protection, projecting as an NFL starter at tackle or guard.
beast_strengths: Wide-framed and his 312 pounds is well-distributed…agile lower body and handles space well…flashes the reaction quickness to adjust on the fly…aggressive extension and heavy-handed to drive rushers wide of the pocket…shows the movement skills to execute combinations, climb and cut off pursuing linebackers…has the play strength to dominate in a phone booth…rolls his hips into contact with the upper body power to stun his target…blocks with a mean streak to overwhelm defenders…works hard to stay conditioned and keep his weight under control…starting experience at both tackle spots. [77]
beast_weaknesses: Late hands and wild placement…abandons his knee bend early in the block, putting his body posture in an upright alignment…straight-legged in pass protection…oversets outside and leaves his inside shoulder susceptible…choppy steps as a drive blocker and needs to clean up his technique…diagnosed with a “mild distal hamstring strain” (February 2019) and missed the scouting combine…sat out the first series of the 2018 season opener for “failing to meet expectations.”

beast_summary: A three-year starter at Alabama, Williams was a model of consistency over his tenure with the Tide, playing right tackle as a true freshman before moving to left tackle the past two seasons once Cam Robinson left for the NFL. While not on the same level as future Hall of Famer Joe Thomas, he overcomes his lack of ideal length in similar ways, including his ability to make split-second reads, quickly find his landmarks and stay square to rushers. Aside from his on-field ability, Williams will win over an NFL coaching staff because he is a tactician with intense work habits and competitive desire. While his college film says he can play left tackle at the next level, his lack of length will push him to guard or center on some NFL draft boards. Overall, Williams is a detail-focused blocker with the foot quickness, technical savvy and attitude to be an above-average run blocker and pass protector in the NFL.
beast_strengths: Plays low and controlled…agile feet and natural knee bend in his kick slide, gaining proper depth…technically sound hands and body posture…drops his lower body to anchor vs. power…generates torque from his hips and runs his feet to move bodies in the run game…controls and forklifts defenders at the second level…very alert player to quickly react and reset…his coaches call him “The Intellectual” because of his detailed preparation and intelligence…eager blocker through the whistle, always looking for the kill shot…natural-born competitor with a goal-oriented mindset…perfectionist attitude in the weight room…graduated with his marketing degree (December 2018) in less than three years…started every game the past three seasons (44 straight starts), spending time at both left and right tackle.
beast_weaknesses: Not physically imposing…shorter-than-ideal arm length and extension…long-armed rushers give him trouble…caught leaning into blocks and ends up on the ground…bull rushers will get him when he allows his base to narrow…doesn’t have starting experience inside at guard or center…outplayed by Clemson edge rusher Clelin Ferrell in his final collegiate game. [76]

beast_summary: A two-year starter at Iowa, Hockenson paired with Noah Fant to form the best tight end duo in college football, lining up inline and slot in the Hawkeyes’ pro-style scheme. He became the second tight end in school history with 750-plus receiving yards in a season and joined Dallas Clark as the only Hawkeyes to win the Mackey Award as the nation’s top tight end. Despite not blocking in high school, Hockenson has developed into an elite blocker with the functional strength and competitive spirit to physically overwhelm defenders at the point of attack. Although he would benefit from added nuance as a route runner, his basketball background is obvious with the agility and catch radius to be an impact weapon downfield. Overall, Hockenson has a complete skill set for the position with outstanding athleticism, pass-catching traits and blocking skills, projecting as an immediate NFL starter with Pro Bowl potential.
beast_strengths: Above-average athleticism…natural pass-catching abilities with his body control, reflexes and hand-eye coordination…reliable hands…clean releases off the line of scrimmage…sticks his foot in the ground and accelerates off his plant to press defenders off the route…finds the sticks and achieves proper depth in his patterns…legitimate downfield threat (averaged 11.5 yards per target in 2018)…ambitious after the catch, flashing tackle-breaking skills (seven catches of 30-plus yards in 2018)…outstanding finisher as a blocker…latches, runs his feet and drives his target off the screen…competitive appetite and wired right for the pro game…productive and durable career in Iowa City.
beast_weaknesses: Doesn’t have ideal size and bulk for the position…overeager at times as a blocker and can get tossed when he arrives off-balance…bad habit of ducking his head into initial contact…tends to rush his routes at times and needs to better set up sitting defenders.

beast_summary: A two-year starter at Mississippi State, Sweat rushed from a two- and three-point stance as the field defensive end in the Bulldogs’ four-man front. Since the start of 2017, his 22 sacks are the second-most by any power-five FBS player during that span (Josh Allen), forming a dominant defensive line duo with Jeffery Simmons (they combined for 58.5 tackles for loss the last two seasons). Sweat wins with first step burst and humongous wingspan, although there is room for better efficiency in his pass rush sequence. Overall, Sweat has average play strength and some stiffness in his rush, but he maximizes his length, both his arms and strides, to consistently threaten blockers off the edge, projecting as an NFL starter in either a 3-4 or 4-3 scheme.
beast_strengths: NFL frame and length…light-footed out of his stance with long strides to quickly eat up grass…core flexibility to lean and maintain his balance…forceful long-arm and introduces various inside/outside moves to keep blockers guessing…improved run awareness and play identification…able to retrace and find the ball…efficient changing directions when tracking the run…comfortable on his feet, dropping in space and covering ground with his long strides…emotional player and not afraid to throw the first punch…effort sustains all four quarters…reached double-digit sacks in both of his seasons in the SEC.
beast_weaknesses: Lean-muscled and lacks ideal bulk on his limbs…questionable growth potential…stiff turning the corner and lacks bend at the top of his rush…needs to play stronger and develop bully tendencies to power through blocks…too often finds himself upfield past the quarterback…flashes pop, but initial hand work still in the development phase…plays tall and rigid once engaged…doesn’t have a great feel in coverage…mysteriously didn’t have any pass break ups in his career despite his length…background requires careful vetting after he spent the majority of his two-year tenure at Michigan State in the coach’s doghouse due to repeated issues …diagnosed with a heart condition at the Scouting Combine, which will require regular check-ups, though it is considered a “low-risk” condition.

beast_summary: A four-year starter at Missouri, Lock was a natural fit in the Tigers’ shotgun, RPO-style offense with an emphasis on vertical option routes, spending two years (2016-17) under the tutelage of Josh Heupel and one season (2018) with offensive coordinator Derek Dooley. He finished his career second in SEC history in passing yards (12,193) and third in touchdown passes (99). Very similar to Derek Carr coming out of Fresno State, Lock is a classic arm thrower who stubbornly believes that every throw is there, but is still figuring out how to use his eyes and piece together his timing. He showed expanded vision as a senior and appeared to eliminate things quicker mid-read. Overall, Lock showcases a live arm and the makeup required to be an NFL starter, but he needs to continue developing his accuracy, mechanics and decision-making to live up to his intriguing potential.
beast_strengths: Blessed with a golden arm and easy velocity…football explodes coming out of his hand with a quick, compact release…easily adjusts his arm angles without sacrificing ball speed…coordinated, quick-footed athlete, using his mobility to move the pocket or pick up chunk yards…NFL frame with room to add more bulk…timing/patience to allow routes to develop…trusts his arm talent to make tight-window and “faith” throws…matured football intelligence and hunger for the game…three-year team captain and handles himself with a calm, commanding presence…productive resume and starting experience.
beast_weaknesses: Inconsistent intermediate touch and downfield accuracy…quick to abandon his mechanics and rely on his arm to compensate, leading to erratic placement…cluttered footwork under pressure, often backpedaling to evade…locks onto his preferred target and needs to mature his eye use and vision…too willing to test heavy coverage, making it tough to trust his decision-making…effectiveness plummets when the design of the play breaks down and doesn’t fully use his athleticism to extend plays…small hands and ball security needs to improve when scrambling, as he holds the football away from his body like a dirty diaper (six fumbles in 2018)…owns a 21-25 record (.457) as a collegiate starter, including an 11-20 record (.355) in SEC play and 1-9 record (.100) vs. ranked opponents.

beast_summary: A two-year starter at Michigan, Gary was exclusively a hand-on-the-ground edge rusher in the Wolverines’ four-man front, occasionally lining up over or inside the tackle. His talent was clear the moment he stepped foot in Ann Arbor, but his production and body of work didn’t consistently match the hype — eight pass rushers in the 2019 NFL Draft class had more sacks in 2018 than Gary had his entire career (10.5). He is the poster prospect for the “traits over production” scouting motto with his freakish athletic skill and overall upside. He currently lacks an efficient move-to-move transition and I often found myself yelling “finish!” at the screen while studying his tape. Overall, Gary is a high risk, high reward prospect because he has rare athletic talent and natural power for his size, but he showed mediocre development in college with lingering questions about his durability and maturity.
beast_strengths: Gifted athlete for his size…flashes the explosive quickness and light feet of a much smaller player…flexible body type with oily hips to smoothly change directions…rare range…plays with low, balanced pad level…wins the corner with powerful strides…violent hands and effective long-arm move…physical edge setter…uses his length to lock out, shed and pursue…accustomed to dealing with chips, double-teams and extra attention…improved discipline to stay home and read the quarterback…competes with urgency…wants to be a leader and not shy joking around or pushing teammates.
beast_weaknesses: Undeveloped pass rush plan and doesn’t set up his moves…hand placement lacks refinement, with too much time hand fighting…streaky snap timing…duck-footed gait and too easily tripped up…needs to lose some baby fat…NFL scouts have concerns about his emotional maturity and ability to play with composure…inconsistent finisher with below-average college production…suffered several minor injuries his first two seasons in Ann Arbor; injured his right shoulder prior to the 2018 season and tried to play through it, missing three games (October 2018).

beast_summary: A two-year starter at Michigan, Bush played inside and outside linebacker in Don Brown’s base 4-2-5 defense and was called the “glue” of the scheme, according to his coaches. He grew up around the game and has a special father-son bond, which has helped mold his football-focused mindset. Bush checks boxes for speed, instincts and tenacity, but he falls slightly below-average in the size department, which will be critiqued differently by each NFL club and system. He will get washed and lost in the sea of bodies near the line of scrimmage, but there is no doubting his toughness, football character and competitive drive (and it isn’t manufactured — he has a genuine energy and enjoyment for hunting the football and playing physical). Overall, Bush doesn’t have ideal take-on skills to thrive inside as a MIKE, but his ability to diagnose, his reaction quickness and his closing speed are special, projecting best as an impact starting WILL in the NFL.
beast_strengths: Above-average speed and lateral range to mirror…elite level reaction quickness due to his instincts and athleticism…displays the range to cover quick screens and flat routes…controls himself well on the move, settling his feet and squaring up his target…fills gaps like a much bigger player, physically taking on lead blocks — doesn’t have the size of a thumper, but that doesn’t stop him from trying to thump…strikes with violence and wraps as a tackler…understands field leverage and pursuit angles…quick to diagnose coverage and find passing lanes…outstanding blitzer with his bend and closing burst…disciplined off the field and passionate on the field, giving 100% effort on every down (Michigan defensive coordinator Don Brown: “This guy is special…plays with a chip on his shoulder and can flat out fly.”)…voted a team captain in 2018.
beast_weaknesses: Undersized and lack of ideal length shows up often on tape…struggles to disengage once locked up…climbing blockers too easily eliminate him from plays…lack of inches leads to broken tackles…knocked around when working downhill in the trenches…will attempt to run around blockers instead of using his hands…room to improve his strike zone as a tackler to avoid hits above the shoulders…competitiveness can go too far at times (i.e. when he scuffed up the Michigan State logo with his cleats after a pregame spat in October, 2018).

beast_summary: A two-year starter at Florida State, Burns lined up primarily with his hand on the ground at field defensive end for the Seminoles. Despite a disappointing 5-7 record in 2018, which snapped FSU’s 36-year bowl-eligible streak, he stayed motivated and set career-bests in tackles, tackles for loss and sacks as a junior. Burns is a loose-jointed athlete with above-average speed off the edge, also showing the agility to drop in space or defend the run. He flashes a variety of pass rush moves, but tends to be over-reliant on his athleticism and needs to develop his timing and set-up skills. Overall, Burns needs to continue to get stronger and sharpen his toolset, but his first step explosion, athletic flexibility and baseline understanding of how to use his length/hands are a recipe for an impact NFL pass rusher, regardless of scheme.
beast_strengths: Twitchy get-off and lateral movements…runs the arc with speed…natural body control to capture the corner and flatten to the quarterback…angular body type with long arms to stab or club-rip blockers…plays with bend and skillfully regains his balance mid-rush…able to change directions with little wasted movement…displays the foot agility and long strides to cover ground and play in space…uses his length to find passing lanes…blocked three kicks over his career…voted a team captain in 2018 and his FSU coaches call him a “humble hustler” who gives “consistent effort” in practice…started every game the past two seasons and played through injuries…his 24.0 career sacks rank fifth in school history.
beast_weaknesses: Lanky limbed athlete and lacks ideal bulk on his frame…questionable max weight…not a power player and can be controlled on the edge (see 2018 Northern Illinois tape)…leaves his chest open and his hand/punch timing requires refinement…hands tend to wander, lacking disciplined counters…prefers to run the arc and needs to develop his inside moves...not much of a talker and is developing his leadership skills. [114]

beast_summary: A three-year starter at Washington State, Dillard played in a two-point stance at left tackle in Mike Leach’s air-raid offense, taking over from another three-year starter (Joe Dahl). With wide splits and a quick-strike passing attack, it can be tough to evaluate offensive linemen in WSU’s offense, but Dillard was dominant over his career (allowed only one sack in 2018) and is the highest-graded senior offensive lineman in this class. There are times when he looks defenseless vs. long-armed linemen, but he plays smooth, intellectually sound and will be even better once he improves his hand placement and reach timing. Overall, Dillard is a better pass protector than run blocker right now, but he is a quick-minded player with the light feet and core power to play multiple positions in the NFL, including left tackle.
beast_strengths: Compact build with an adequate frame for the position…balanced feet with lower body flexibility…hands and feet stay in sync in his pass sets…able to bend, redirect and move smoothly as a puller…aggressive with his reach to initiate contact, using a violent swipe to knock down hands…plays with the core strength to control the edge…processes everything well and doesn’t panic…graduated with a degree in social science…added 60-plus pounds since enrolling as a skinny 240- pounder…durable and started all 39 games the past three seasons.
beast_weaknesses: Inconsistent punch timing, and long-levered rushers can reach his chest…his struggles with length also show in the run game, causing him to overextend…needs to better use his hips and leverage as a run blocker…needs to show better finish and sustain skills…scouts want to see more of a mean streak in his game…looks clean pulling but doesn’t always hit his target.

beast_summary: A three-year starter at Clemson, Wilkins worked his way into the defensive line rotation as a true freshman and was a key reason behind the Tigers’ two national titles the last three seasons. Lining up primarily over the B-gap, he became the school’s fifth unanimous All-American (2018) and the first Clemson player to win the William V. Campbell Trophy, also known as the Academic Heisman. Moving differently than most his size, Wilkins uses his loose lower body, contact balance and active hands in conjunction to squirt through gaps. His high-character intangibles will be a strong selling point for an NFL team looking for a high-floor prospect. Overall, Wilkins is an inconsistent run defender, but his quickness, body flexibility and ball awareness lead to backfield production, projecting as a penetrating three-technique in a four-man base.
beast_strengths: Initial quickness to live in the opponent’s backfield…flexible hips and joints, contorting his good-sized frame and staying balanced through gaps…fluid redirection in pursuit with the chase speed to track down ballcarriers…plays underneath blocks and keeps his lower body working to grind out movement…gap quickness helps clog things up in the run game…recognition skills reflect his experience…well-versed on special teams coverages…scored three touchdowns (two rushing, one receiving) on offense…two-time team captain with the type of work ethic and intangibles that are “up there with Deshaun (Watson) since we’ve been here,” according to a Clemson assistant coach…graduated with a degree in communications (December 2017), becoming the first scholarship player in school history to graduate in two-and-a-half years…his 59 career games played is tied for the most in school history.
beast_weaknesses: Lacks ideal length and point-of-attack power…inconsistent shed technique and timing…can be bullied in the run game…inconsistent base strength and can be displaced by blockers, especially when his pads rise…doesn’t always replace his hands on his get-off, stalling his pass rush…always looking for an edge, but developed a reputation for being a borderline dirty player due to questionable hits…older prospect and will turn 24 during his NFL rookie season.

beast_summary: A three-year starter at Duke, Jones was groomed in the Blue Devils’ spread, no-huddle offense, which incorporated RPO concepts and asked him to use his legs (averaged double-digit carries per game over his 36 starts). A late bloomer, he developed under Cutcliffe’s watchful eye and it is easy to see the Manning influence with his footwork, pocket mannerisms and his release. While he doesn’t have a very impressive resume on paper, Jones elevated the average talent around him on the Duke offense, relying on both his arm and legs. His low-key personality might not immediately win over a room, but he competes with a quiet confidence and doesn’t show any fear on the football field. Overall, Jones doesn’t have any exceptional physical traits and his internal clock requires work, but he is a cerebral passer who makes accurate reads with active eyes and feet, projecting as a B-level NFL starter.
beast_strengths: Tall, average-sized frame…quick trigger to read and fire…recognizes coverage assignments and finds the out…has a pre-snap plan…slightly above- average arm strength…understands placement on downfield routes (posts, corners, etc.), setting the school record with 10 career touchdown passes of 50-plus yards…places the ball where his receiver can attack and make a move (holds the Duke career record with a 26.3 completion-to-interception ratio)…not a twitchy athlete, but mobility is an asset (comfortable throwing off platform)…excellent pocket movement, stepping up and keeping his eyes elevated…stronger and tougher than he looks to brush off contact – missed only two games following left shoulder surgery (September 2018)…graduated with a degree in economics (December 2018)…two-time team captain with “impeccable character,” according to Cutcliffe.
beast_weaknesses: Eye manipulation and internal clock are undeveloped…needs to find better balance between not rushing his process, but also playing with urgency…caught staring down routes, leading defenders to the target…still finding his touch as a passer…deep-ball timing is an issue, increasing the difficulty level…lacks elite arm strength to easily add extra RPMs…needs to take better care of the football…mild-mannered personality and still finding his voice as a leader…pedestrian career production with 59.6 percent completions and a 17-19 record as a starter – never earned All-ACC honors.

beast_summary: A three-year starter at Clemson, Ferrell earned a starting role as a redshirt freshman and helped fill the shoes of Shaq Lawson and Kevin Dodd, lining up primarily at right defensive end in the Tigers’ four-man base. He had outstanding production the last three years and ranks tied for fourth-best in school history with 27.0 career sacks. Ferrell is a much better NFL prospect than Lawson or Dodd because of his advanced hand tactics and awareness to see plays develop and set up his pass rush sequence. Similar to Preston Smith, he isn’t ultra-twitchy and won’t capture the corner on speed alone, but he has terrific contact balance and power to work off blocks. Overall, Ferrell has only average athleticism for his size, but his mix of power, handwork and recognition skills lead to production, projecting best as a hand-on-the-ground rusher in a 4-3 base.
beast_strengths: Good-looking on the hoof with long arms…advanced hand use, displaying strong rip, chop and swipe moves…times up the snap well with quick initial movements…understands depth and how to create rush lanes for himself…lower and upper body mechanics stay on the same page…effective spin and sets up inside moves…uses his length to set a hard edge and stay clean…holds his ground vs. power…disciplined eyes to read/track the football, staying away from mistakes…keeps his head on a swivel and anticipates angle blocks…consistent effort and plays through the whistle, making opposite hash stops…named a 2018 team captain…called a “humble worker” by his coaches…productive resume and started more games (44) than any other pass rusher in Clemson history, passing Levon Kirkland (43).
beast_weaknesses: Not naturally twitchy or explosive in his get-off…only average bend and cornering skills, causing his rush to stall…thrives on jumping the snap, which will lead to offsides penalties…can be squeezed out of gaps by power…lost outside contain more times than expected on tape…didn’t miss time the last three seasons, but didn’t play his senior year in high school due to a torn ACL in his right knee (August 2014), which also forced him to redshirt in 2015; didn’t work out at the pro day after re-aggravating a right turf toe injury (March 2019).

beast_summary: A three-year starter at Oklahoma, Ford spent two seasons in the left guard rotation before flourishing at right tackle as a junior, lining up primarily in a two-point stance. He was arguably the best player on college football’s best offensive line in 2018, helping the Sooners rank No. 1 in the FBS in total offense (570.3 yards per game) and scoring offense (48.4 points per game).
