br_positives: — Versatile player who has shown the ability to play in both press- and off-coverage from the slot and outside cornerback position. | — Very good vision and anticipation when playing in zone coverage. Can bait the quarterback into throws. | — Shows up in both run and screen games. Takes on blockers to declare leverage.
br_negatives: — Decent hip mobility but can be slow at times when flipping or sinking hips. Shows some trouble closing space out of breaks. | — Below-average functional strength. Can get pushed around at times. Especially from bigger blockers. | — Inconsistent tackling. Can come in out of control while also diving at legs or throwing arms out to tackle.

beast_summary: Davontavean “Tay” Martin was a three-sport (basketball, football, track) star at Ellender Memorial in Houma. He earned first team all-state as a senior with 45 catches for 751 yards and eight touchdowns, adding two interceptions on defense. A three-star recruit, he flipped from Tulane to Washington State, where he started for two seasons. In order to be closer to home (has a three-year old daughter and three younger siblings), he transferred to Oklahoma State, backing up Tylan Wallace in 2020 and leading the team in receiving in 2021. Martin is a tall, lean athlete with natural flexibility and route pacing to give his quarterback a target. He uses his length to make athletic adjustments on the football, and crowded catch points don’t bother him, which is important because he struggles to separate on his own. Overall, Martin is a quicker-than-fast athlete who must improve his drop rate, but he plays strong through contact with the mindset of an X wideout.

LaBryan Ray, who is one of three boys, was raised by his father (Gary Sr.) in northern Alabama after his mother (Angela) passed away when he was 6. He attended James Clemens High, where he combined for 237 tackles, 45.0 tackles for loss and 25.0 sacks on the defensive line in his final two seasons. A five-star recruit, Ray was the No. 1 player in the state and a top-30 recruit nationally, committing to Alabama over several other SEC schools. However, an extensive injury history limited his impact in Tuscaloosa. Ray doesn’t have the power, range or explosiveness to be disruptive, but he is stout at the point of attack with the hand strength and play recognition to control single-blocks and create gap congestion vs. the run. Overall, Ray has the build and quickness of a rotational 4i or five- technique lineman in the NFL, but strong durability concerns and his inability to stay on the field (only 850 defensive snaps in five seasons) are red flags.

Slade Bolden was a standout baseball and football player at West Monroe High (No. 1 in his class academically with a 4.0 GPA). He earned 2017 Gatorade Player of the Year honors in Louisiana as a dual-threat quarterback with 3,082 yards (1,622 passing, 1,460 rushing) and 40 total touchdowns. A three-star recruit, he committed to Alabama over TCU as a wide receiver and became a starter in 2021, finishing third on the team in receptions behind Jameson Williams and John Metchie. Operating primarily out of the slot, Bolden is quicker than fast with an instinctive feel in the underneath passing game, allowing him to find zone pockets. Quarterbacks will appreciate his dependable hands and initial separation, but his catch radius is average, and he struggles to create his own space before and after the catch. Overall, Bolden is an ordinary size-speed athlete with clear limitations, but his toughness on special teams could help him secure an NFL slot role.

Michael “Mike” Woods II was a three-year starting receiver at Magnolia High, where he combined for 155 catches, 2,988 receiving yards and 41 touchdowns in 31 games over his final three prep seasons. A three-star recruit, he originally committed to SMU before following Chad Morris to Arkansas when he became the Razorbacks’ head coach. After three seasons, he sought out a more explosive offense and transferred to Oklahoma for the 2021 season. Woods has a long, slender frame with some build-up speed to stack coverage on vertical patterns. He uses his length to reach back or snatch the ball outside of his frame, but focus drops plagued him during his career. He is a linear route runner and lacks the instincts or stem deception to routinely snap his hips and create easy separation. Overall, Woods displays a rangy catch radius and long-striding athleticism, but doesn’t have any special qualities to distinguish him on an NFL depth chart.

Devin Harper was born in Atlanta and attended Karns High in Knoxville, where he was a standout running back and linebacker. He rushed for 1,403 yards and posted 40 tackles as a senior to earn all-conference honors. A three-star athlete recruit, he signed with Oklahoma State, where he was primarily a subpackage defender his first five seasons. He took advantage of the extra year of eligibility from the pandemic and excelled as a super senior, finishing second on the team in tackles. Harper is a rangy run defender and weakside blitzer with the quickness to squeeze gaps and the closing burst to chase down perimeter plays. His tackling technique and strike zone are inconsistent and need to mature for the pro game. His situational awareness and coverage anticipation also must improve for the NFL. Overall, Harper’s coverage lapses on tape are bothersome, but he shows the downhill speed and demeanor to be a nickel defender and special teams standout.

Isaiah Pola-Mao comes from a football family, including his Hall of Fame uncle, Troy Polamalu. Isaiah was an All-American senior receiver and safety at Mountain Pointe High, posting 100 tackles, 10 interceptions and nine touchdowns on offense. A four-star recruit, he committed to USC over Washington. After his first two seasons were wiped out because of shoulder injuries, he put himself on the NFL map in 2019, although his 2020 and 2021 seasons didn’t quite live up to the expectations. Lined up as a deep safety, Pola-Mao has terrific range and the situational awareness to understand what the offense wants to do. However, he appeared to battle confidence issues as a senior, overthinking things instead of relying on his instincts, which led to a high completion rate when he was targeted. Overall, Pola-Mao is a tall, athletic safety with NFL speed and twitch, but his negative plays in coverage and vs. the run in 2021 are a concern for NFL scouts.

Peyton Hendershot grew up outside of Indianapolis and attended Tri-West High where he lettered in basketball and football (defensive end and tight end). He earned All-State honors as a senior with 67 catches for 896 yards and nine touchdowns. A three-star recruit, he flipped from Ball State to Indiana, where he became the program’s all-time leader in catches and receiving yards by a tight end. Although he lacks explosive traits and is a limited blocker, Hendershot has solid size and speed for the position with excellent hand-eye coordination as a pass-catcher (one drop on 62 targets in 2021). He was arrested (February 2020) after his ex- girlfriend said he grabbed her by the neck and shoved her against the wall. He pled guilty in June 2020 as part of a plea deal that required he enter into a batterer's treatment program. Overall, Hendershot has draftable pass-catching talent, but his off-field character warrants close inspection following his domestic incident.

Nolan Turner lettered in basketball and football at Vestavia Hills High (outside of Birmingham), posting 63 tackles and five interceptions as a senior. A two-star recruit, he had only one offer (UAB) until a last-minute offer from Clemson. His father (Kevin), who passed away in March 2016 from ALS, was teammates with Dabo Swinney at Alabama and played eight years at fullback in the NFL. Turner was a two-time team captain for the Tigers and had an All-American 2020 season at free safety. He posted above-average testing numbers pre-draft but doesn’t play that fast with inconsistent cover anticipation and tightness when reacting to routes. Though he does a nice job throttling down as a run defender to break down in space, his finishing skills as a tackler were below par on his 2021 tape. Overall, Turner’s up-and-down tape tempers NFL expectations, but his athleticism, football character and special teams experience (759 snaps in college) work in his favor.

A three-year starter at Washington State, Borghi was a versatile back initially in Mike Leach’s Air Raid scheme followed by two seasons in Nick Rolovich’s run-and-shoot pass offense. He averaged 98.2 yards of total offense per start in college and is one of the few running backs in this class with 150-plus career catches. Borghi runs with a good mix of quickness and patience and routinely gets what is blocked for him. However, he doesn’t force many tackles and is more likely to run away from contact that run through it. Overall, Borghi’s role will be limited in the NFL because of his average size, run strength and agility, but he is an instinctive runner and natural hands-catcher. He is a poor man’s Danny Woodhead who can make an NFL roster as a change-of-pace option.
beast_strengths: Built low to the ground with natural thickness in his chest, legs and wrists … accelerates well into the hole and when attacking the perimeter … savvy runner at the line of scrimmage, with the vision and patience to allow blocks to develop … runs with low pads and won’t waste time dancing … soft-handed receiver out of the backfield, with outstanding body control to immediately become a threat once the ball hits his mitts … his pass protection needs continued development, but it is much better than his underclassman tape … fumbled twice in college, and both came his freshman season … scored 41 total touchdowns in 39 games played.
beast_weaknesses: Muscle-bound in his core, hindering his quick directional change … doesn’t play with the explosive lateral burst for easy lane change … has marginal run power and struggles to keep his feet flowing with energy through contact … small target as a receiver, and doesn’t have an extensive catch radius … his lack of length also hinders him as a blocker … missed the first three games of his junior season with a back injury (September 2020); suffered a torn ACL and MCL in his knee as a junior in high school (November 2016) … didn’t play on special teams in college and hasn’t returned kicks since high school.

beast_summary: A three-year backup at Ole Miss, Conner was part of a crowded backfield in head coach Lane Kiffin’s RPO-based scheme. He spent most of his career as a third-stringer, but the Rebels spread out their rushing production as Ole Miss was the only FBS team in 2021 with four players with at least 500 rushing yards. Conner was at his best near the goal line, with 19 of his 26 career rushing touchdowns coming from five yards or less, including 14 one-yard runs. Although he doesn’t run with the creativity to be a home-run hitter (only two carries of 25-plus yards in 2021), he will hit plenty of singles and doubles (led Ole Miss running backs with 22 runs of 10-plus yards in 2021). Overall, Conner needs to improve his run tempo and third-down skills to see regular NFL work, but he has the vision, balance and toughness to be more than just a goal-line back. Like in college, his ideal NFL fit will be part of a committee.
beast_strengths: Well-built with thickness in his lower and upper halves … runs compact with square pads and an angry attitude … oiled up with the run strength that leaves defenders sliding off him … it often requires multiple tacklers to get him on the ground … excellent vision on stretch plays, where he can get going downhill and maneuver around road blockers … willing in pass protection, and was often used as a lead back on designed quarterback runs … wasn’t heavily targeted but showed soft hands and reliable focus as a screen target (zero drops the last two seasons) … durable and logged only 336 touches in college, leaving plenty of tread on his tires … has a nose for the end zone and leaves Ole Miss No. 3 in school history with 26 career rushing touchdowns (one spot ahead of Archie Manning).
beast_weaknesses: Takes a moment to get going or change directions after gearing down … impatient at the line of scrimmage, and prematurely gives up on developing run lanes … gets bounce happy, and that won’t fly vs. NFL speed … not a make-you-miss back at the second level … only two of his 144 offensive touches in 2021 resulted in a 25-plus yard play … doesn’t have an extensive receiving background … squares at contact in pass protection but doesn’t play up to his size because of poor technique (drops his eyes, doesn’t anchor) … was never asked to be a workhorse in college (only three times in 35 career games did he have 15-plus offensive touches).

beast_summary: Jordan “JJ” Jackson grew up in Jacksonville and attended The Bolles School, where he was a four-year letterman on the defensive line. He led Bolles to a 12-1 record as a senior and earned Honorable Mention All-State honors. A two-star recruit, he committed to Air Force, following in the footsteps of his mother, who served almost two decades in the Army. Aside from missing the 2020 season because of corrective shoulder surgery, he was productive for the Falcons, averaging double-digit tackles for loss each season. Jackson is a smooth, active athlete with a relentless motor that directly leads to backfield production, but he doesn’t play explosive as a pass rusher. As a run defender, his hand placement, base strength and instincts are inconsistent and he needs to show more grit at contact. Overall, Jackson lacks direction once engaged, but he has a projectable frame with functional length and initial quickness to compete for a rotational three-technique role.

Tayland Humphrey prepped at Klein Oak High in Spring, Texas before a two-year stint at Hutchinson Community College. A four-star JUCO recruit, he bypassed offers from Alabama, Georgia and others to sign with FIU to play with his brother (John Bolding) in 2018. He left after one year (NFL scout: “He had a lot of growing up to do.”) and transferred to Louisiana, where he earned All-Sun Belt honors each of the last two seasons. Nicknamed “Big Saucy,” Humphrey fires out of his stance to out-leverage blockers and squeeze gaps, using his long arms to corral or rag doll ball carriers. He struggles to redirect in short spaces and won’t offer much of a pass rush, but when the motor is revving, he can be more than just a space-eater. His physicality is currently more advanced than his run instincts. Overall, Humphrey must continue to keep his candle lit both on and off the field, but he can be disruptive on early downs with his frame, length and athletic lower body.

A part-time starter at Baylor, Ebner was a do-it-all weapon in offensive coordinator Jeff Grimes’ wide-zone scheme, playing second-fiddle to Abram Smith in 2021. Though his rushing production increased in his final season, he was the most productive as a receiver and return man, earning back-to-back Big 12 Special Teams Player of the Year honors the last two seasons (finished his career No. 2 in school history with 4,582 all-purpose yards). Ebner is comfortable running routes from the backfield or slot with the coordinated ball skills to adjust and finish grabs. He has above-average speed with balance and a compact build, although his creativity and decision-making at the line of scrimmage are not strengths to his game. Overall, Ebner probably doesn’t make an NFL roster as a running back alone, but his pass-catching versatility and special teams experience will give him an advantage in an NFL camp.
beast_strengths: Compact ball carrier with plus speed … shows rhythm and timing in his lateral movements to escape trouble … his eyes instinctively find open space to redirect his course … solidly built with a low center of gravity to consistently pick up positive yards after contact … high school wide receiver, and shows a natural feel as a route runner … dependable hands, and drops were scarce on film (holds the Baylor record for career catches by a running back) … experienced special teamer and return man with three career kickoff return touchdowns, averaging 25.3 yards per return (47/1,187/3) … durable and set the school record for games played (61).
beast_weaknesses: Undersized by NFL standards for the position … inconsistent tempo and stop-start skills as he sorts through blocks … shows hints of hip and ankle stiffness when he attempts to make sudden plant-and-go cuts … runs quick and tough, but not explosive or physical through contact … smaller target as a pass catcher, forcing his quarterback to be precise with throws … his technique and awareness as a pass blocker are both underdeveloped … his ball security is a problem, fumbling four times as a senior … his career rushing production won’t get you excited.

beast_summary: Doug Kramer Jr. started playing tackle football in fifth grade and continued as a three-year starter at Hinsdale Central High, where he earned conference offensive lineman of the year honors as a senior. A three-star recruit, he grew up in an Illinois family (his parents’ alma mater) and was ready to walk on until he received his dream offer weeks before 2016 signing day. Aside from a few missed games because of injury, he started every game the past five years with more than 3,000 career snaps on offense (100% of those at center). Kramer is quick with his snap and step and uses his lower body bend and natural leverage to stay under his blocks. He is technically sound and recovers well, but his short arms will keep him at a disadvantage vs. rushers across his face and long defenders in the run game. Overall, Kramer is undersized and doesn’t offer position flex, but he is quick, smart and the type of grinder capable of carving out a multi-contract NFL career.
pff_overview: Kramer is just your run o fthe mill five-year starter who's never taken a snap at anything other than center. Kramer was part of Lovie Smith's first recruiting class with the Illini and one of his most prolific players. He's a high-end athlete for the position, but doesn't possess the requisite physicality to fit into most schemes in the league. You saw that even in his grading profile at the collegiate level. Hinsdale, IL
pff_pros: Above-average get-off. Wins by getting on you in a hurry. Can fly between assignments. Foot quicks and processing speed to clean up stunts/slants. Natural leverage at his size. If he catches DTs off balance he can run with them.
pff_cons: Not much to his lower half and won't fully unlock hips into contact. Looks ready to topple over at any moment on the move. Sixth-year player. Turns 24 in June.
pff_bottom_line: Kramer is a physically limited center who won't register on the radar of teams that aren't outside zone heavy.

beast_summary: A four-year starter at Utah, Tafua lined up at defensive end in defensive coordinator Morgan Scalley’s four-man front, standing up or rushing with his hand on the ground. He put together a standout final season in Salt Lake City with a conference-best in pressures and sacks and was awarded the 2021 Morris Trophy as the top defensive lineman in the Pac-12 (as voted by conference offensive linemen). Tafua, who will turn 26 as an NFL rookie, is the Energizer bunny as a pass rusher with his quickness and efficient rush plan to create backfield disruption. He is a strong edge-setter and plays with discipline vs. the run, but he will struggle to quickly shed once engaged. Overall, Tafua falls short of what NFL teams ideally want on the edge in terms of length and explosiveness, but he wins with developed rush moves and relentless energy to challenge blockers. He projects as a potential NFL backup, ideally suited as a wide-nine defender.
beast_strengths: Improved his pass rush maturation each season ... quick off the ball with the slant quickness to infiltrate gaps ... understands rush depth and skillfully anticipates blocking landmarks ... attacks with a variety of power moves, including a stab-rip to swipe away the reach of blockers ... stout edge-setter who knocks tight ends into tomorrow ... disciplined run-stopping defender, quickly reading and leveraging gaps ... his gas tank is always full, giving relentless effort, which directly leads to production ... voted a team captain as a senior, and toughs out injuries ... above-average backfield production as a senior in 2021.
beast_weaknesses: Doesn’t have ideal length ... plays quick but not twitchy or explosive ... shows hints of hip stiffness at times when attempting to bend the corner ... his snap timing has room for improvement (three offsides penalties in 2021) ... his countering skills can be better once he is locked up by blockers ... will leave some production on the field with his inability to make quick gear changes in the backfield ... doesn’t have the requisite foot speed to drop and be a playmaker in coverage ... older prospect because of his two-year church mission between high school and college ... stayed durable throughout college but played through a sports hernia over the final three games of his senior season (November 2021), requiring surgery.
br_positives: — Above-average first step at the snap. | — Good hands versus the run. Consistent punch allows him to control blocks. | — Moments of great upper-body strength. Knocks blockers back from time to time. | — Effective setting the edge. | — Decent flexibility and balance when working around blocks in the run game.
br_negatives: — Physicality and energy comes and goes. | — Does not attack around the edge very well. Bend does not show up as well as it does versus the run. | — Does not have the lower-body strength to consistently drive blockers back. | — Range and movement in space is average at best.

beast_summary: Chris Oladokun (oh-la-DOE-kun) was born and raised in Tampa, Fla., and started playing quarterback at the youth level. He attended Alonso High before transferring to Sickles High as a senior, posting 15 touchdowns in 2015. A three-star recruit, he committed to South Florida, where he spent three years before transferring to Samford. After two years, he transferred to South Dakota State in June 2021 and won the starting job, becoming the third player in school history to reach 3,150 passing yards in a season. An athletic mover, Oladokun effectively moves the pocket and creates off-schedule with his quick feet and whip of an arm. He has a quick release, but needs to be more controlled and repeatable with his mechanics, which should give a boost to his ball placement. Overall, Oladokun needs to fine-tune his read timing, decisions and technique, but he is a poised passer with functional athleticism and arm strength to warrant practice squad consideration.

Andrew Rupcich (Rup-sitch) was a two-way player at McHenry High (one hour north of Chicago) and was an all-conference right tackle as a senior. He was late to qualify out of high school and signed with NAIA-level Culver Stockton in northeast Missouri instead of going the juco or walk-on route. He earned the starting left tackle job as a true freshman and started every game the last five years (48 consecutive starts), earning all-conference honors all five seasons. Rupcich is a solid athlete for his size and relies on his physical hands to control or drive blockers. NFL scouts praise his toughness and willingness to fight through injuries. His pads are much too high, his arms are too short and his technique needs an overhaul, especially with a move to the interior (played left guard at NFLPA Collegiate Bowl). Overall, Rupcich is one of the best offensive linemen to ever come from the NAIA level, but he must improve his contact balance and recovery skills for the NFL.

A two-year starter at Georgia Southern, Baker was an outside cornerback in former defensive coordinator Scot Sloan’s man-zone scheme. A former walk- on, he went from fourth-string to starter, earned a scholarship and earned a spot on Bruce Feldman’s 2021 Freaks List, which he backed up with his impressive pro day numbers. Baker checks boxes with his height, length, speed and explosiveness, but his coverage anticipation and consistency in run support are subpar. He has a bad habit of losing his balance when peeking into the backfield and struggled vs. some of the better opponents on the schedule (two touchdowns allowed on the 2021 Arkansas tape). Overall, Baker is experienced in various coverages with top-tier athletic traits, but he lacks poise downfield and the key for him to carve out an NFL career will be his mental development. He projects best as a press-man corner and special teamer.
beast_strengths: Freaky height-weight-speed athlete with plus arm length … rangy cover man and makes plays at every level of the field … shows off his top-level closing burst in his plant and drive or when taking playmaking angles to passing windows … displays the hip flip and foot quickens to recover from wasted steps and coverage lapses … showed improved discipline downfield (only one pass-interference penalty in 2021) … looks like a wide receiver when he attacks the ball, showing outstanding leaping skills, timing and hand strength … has versatile experience at safety, cornerback and nickel … was a gunner on punt coverage.
beast_weaknesses: Undeveloped coverage anticipation and doesn’t put himself in situations to make plays on the ball … late to sort through route indicators and feel route breaks … struggles to accurately balance his eyes between quarterback and route runner, especially in zone … can be beaten over the top because of inconsistent transitions … low interception total reflects his tardiness to the catch point … slender build with below-average play strength … inconsistent run defender with too many missed tackles on his résumé.

beast_summary: A one-year starter at Massachusetts, Watts was an outside cornerback in former defensive coordinator Tommy Restivo’s scheme. After starting opposite Caleb Farley at Virginia Tech in 2018, he spent two seasons on the sideline at North Carolina before transferring to UMass in 2021, where he attracted attention from NFL scouts. Watts has outstanding play speed with the lower-body twitch and pattern-reading skills to play tight coverage or drive on plays at the line of scrimmage. However, he needs to play with more control in his transitions, which should lead to improved ball production. Overall, Watts needs to improve his coverage discipline and play strength for the next level, but he has the athletic traits and reaction skills to develop into reliable contributor in an NFL secondary. His testing numbers and experience on special teams will only help his chances.
beast_strengths: Fluid athlete with sudden footwork … quick to flip his hips and accelerate to top speed … able to stay in phase down the sideline … drives downhill to attack screens and quick throws before they can get going … stays in position to recover and closes out break separation in a blink … alert in coverage and shows minimal lag in his diagnose and response to routes … looks comfortable crowding receivers to achieve body position and defend windows … scrappy tackler and toughness won’t be questioned … NFL scouts call him “coachable” and a player who has yet to play his best football … was a standout on punt coverage on the 2021 tape.
beast_weaknesses: Lacks ideal perimeter size with his slender build with thin hips … only two career takeaways … showed grabby tendencies on the 2021 Toledo tape … doesn’t play with a natural feel with his back to the football … savvy receivers know he will jump at first movement … inconsistent press technique and play strength … leaves his feet prematurely as a tackler and will throw his body around instead of a controlled wrap up process … doesn’t lack for toughness but will take himself off track to avoid blocks … suffered a fractured left arm (November 2018) and had plates and screws inserted, missing only one game … spent time at three schools the last four seasons and missed two seasons of development in 2019 and 2020.

beast_summary: Nicholas “Nick” Muse, who is the younger brother of NFL LB/S Tanner Muse, grew up in Belmont and attended South Point High. He was a four-sport athlete and led the team to the 2016 3A state title as a linebacker and tight end. A no star recruit, he committed to FCS William & Mary where he played two seasons. He transferred to South Carolina and was ruled eligible early in the 2019 season. He tore his ACL late in 2019, but finished top three on the team in receiving the last two years. Lined up inline and on the wing, Muse is a good-sized, presentable target with plus foot-speed, but needs a runway to create separation as a route-runner. While he is a rugged blocker at the line of scrimmage and second level, his lack of length will leave him out-leveraged, especially on the edge. Overall, Muse is up and down as a blocker and needs to cut down on the drops, but he is a “make it” competitor with enough athleticism to compete for a backup role in the NFL.
beast_strengths: Executes outside zone with rare movement skills for his size ... high-level feet and balance on the move ... long arms and explosive hands ... has the grip strength to turn, torque or toss his man ... caves in the line on down blocks ... his violent knockdowns would be felonies anywhere other than the football field ... mauling latch-and-drive skills to escort bodies away from the play ... creates a firm base to anchor his pass sets ... flips his hips with fluid body adjustments to answer twists/loops ... wide, engulfing frame to absorb contact and quickly recover after a misfired punch ... easily pulls cross-formation or downfield ... looks to snatch souls and competes with the same nasty streak for all four quarters ... loves football and carries himself with an uplifting attitude ... his coaches say his love for football is genuine and he started showing leadership traits as a true freshman (NFL scout: “He kept praising his teammates when all I wanted to do was talk about him.”) ... officially credited with 154 pancakes (67 in 2021) and 47 knockdowns in his career ... durable college career (31 consecutive starts) and played interchangeably at left tackle and left guard.
beast_weaknesses: Habitual over-setter and surrenders inside leverage ... allows his fundamentals to lax and break down too often ... his inefficient pass sets and eagerness to connect with defenders leads to lunges and misfires with his initial punch ... his hands are powerful, but not always disciplined ... responsible for 10 penalties over his three years in college, including multiple flags for playing beyond the whistle (his amped up play personality can get away from him at times).

beast_summary: Isaiah Graham-Mobley was born in Bryn Mawr, Pa., and grew up in Philadelphia before attending Upper Merion High, where he was a three-sport star. He was a receiver and defensive back and was the team MVP with six interceptions. A three-star recruit, he stayed close to home and signed with Temple (his only FBS offer), where he wasn’t a full-time starter and had season-ending injuries in 2019 and 2020. He transferred to Boston College for his final season, where he was the starting middle backer. Graham-Mobley has struggled to stay healthy (missed 14 games the past three seasons) and was an inconsistent performer, especially on his 2021 tape. When he diagnoses properly, he has above-average speed for the position to unlock, flow and beat blockers to the contact point. Overall, Graham- Mobley is a good-looking athlete with some untapped ability, but his inconsistent play recognition vs. both the run and the pass will stand out vs. NFL offenses. [223]

CJ Verdell was a four-year letterman at Mater Dei Catholic, leading the team to the 2015 state championship. He combined for 4,740 rushing yards in his junior and senior seasons and was named the San Diego Offensive Player of the Year. A three-star recruit, he committed to Oregon over other Pac-12 offers and enjoyed immediate success with back-to-back 1,000 yard rushing seasons in 2018 and 2019. However, he was limited by injuries his final two seasons, including a major leg injury as a senior. Verdell is an athletic and urgent runner to shoot through holes and quickly attack open space. Though he runs decisive and tough, his lack of run power limits him between the tackles. On passing downs, he shows adequate screen game skills, but was barely a speed bump at times in pass pro. Overall, Verdell battled unfortunate injuries over the second half of his Ducks career, but his quick feet and contact balance will give him a chance to make an NFL roster.
br_positives: — Very good speed. Can threaten a big play from anywhere. | — Great straight-line acceleration. Hits top speed quickly once he turns upfield. | — Smooth mover in space. Weaves around defenders comfortably. | — Tough, scrappy runner. Fights for yardage. | — Comfortable pass-catcher in space. Transitions to being a ball-carrier with ease. | — Competent in pass protection. Consistently finds work.
br_negatives: — Average balance and power. | — Not as quick as he is fast. More of a straight-line threat. | — Could stand to be a bit more decisive and commanding as a runner. | — Consistently banged up. Has not proved he can sustain a heavy workload.

beast_summary: Andrew Ogletree lettered in basketball and football at Northridge High and earned all-state in both sports as a senior (also named the 2015-16 Division-III player of the year in basketball, averaging 14.5 points per game). He signed with Division-II Findlay as a receiver and set career-bests as a junior in 2018. After sitting out the 2019 season with a knee injury, he transferred to FCS-level Youngstown State for his final two seasons, starting every game at tight end in 2021. Ogletree plays with the agility and control of a smaller athlete and uses his long, galloping strides to work to open space. He has the catch radius to pull in difficult throws over defenders, but will also drop too many easy ones. He didn’t find the end zone at YSU. As a blocker, he is willing, but needs to improve his knee bend and aiming points to leverage his man. Overall, Ogletree’s stats don’t jump off the page, but his tape shows an agile-footed big man who is still discovering how good he can be.

A one-year starter at Oklahoma State, Warren emerged as the starting back in offensive coordinator Kasey Dunn’s zone scheme. After showing promise at Utah State, he bet on himself by joining a crowded Oklahoma State backfield in 2021 and was a playmaker in the Big 12, announcing himself as a possible draft pick. Warren has outstanding initial footwork and vision to put himself in position to find the vulnerable areas at the line of scrimmage. He runs with competitive violence, although he will struggle to keep his momentum through early congestion. Overall, Warren’s broken tackles will be harder to come by vs. NFL pursuit, but he impulsively reads his blocks and uses foot quickness to dart his way to greener pastures. He will compete for a complimentary role in an NFL backfield.
beast_strengths: Sturdy and compact build … quick, decisive footwork to efficiently scan and execute zone runs … instinctively sets up his cuts to force fly-by tackles by defenders (see 2021 Boise State tape) … his low center of gravity helps him absorb hits and bounce off contact … his leg drive and competitive run style makes it tougher for defenders to ground him in the open field … resets his eyes after he clears the line of scrimmage and shows enough speed to take it the distance … takes care of the football (only two fumbles on 218 offensive touches in 2021) … caught the ball well on his 2021 tape, with zero drops charted.
beast_weaknesses: Average run power at the line of scrimmage … more quick than explosive as a runner, and needs to gather his balance before making cuts … inconsistent patience that will lead him to freelance off-script at times … might have trouble gaining the corner vs. NFL-level pursuit … has reliable hands out of the backfield but wasn’t a dynamic screen target at Oklahoma State … put some decent blocking reps on tape, but the below-average reps that resulted in direct disruption of the quarterback are tough to overlook … missed one game as a junior because of a spine disc injury (September 2019). [40]

beast_summary: Blaise (BLAYZ) Andries (AN-dreez) grew up in Marshall (same hometown as Trey Lance) and was a three-sport letterman at Marshall High. He earned first team All-State honors as a senior left tackle and was the No. 1 ranked recruit in the state. He was courted by national programs like Florida, Oklahoma and others, but the chance to play in front of his family led him to Minnesota. He was an iron man for the Gophers and started every game over the last four seasons, starting at [138] multiple positions each year (played every position except center in college). Predictably for a math major, he understands angles and gets his hands involved to tie up defenders. However, his lower body lacks controlled movements and he isn’t a people-mover or physical finisher at the point of attack, leading to fit concerns. Overall, Andries is a smart, experienced veteran who works hard to position his run-blocking fits, but his below average contact balance lowers his NFL ceiling.

Joshua Onujiogu (oh-new-jah-WAY-go), who is one of six children, grew up playing football and was a multi-sport athlete at Wareham High (school- record 15.49 in 110-meter hurdles). Playing at a small school (only 22 players on his varsity team), he went underrecruited, and Division III Framingham State was his only offer. He started as a true freshman and posted impressive backfield production each season, finishing his career with 67.0 tackles for loss in 47 games. Onujiogu is undersized with questionable edge-setting strength, but he stays low and flexible in his pass rush with the burst to skim the corner. He stays active with his hands, either taking away his stab at the top of his rush or converting speed to power and barreling through blocks with his forward lean. Overall, Onujiogu has tweener traits and is inexperienced vs. high-level blocking, but he rushes with quick feet, hands and hips and displays the motor and upside worth bringing to an NFL camp.

Josh Sills grew up in rural southeast Ohio and started playing football in third grade. He was a two-year starting left tackle at Meadowbrook High and also handled the kicking/punting duties. A three-star recruit, he committed to West Virginia over Michigan and spent four years in Morgantown. After a season-ending shoulder injury in 2019, he entered the transfer portal and landed at Oklahoma State and started 24 games over the last two seasons. Sills competes with a touch of wildness and is the type of guy you want on your side in bar fight. His bully attitude on the field makes him a great run finisher, but sometimes at the expense of his balance, falling off blocks. He has solid athleticism for a big man with a forceful punch as a pass blocker, but his timing needs refinement. Overall, Sills is one of the few players in this draft class with college starting experience at all five offensive line spots, but he must play with better control to counterbalance his aggression.

br_positives: — Tall, rocked-up build with good length. | — Energetic and physical player. Scraps and works to the ball until the whistle. | — Consistent punch in the run game. Helps him anchor fairly well. | — Flashes of good upper-body strength and power to control blocks. | — Decent range in space.
br_negatives: — Poor snap get-off. False steps out of his stance all the time; not particularly explosive. | — Not a natural bender. Shows stiffness when trying to round the corner as a pass-rusher. | — Hand usage as a pass-rusher is a bit wild right now. Needs to be more planned out. | — Does not have a clear dynamic pass-rushing trait. More of a hustle player than anything.

beast_summary: A two-year starter at Oregon, Williams was an outside receiver in former offensive coordinator Joe Moorhead’s scheme. A former top recruit, he spent less than two seasons at USC before transferring to Oregon, where he led the Ducks in receiving each of the past two seasons, but his career production looks more like single-season numbers. Williams is a large target for his quarterback thanks to his frame, body control and ball skills to go get the football. However, he is a one- speed route runner who doesn’t consistently play up to his size or physicality. Overall, Williams has rangy leaping skills when the ball is in the air, but he struggles to create consistent separation and requires extensive route work to secure a roster spot in the NFL.
beast_strengths: Large-framed, long-limbed athlete ... rangy pass catching skills when the ball is in the air ... accurately times his attack to high-point and out-jump defenders to the football ... consistently works himself past the sticks (74.3 percent of catches in 2021 resulted in a first down or touchdown) ... focus drops were tough to find on tape, and hand strength stands out ... physical after the catch to be more than a possession target ... doesn’t take blocking duties lightly, using size to his advantage ... led Oregon in receiving each of his two seasons in Eugene.
beast_weaknesses: Questionable route awareness, and late to recognize coverages ... stems are more rounded than sharpened ... needs a moment to get back up to full speed after being slowed mid-route ... will struggle to escape the jam of NFL press corners ... physical defenders give him trouble ... hears footsteps when attempting to work the middle of the field ... doesn’t always play up to his size, with a low success rate in contested situations ... below-average elusiveness to routinely force missed tackles or create as a ball carrier ... offers very little on special teams coverages ... production doesn’t jump off the page.

beast_summary: Master Teague III grew up outside of Nashville and rushed for 2,031 yards as a junior at Blackman High in Murfreesboro before missing most of his senior season (ankle injury). A four-star recruit, he signed with Ohio State over several SEC schools, and although he didn’t quite live up to expectations, he was a productive second fiddle behind JK Dobbins (2019), Trey Sermon (2020) and TreVeyon Henderson (2021). Teague finished his OSU career with 5.5 yards per carry and plenty of tread left on his tires. He is built like a tank to run with downhill power, but also has the speed of a race car to out-leverage pursuit. Though straight-line explosive, he isn’t slippery or shifty to patch together multiple moves. Despite his thick frame, he can be run over in pass pro because of poor base and fundamentals. Overall, Teague has underwhelming film, but there is meat still left on the bone, and his height/weight/speed have NFL teams interested for offense and special teams.

Alexander “Zander” Horvath (HOR-voth) was a two-year starter at Marian High and finished with a school-record 3,373 rushing yards and 50 touchdowns in his career. A no-star recruit, he didn’t receive any FBS scholarships and originally accepted a preferred walk-on spot at Indiana to play linebacker before flipping to Purdue as a fullback. He shared the rushing duties over the last four seasons, setting career bests in rushing and receiving as a junior in 2020. Horvath has linebacker size with sculpted muscle and pop at contact as a lead blocker. He tested well above average for a fullback, and although his tape doesn’t show an explosive athlete, his agility, balance and straight-line speed are impressive. He needs to improve his patience and pad level if he hopes to receive NFL carries. Overall, Horvath lacks the instincts of a full-time ball carrier, but he has the blocking upside, pass-catching skills and special teams experience to compete for an NFL roster spot.

A four-year starter at Iowa State, Allen shared the Y tight end duties with Charlie Kolar in offensive coordinator Tom Manning’s scheme, lining up inline and detached. He wasn’t a highly targeted part of the offense (never finished a season better than fifth on the team in catches), but he played a lot of football at ISU (more than 2,000 offensive snaps) and was productive when given opportunities. Allen is a coordinated athlete with decent speed to work his way to open zones or make grabs down the seam over linebackers. Although he lacks the play strength or body control as a blocker to stay connected, he can set the edge and consistently works to reestablish his body leverage. Overall, Allen doesn’t have a distinguishing trait that helps him pop on film, but his game shows equal parts toughness and intelligence with the ball skills to gain the trust of an offensive play caller. If he gets an opportunity in the NFL, he has a chance to stick as a rotational player.
beast_strengths: Light-footed athlete with outstanding length … skillfully mixes gears and adjusts his routes to the coverage … decent fluidity and doesn’t get hung up by his stem mechanics … quick hands and reflexes to snag throws outside his frame … registered only two drops over his final 90 targets in college … has the balance to efficiently go from pass-catcher to runner … rides blocks with the expected level of grit and toughness … uses his length to extend into contact and create an initial surge … high intelligent and a five-time Academic All-Big 12 recipient … played through most of the 2018 season with a torn groin, which required offseason surgery.
beast_weaknesses: Narrowly-built and lacks desired bulk, especially in his lowers … unimpressive play strength across the board … can get bogged down by physical defenders in man coverage … runs too upright in his routes and needs to show better sink … missed tackles were scarce on his film and YAC opportunities will be tougher vs. NFL defenses … not going to create consistent movement in the run game … doesn’t have the stout base to put down roots vs. bull rushers … older prospect and will turn 25 before his first NFL training camp … below average career receiving production.

beast_summary: George “Trae” Barry was born and raised on the Alabama Gulf Coast and was a three-sport standout at Spanish Fort High, playing quarterback and receiver. A two-star recruit, he committed to FCS Jacksonville State where he was an immediate contributor as a pass-catcher. After four seasons, he entered the transfer portal and landed at Boston College (over Ole Miss) for his final season. Despite missing time with a knee injury, he finished second on the team in receiving in 2021. Barry has a long and lean frame and looks like a basketball small forward with the way he expands his catch radius and out-muscles defenders to catch the ball cleanly. He has stride speed to create downfield plays, but needs to be more efficient at the top of his routes. He is raw, but promising as a blocker. Overall, Barry’s medicals (knee) will be important, but he is a supersized wide receiver with stride athleticism, ball skills and blocking upside to stand out in camp.

Leddie Brown started his prep career at Eastern Christian Academy (Md.), which was run by David Sills IV, but the program shut down after his sophomore year. As a junior, he led Smyrna High (Del.) to the 2016 state title before transferring to Neumann-Goretti High in Philadelphia as a senior, rushing for 899 yards and 11 touchdowns. A three-star recruit, he followed his West Virginia connections and eclipsed 1,000 rushing yards as a junior and senior in Morgantown. A physical grinder, Brown lowers his pads into contact to finish while also showing the lateral footwork to sidestep road blocks and switch run lanes at the line of scrimmage. While fumbles were an issue for him (five in 2021), he is willing in pass protection and catches the ball smoothly away from his frame. Overall, Brown doesn’t have explosive traits that will scare NFL defenses, but he has the run balance to stay afloat and the third-down upside that gives him a fighting chance.

A three-year starter at Oregon State, Quitoriano was the Y tight end in head coach Jonathan Smith’s balanced offense, lining up primarily inline. Underutilized as a pass-catcher, he had his most productive season as a senior, which ranked him seventh on the team in receiving yards in 2021. A highly decorated basketball player in high school (led the state of Oregon in points and rebounds in 2017), Quitoriano plays football in a similar way as a power forward, relying on his size, strength and ball skills to be productive. While he is a coordinated athlete, his average play speed creates little separation and his blocking tends to get out of control. Overall, Quitoriano shows the promise of an NFL combination tight end because of his size and toughness as a pass-catcher and blocker, but he struggled to show playmaking skills in either area on tape. He will have the chance to earn a backup Y role with a club.
beast_strengths: Big-bodied target and plays like a power forward in the post … above average hand strength (zero drops as a senior) … crowded catch points don’t bother his concentration, routinely extending and finishing in a crowd … doesn’t move with stiffness in his routes and flashes a little something after the catch … experienced run blocker with grappling strength and long-levers at the point of attack … looks to roll into contact, which helps him create thump and movement … his competitive temperament shows in a variety of ways on film … played almost 600 snaps on special teams coverages in college.
beast_weaknesses: Sluggish off the line with speed that is more build-up than immediate … will have a tough time uncovering vs. man in the NFL … reaches his depth, but lacks instincts or set-up as a route-runner … can get crazed when attempting to finish as a zone blocker … his feet and hips need to keep up with his hands once he slams into contact … inconsistent edge-setter … wasn’t asked to pass block a ton and his below average technique reflects that … penalized five times as a senior, including three false starts … lackluster receiving production with 40 career catches (only three career catches of 30-plus yards).

beast_summary: Jonathan “Jon” Ford grew up in south Florida and attended Dillard High, where he made varsity as a freshman. He had a breakout junior season with 98 tackles and 12.0 sacks to earn All-County honors. A three-star recruit, he had almost 30 offers, including Ohio State and USC, but he always dreamed of becoming a Hurricane. He started each of the last three seasons at Miami with inconsistent results, managing only 8.0 tackles for loss over 50 career games. Ford has controlled footwork at contact with the size to engage, anchor and maintain his gap integrity. He has the physical hands to get into blocks, but doesn’t have the countering quickness or instincts to track down ball carriers. As a pass rusher, he is sluggish transitioning his first step into a disruptive rush sequence. Overall, Ford looks the part and flashes point-of-attack strength and handwork to two-gap, but his lackluster impact on tape is unlikely to improve vs. NFL-level blocking.

James Skalski (SKAL-skee) started playing football at age 5, learning from his father (John), who played at Oklahoma and passed away in 2016. He started three years in football and soccer at Northgate High (Atlanta area), earning Region Defensive MVP as a senior with 170 tackles. A three-star recruit, he picked Clemson because of coach Brent Venables and became a three-year starter, two-time team captain and the “heart and soul” of the defense, according to head coach Dabo Swinney. Skalski, who set an FBS record with 69 games played, is intense in pursuit and was a standout on special teams during his career (22 career tackles). Although he tested well, his lack of twitch is noticeable in his change-of-direction movements, and he finds himself out of control as he attempts to unwind and finish. Overall, Skalski will be limited at the next level, but he is a physical take-on player with an excess of gritty intangibles that could be his ticket to sticking in the NFL.

A two-year starter at Georgia, FitzPatrick was the Y tight end in offensive coordinator Todd Monken’s balanced scheme. Lining up primarily inline with some detached snaps, he was an understated yet important part of the Bulldogs offense and national title run, playing through broken bones in both feet over the second half of the 2021 season. FitzPatrick blocks with a balanced, square base and the frame, play strength and toughness to be an asset in the run game. With only 32 career targets and two multi-catch games (none in 2021) in his college career, his evaluation as a pass catcher feels incomplete and unproven. Overall, FitzPatrick doesn’t have the tape or résumé of a playmaking receiver, but his inline blocking and intangibles are what makes him a draftable prospect. He can find a niche as a productive Y tight end in the NFL.
beast_strengths: Imposing size with solid muscle tone and room to get bigger … moves with big-man fluidity as both a blocker and receiver … bends his knees and shuffles his feet to achieve blocking angles … stout at contact to absorb contact and wall off lanes … effective on pins and outside-in blocks … runs with high knees and strong strides mid-route to leak into space or drag across the field … presents a large target for his quarterback with solid hands … heavy traffic didn’t appear to faze his concentration as a receiver … half of his six catches in 2021 resulted in a 20-plus yard play … intelligent on and off the field and his coaches call him a “high-achiever” who could be a millionaire financial investor if he wanted … played through broken bones in his feet over the second half of the 2021 season.
beast_weaknesses: Minimal receiving production in college with only 200 career receiving yards spread out over three years … unproven consistently scooping the ball at his knees or making full-extension grabs … doesn’t have the route speed to threaten coverage horizontally or down the seam … not going to make tacklers miss after the catch and can be grounded by single defenders … taller pad level with room to clean up his handwork as a pass blocker … can be caught leaning with his desire to generate movement at contact … flagged twice for holding in 2021 … underwent surgery to repair stress fractures in his fifth metatarsal bone on his left foot (January 2022); underwent surgery for the same issue for his right foot four weeks later (February 2022).

beast_summary: Curtis Hodges Jr. was a late bloomer at Mountain View High and switched his focus from basketball to football as a senior, posting 50 catches for 733 yards and seven touchdowns as a 190-pound receiver. A three-star recruit, he committed to Arizona State over Iowa State, but struggled to see consistent playing time because of injuries and lack of development. He had a breakout senior year and led ASU in yards per catch (18.7) in 2021 with eight catches of 25-plus yards. Hodges wasn’t asked to make plays in traffic on tape, but he can work the seam with his stride acceleration (before and after the catch) and fluid adjustment skills. His impressive body control also translates to his blocking, but his hands are wild and grabby (three holding calls in 2021). Overall, Hodges is undeveloped as a route- runner and lacks the power to sustain inline blocks, but he is a long, flexible athlete with enough pass-catching traits to warrant practice squad consideration.

DaMarcus Fields was a three-sport standout in basketball, track and football at Taylor High. He played primarily at receiver before moving to defense as a senior, finishing with 101 tackles and four interceptions to earn all-district honors. A three-star recruit, he committed to Texas Tech the summer before his senior year. After redshirting with shoulder issues in 2016, he became a five-year starter for the Red Raiders and earned All-Big 12 honors four consecutive years, finishing his career with 49 passes defended. Fields has bounce in his feet and the processing ability to work from either press or off. He will have his share of judgment errors and false steps and he turned only four of his 49 passes defended into turnovers (seven touchdowns allowed, zero interceptions since 2020). Overall, Fields is an aggressive and proven disruptor at the catch point, but his balance concerns and lack of explosive twitch might hinder him at the next level.

Ronnie Rivers was born in Castro Valley and attended Freedom High, where he rushed for 2,239 yards and scored 33 touchdowns as a senior in 2016. A two-star recruit, he grew up in a Fresno State family, and there was no doubt where he would commit once he received the offer. He logged at least 100 carries all five seasons with the Bulldogs and led the team in rushing each of his final four years. He finished No. 3 on the school’s all-time rushing list, only 56 yards behind his father (Ron), who played six years in the NFL (1995-2000). Ronnie has explosive feet and lateral agility to cut away from defenders and bounce off contact. He doesn’t have the base strength to slow down rushers, but he thrives in the screen game with his quick hands and offers punt return experience (7.8 career average). Overall, Rivers lacks the size or skill set to be anything more than a complimentary back, but his shifty feet and receiving skills could earn him a Boston Scott-like role.

Marcus McKethan (muh-KEE-thuhn) was a three-sport star at Barnwell High, lettering in basketball and winning the discus state title as a junior (151’6). He was a three-year starter at offensive tackle and didn’t allow a sack as a senior. A three-star recruit, he committed to North Carolina prior to his senior year and started 37 of the past 38 games at right guard for the Tar Heels (he was a right guard only at UNC). McKethan is a wide, burly blocker with bear claw hands and the strength at contact to be a people-mover in the run game, but he will fall off blocks and lose connection because of below-average contact balance. He jars rushers at contact when he properly times his initial punch, but he is heavy in his shuffle, and his recovery quickness will be challenged by NFL athletes. Overall, McKethan looks straight out of central casting with his frame, length and power, but the key to him locking down an NFL roster spot will be developing his reactive athleticism.

Britain Covey was a do-everything quarterback at Timpview High, leading the team to 26 consecutive wins, including back-to-back 4A state titles. He signed with Utah and was a Freshman All-American before taking a two-year religious mission in Chile. He returned in 2018 and was the team’s leading receiver before a right knee injury hindered him during the 2019 season. He returned in 2021 and again earned All-American status as a return man. Covey is an electric athlete with the innate proximity awareness and cutting quickness that makes him a dangerous returner. He averaged 11.7 yards per punt return with five career touchdowns on special teams (four punt returns, one kick return). He is an undersized target in the passing game, but he separates underneath and creates YAC plays for himself. Overall, Covey is role specific, but his instinctive vision and suddenness give him a realistic chance of playing in the NFL as a slot and return man.

TJ Pledger started his prep career at Chaminade High in Los Angeles, rushing for more than 4,000 yards in three seasons. He transferred to IMG Academy in Bradenton, Fla., for his senior year. A four-star recruit, he signed with Oklahoma over Nebraska and spent three seasons as a backup (split carries with Rhamondre Stevenson in 2020). He entered the transfer portal and landed at Utah, where he finished second on the team in rushing and averaged 6.7 yards per carry in 2021. Studying his tape, there was a consistent theme: Pledger always had an escape plan and consistently picked up yardage after contact. He is compactly built and quick to press, sort and finish each run with urgency. He appears to have soft hands, although he needs to expand his horizons as a blocker and third-down player. Overall, Pledger was a dependable backup in college, and his short-area burst and contact balance could land him in a running back rotation in the NFL.

Jack Cochrane was a four-sport letterman at Mount Vernon High and finished his prep career with 3,615 total yards (2,505 rushing, 1,110 receiving) and 66 touchdowns (school’s all-time leading scorer). He also posted 218 career tackles and seven interceptions on defense. He signed with South Dakota, where he was highly accomplished off the field (4.0 GPA student, three-time captain) and on the field (only FCS player with 100-plus tackles and four-plus interceptions in 2021). Cochrane is a smart, technically-sound player vs. the run and the pass (see 2021 Kansas tape). He does a nice job staying square and mirroring at the line, but his lack of length will make lateral scrapes tougher to execute in the NFL. He shows some hip tightness in space, which might restrict his coverage range in the NFL. Overall, Cochrane was a longshot to be drafted at this time last year, but his improvements and production on his senior tape have put him in the late round mix.

Qwynnterrio Cole attended Memphis East High, where he was a late bloomer and enjoyed a breakout season as a senior wide receiver and defensive back. A no-star recruit, he had a few FCS offers and signed with Alcorn State, where he was named an HBCU All-American as a sophomore and junior. After the 2020 season was canceled, he graduated and transferred to the FBS, where he earned the starting strong safety job at Louisville, finishing second on the team in tackles. Cole passes the eye test with his lean-muscled build and is at his best in the box or when working downhill to trigger-and-drive. His production and performance showed no drop-off in his one year in the FBS. His toughness and physicality were evident after five plays on tape, but so were his tight hips and redirection skills. Overall, Cole is a long, explosive athlete with aggressive run-defending ability, but his lack of range and transitions, especially in coverage, will limit his NFL ceiling.

Clint Ratkovich grew up outside of Chicago and led Crete-Monee to a 2015 conference title as a do-everything offensive back and linebacker. A no-star recruit, he landed at Western Illinois, where he dabbled at safety before becoming a productive pass-catching fullback. He transferred to Northern Illinois for his final season and played a hybrid fullback role (“superback”) and accounted for 15 total touchdowns. Ratkovich has the thick, muscular body of a fullback, the instincts of a running back and the reliable ball skills of a receiver. He isn’t much of a creator and didn’t break many tackles on tape, but he runs with a head of steam and a nose for the end zone/first down. As a blocker, he has a solid batting average, but needs to rely more on technique over physicality to execute at the next level. Overall, Ratkovich isn’t on the same level as 49ers’ Kyle Juszczyk, but he has the versatility to play a similar role and make an immediate impact on special teams.

Johnny Johnson III transferred from Buckeye Verrado to Chandler High prior to his junior season (teammates with N’Keal Harry). As a senior, he led Chandler to the 2016 state championship with 77 catches for 1,274 yards and eight touchdowns. A three-star recruit, he had only one offer (UNLV) until Oregon reached out with a scholarship. He had his best season in 2019 with a team-best 836 receiving yards and finished his Ducks career with 139 receptions. Johnson has experience working inside, outside and at every level of the field and put a deep inventory of routes on tape. He flashes short-area burst for quick passing windows and some juice after the catch. However, he can be outmuscled up and down the field and needs to be more of a playmaker when the ball is in the air. Overall, Johnson is a quality pass catching prospect who lacks distinguishing traits, which will make it tough for him to pass more talented receivers on the depth chart.

Greg Bell was born in San Diego and starred at Bonita Vista High, rushing for 2,632 yards and 34 touchdowns as a senior. He went the junior college route after high school because of academics and then landed at Nebraska. Unhappy with his playing time, he transferred closer to home at San Diego State, but missed all of 2019 after a resistance band snapped and hit him in the eye. He battled a foot injury throughout 2020, but returned healthy with career-bests as a super senior in 2021. Bell doesn’t have breakaway speed, but he follows his blocks and is quick to clear holes. He is below average in two critical areas that lower his draft grade: ball security (fumbled six times in 2021) and third-down ability. He doesn’t have the foundation of a sturdy pass blocker and was rarely targeted as a receiver. Overall, Bell is a highly determined competitor with vision and cutting skills, but needs to prove his reliability, especially on passing downs, for an NFL team to trust him.

Nazeeh (NAH-zee) Johnson was an all-conference receiver and defensive back at Millbrook High, rushing for 1,093 yards and posting four interceptions as a senior. He heard from several FCS programs but accepted a preferred walk-on spot at Marshall (put on scholarship in spring 2018). A four-year starter, he rotated between nickel and free safety and recorded consistent production each season. Johnson plays with outstanding balance in coverage with the athletic twitch to mirror and make sudden start-stops (his elite testing numbers match his athleticism on tape). He is a solid wrap tackler, although his lack of ideal length and play strength might be an issue in the NFL. A team captain, the coaches use phrases like “unselfish dude” and “tough as dirt” to describe him. Overall, Johnson lacks ideal size and will be tardy with his reads at times, but his explosiveness and resilient attitude are traits worth the investment as a nickel defender and special teamer.

Jacob “Jake” Hansen was a three-sport athlete at East Lake High, posting 103 tackles as a senior. He was introduced to football by his father (Shad), who played linebacker at BYU (1989-92) and holds the Cougars’ single-season tackle record (193). A three-star recruit, Hansen flipped from Iowa State to Illinois and had a productive career for the Illini, leading the team in tackles twice (his 12 forced fumbles are second in school history behind Simeon Rice’s 13). However, his career also included three season-ending injuries, including a torn ACL to each knee. Hansen is quick to key and get a head start, and his quick recognition skills expand his range as a defender (averaged 7.9 tackles per game the last four years). He needs to be more fierce as a block-shedder, and his man-cover awareness is suspect. Overall, Hansen is a tone-setter with above average read-react and tackling skills, but he can be eaten up by blockers, and his injury history is an obvious concern.

Dion Novil (no-VILL), who is one of six boys, grew up in West Palm Beach, Fla. before moving to Abilene prior to his sophomore year. He enrolled at Wylie High, where he earned All-District honors as a junior and senior defensive lineman, finishing his senior year with 41 tackles, 14.0 tackles for loss and 4.0 sacks. He was also the District MVP in basketball. A two-star recruit, he signed with North Texas and started every game at nose guard the last three seasons (only the fourth player in UNT history to reach 37.0 tackles for loss). Novil can be moved when he is late out of his stance, but he is built like an ox with his broad, strong frame, forcing holds when he gets rumbling downhill. He played a lot of snaps for a nose (averaged 52 snaps per game over the last three years) and always gave steady effort on tape. Overall, Novil won’t create many pass rush opportunities, but he is active with above-average gap power when he plays on time, projecting as a potential backup.

Jeremiah Hall played on the offensive line in youth football in Charlotte before shifting to tight end and more of an H-back role at Zebulon B. Vance High, posting 1,005 yards of total offense and 22 touchdowns as a senior. A three-star recruit, he filled the Dimitri Flowers role in Lincoln Riley’s offense for the Sooners, lining up in the slot, inline and backfield. He tied for third on the team in receptions as a senior captain, averaging double-digit yards per catch each of the last four years. Hall is a sure-handed receiver (good luck finding drops on his film) and runs like a jackhammer with the ball in his hands. He isn’t the most instinctive blocker, but there are no doubts about his competitive toughness as a lead back and alert pass protector with his wide base and eager hands. Overall, Hall isn’t a dynamic athlete and there are only so many NFL roster spots for his skill set, but he is a sturdy blocker and dependable pass catcher with the makeup for special teams.

Ryder Anderson, who is the younger brother of former Oklahoma running back Rodney Anderson, helped Katy High to a state championship as a junior, lining up at defensive end and tight end. A three-star recruit, he was courted by SEC and Ivy League programs, signing with Ole Miss. After four seasons of steadily improving production with the Rebels, he transferred for his final season, joining the Hoosiers. He posted career-best numbers and earned All-Big Ten honors as a senior. Anderson looks the part with his size, strength and length to lock out and control the point of attack. He has a powerful stab move, but his first step quickness [179] is average with heavy legs that lack shifty movements. He offers inside-outside versatility, although his lack of twitch might limit his playmaking radius vs. the run. Overall, Anderson doesn’t have much in his bag of tricks as a pass rusher, but he is a bulldozer downhill with ammo in his hands to power through soft shoulders.

Jequez Ezzard (Ezzurd) was born in Atlanta and attended Hapeville Charter Academy, where he was an All-Conference receiver and return man. Lightly recruited, he signed with FCS-level Howard, where he had back-to-back standout seasons before missing the 2019 season because of injury. He transferred to Sam Houston State and led the Bearkats to the 2020-21 FCS National Championship, earning All-American honors as a junior and senior. Ezzard has outstanding instincts with the ball in his hands, using elusive start-stop quickness to zig when defenders zag. He accounted for 10 receptions of 40-plus yards during the past two seasons but will struggle with physicality at the line and the catch point. He scored a touchdown once every 4.7 catches in college and averaged 12.3 yards as a punt returner. Overall, Ezzard is undersized and lacks ideal top-end speed, but he catches the ball well and skillfully shifts gears to force pursuit off-balance as a slot or returner.

Chase Garbers was a three-year varsity starter at Corona del Mar, finishing his prep career with 69.0 percent completions, 7,970 passing yards and 90 passing touchdowns. A four-star recruit, he was courted by SEC and Ivy League programs, but he stayed on the West Coast, where he was a four-year starter. He was the team MVP as a senior and set several career highs as a passer and rusher, finishing with the school records for rushing yards and rushing scores by a quarterback. Garbers is a good-sized athlete with the body movements to maneuver the pocket and work his feet to his target. He delivers with touch to layer throws over coverage, although his deep-third placement isn’t a strength. His read-to-read timing is inconsistent, and he tends to lock on his preferred option. Overall, Garbers doesn’t have too many traits to get excited about, but he has enough mobility and short-to-intermediate accuracy to get the attention of coaches in an NFL camp.

Samuel Womack III earned first team all-city, all-metro and all-state as a senior at East English Village Prep, eclipsing 1,000 receiving yards on offense and recording 11 interceptions on defense. He also played basketball, and his focus on AAU tournaments instead of recruiting camps contributed to him not receiving any Division I offers out of high school. He walked on at Toledo and led the MAC in passes defended three consecutive seasons, finishing with a school-record 45 passes defended. Even though he received a scholarship in 2018, Womack still competes with that underdog mentality and shows the innate ability to judge the catch point. He is a composed athlete with oily hips and quick acceleration to attach himself to routes. He has the toughness for the run game, but his consistency can improve. Overall, Womack will be overlooked due to his size, but his competitive nature, body control and on-ball production belong in the NFL, ideally suited in the nickel.

Zyon Gilbert was born and raised in Montgomery and was a two-way player at Jefferson Davis High. He finished his prep career with eight interceptions and five total touchdowns, twice earning all-state honors. A three-star recruit, he committed to Florida Atlantic, where he saw immediate snaps at safety before moving full-time to cornerback in 2020. He led FAU in passes defended each of the past three seasons. Gilbert is a tall, slender athlete with light feet to quickly change directions and accelerate to top speed. He got away with it in college thanks to his athleticism, but he plays too much on his heels and can be late to anticipate route breaks, especially in bail coverage. He isn’t shy getting physical vs. the run, although he needs to be more subtle with his aggressiveness to avoid flags. Overall, Gilbert isn’t a technically refined player, but he mirrors well from his pedal and has the vertical speed to compete for corner snaps on the perimeter.

Sam Okuayinonu (oh-KOO-whan-ohh) lived in Liberia until he was 12, when he and his mother fled the country for the U.S., settling in Lowell, Mass. He was a soccer player who tried and quit football as a junior at Lowell High before picking it back up as a senior. Because of grades and his inexperience on the football field, he spent three seasons at the junior college level. He transferred to Maryland (over Oregon), where he spent the past three seasons, posting career bests as a senior in 2021. Okuayinonu has a stout, muscular body type and flashes the violence in his hands to work through and off blockers to the quarterback. He is somewhat of a tweener, lacking ideal length and arc speed for the outside and struggling to find consistency as an interior defensive lineman. Overall, Okuayinonu plays with more effort than instinct, but his active hands and natural power wear down blockers and allow him to be disruptive from different alignments.

Craig “Russ” Yeast II transferred from Fremont Ross High (Ohio) to Center Grove (Ind.) as a senior and was the Gatorade Player of the Year with 2,127 yards of total offense. A four-star recruit, he signed with Louisville as a cornerback before moving to safety in 2019. After four seasons, he transferred to Kansas State and put himself on the NFL radar with a career year. His father (Craig Yeast) is the head football coach at Kentucky Wesleyan and set the SEC receiving record at Kentucky before a nine-year career in the NFL (1999-2006). Russ is a competitive yet disciplined player to react quickly in short zone or show his range from the post. He has a knack for timely swats at the catch point (led Big 12 in passes defended in 2021). He is willing in the run game, but can find himself attached to blockers. Overall, Yeast has cornerback-safety tweener traits, but he is an urgent player with the flow skills and cover awareness to compete for a nickel role in the NFL.

Benjamin “BJ” Baylor was a four-year starting running back at Wharton High and earned District MVP honors as a senior with 1,997 rushing yards. A three-star recruit, Oregon State was his only Power 5 scholarship offer, and he signed with the Beavers. After waiting his turn behind Jermar Jefferson and Artavis Pierce, he became the starter as a senior and was the only player in the Pac-12 to average better than 100 yards rushing per game in 2021. Although indecisive at times when the defined run isn’t there, Baylor runs with burst and attitude to maximize yardage when he picks a lane. He is able to work around early traffic thanks to his agile footwork and acceleration to escape out the back door. There is plenty of tread left on his tires, but he is also inexperienced in areas (four fumbles in 2021). Overall, Baylor needs to become more reliable with his ball security, blocking and pass-catching, but he runs with foot speed and pacing to gash defenses.

Jake Hummel was an all-state performer in football and track at Dowling Catholic and won three state championships in three years in varsity football. A three-star recruit, he signed with Iowa State and followed in the footsteps of his father (Perry), who was an All-American wrestler with the Cyclones (1979-82) and the runner-up national champion in 1980. Jake was a reserve (886 career special teams snaps) during his first three years and combined for 157 tackles as an All-Big 12 starter the past two seasons. Hummel floats well in space with terrific diagnose skills and a feel for angles to find the quickest route to the play. He battles his tail off at contact, but he can be overwhelmed by blockers and has room to tidy up his tackling. His active feet and alert eyes will lead him to the football in coverage. Overall, Hummel doesn’t always play up to his testing numbers, but he processes well with NFL worthy athleticism and toughness to be a core special teamer.

Quandre (QUAN-dray) Mosely was born and raised in Brunswick and played basketball and football (wide receiver) at Glynn Academy. He went the junior college route and spent two seasons at Eastern Arizona Community College, playing both receiver and cornerback. A three-star juco recruit, he committed to Kentucky over Oregon and Utah. He primarily came off the bench for the Wildcats the past three seasons but saw his role expanded as a senior (36.7 defensive snaps per game). Mosely is a long-limbed athlete with impressive plant, drive and burst ability to jump passing lanes or arrive with the ball at the receiver. He plays with light feet, but needs to show more trust in his transitional movement skills. He tends to misjudge when to take gambles. Overall, Mosely must continue to develop his play recognition and press technique, but he displays the foot quickness, twitch and length to be a developmental cornerback for a press-man NFL defense.

Diego Fagot (fuh-GO) was home-schooled by his mother (Annmarie) and played sports at Calvary Christian Academy. At linebacker, he earned All-State honors three times and was named the county’s top athlete in both football and track as a senior (won back-to-back state titles in the shot put). A three-star recruit, he considered Pitt and UCF before connecting with Navy. He settled in as the middle linebacker and led the team in tackles each of the past three seasons. Fagot is a physical, downhill defender who triggers without wasting steps, hitting gaps with purpose and balance. He plays with relentless pursuit traits and the thumping skills to work off blocks and be a sound tackler.
