Campbell Trophy, which is known as the "academic Heisman") … two-time team captain and Strength and Conditioning Award winner as a senior … durable and dependable, starting 47 straight games to finish his career.
beast_weaknesses: Stubby arms with an undersized, maxed-out body type … his lack of length will limit his ability to control NFL-level nose tackles … spends a lot of time hand-fighting without creating movement in the ground game … tends to get grabby when he falls behind … has room to improve his balance once he gets out in space … was almost exclusively a right guard at South Carolina, with only 14 of his 3,195 offensive snaps coming at center … missed the 2018 season because of a non-football foot injury from high school that required surgery (September 2018).

beast_summary: A four-year starter at Duke, Heyward played MIKE linebacker in head coach Mike Elko’s 4-2-5 base scheme. He posted 80-plus tackles each of the past three seasons and consistently filled up the stat sheet without missing games. Heyward is a smart, instinctive run defender who is quick to respond, see through blocks to avoid engagement and get the ball carrier on the ground. He needs to play with more patience and control for better positioning as a take-on player and tackler, but his long arms help compensate. Overall, Heyward doesn’t have ideal agility or change of direction with questionable range in coverage, but he is long, fast and dependable and should at worst be a regular special teamer in the NFL. He has the skill level to be this year’s version of Ernest Jones.
beast_strengths: Workable frame with above average arm length … reads his keys and feels blocking pressure to find the ball carrier … extends his long, stiff reach and presses into blockers to separate and make plays at the line of scrimmage … shows the pursuit speed to chase down his prey … his long arms allow him to lasso ball carriers other linebackers can’t … strong fingers/hands/wrists to finish tackles once he makes contact … team captain who leads by the example of his work habits … durable and finished his career with 40 consecutive starts … averaged 8.0 tackles per game over his junior and senior seasons … was a regular on kick and punt coverages the last four seasons (14 tackles on 629 special teams snaps).
beast_weaknesses: Moves with some stiffness in his lower body and midsection, slowing his quick direction changes … accelerates well to close, but doesn’t play with explosive movements … needs a clear runway to really see that 4.5 speed … reads too quickly at times and runs himself into blocks or misdirection … lead blockers can pick him off before he finds the football … was mugged up on the 2022 North Carolina tape and needs to get stronger to fill this type of role vs. NFL offensive linemen … lacks desired coverage range and will struggle to match NFL athletes in space.

beast_summary: Jacob Slade grew up in the heart of Buckeye country and attended Olentangy High. As a senior, he earned All-State honors as a left tackle while also being named All-District on defense with 73 tackles and 13 tackles for loss. A three-star recruit, he committed to Michigan State along with his twin brother (Zachary), who is also a defensive end. His college production doesn’t jump off the page, but he was disruptive versus the run on his 2021 tape and when healthy in 2022. Slade plays under his pads with the quick hands to get into blocks and establish gap leverage. Against double-teams, he can hold his ground or knife through to make stops in the hole. His pass rush is based more on effort and desire than a technically proficient attack. He missed too many tackles on his 2022 tape. Overall, Slade’s tight lower body restricts his range and movements, but he is stout and instinctive at the point of attack, projecting as a rotational one-technique run stuffer.

Kahlef (kuh-LEAF) Hailassie (huh-LOSS-ee) started playing football at age 7 and eventually became an All-Conference safety at Elk Grove High. He also was a standout receiver and returner. A three-star recruit, he flipped from Colorado to Washington State on signing day before making a late switch to Oregon. He spent two years at the juco level before transferring to WKU for his final two seasons, and he earned All-CUSA honors at cornerback as both a junior and senior. Hailassie is a twitchy athlete who can mirror and match, although he will surrender separation when caught upright and on his heels. He has outstanding length to crowd the catch point but must do a better locating to pick off passes. As a tackler, he stays balanced as a finisher when working from high to low. He plays fearless with a brash attitude. Overall, Hailassie needs to play with more disciplined eyes, but he is long, fluid and controlled in his movements to cover from press or off coverage.

A four-year starter at North Dakota State, Gindorff was an inline Y tight end in offensive coordinator Tyler Roehl’s run-heavy, gap-power scheme. Despite never playing the position before college, he joined the tight end room (which included Cody Mauch) when he arrived in Fargo and turned himself into an NFL prospect. Gindorff graduated with an accounting degree at North Dakota State, but he also earned a master’s in blocking and takes a lot of pride in that being the strength of his game. He made his limited pass-catching targets count, but his ordinary athleticism will limit ways to get him the football. Overall, the medical feedback after back-to-back season-ending ankle surgeries will determine if Gindorff is drafted or not, but when healthy, he catches the ball well and relishes the dirty work as an inline blocker. He projects as a throwback Y tight end capable of winning a No. 2 blocking role.
beast_strengths: Looks the part with a thick, long torso and strong build … quick first step to gain early blocking advantages … fits his hands and gets his hips/feet into position to wall off or seal … flashes the play strength to create pop and re-leverage himself mid-engagement … enjoys the dirty work as an inline blocker … drives his feet until the echo of the whistle … has the ability to adjust and snatch the football … enormous wingspan expands his catch radius … at his best when operating with short-area routes … his post-catch determination and balance will help him slip tackle attempts … hard worker and intelligent (34 out of 36 on his ACT) and voted a team captain.
beast_weaknesses: Average athletic profile with tightness in his hips … doesn’t have the short-area quickness to sink and separate at the top of routes … will struggle to threaten the seam versus NFL man-cover talent … a lot of his route spacing was created by play action in college … guilty of relying on his body to finish catches … head ducker and willing to stray from his blocking technique to overwhelm defenders … already 24 years old … faced primarily FCS competition (only three of his 44 catches in college came against an FBS opponent) … suffered a broken fibula and damaged right ankle ligaments during the playoffs (December 2021); the injury didn’t heal correctly and he required a second procedure (October 2022), which ended his 2022 season.

beast_summary: A three-year starter at Washington, Bainivalu held down the right guard spot in offensive coordinator Ryan Grubb’s pro-style spread scheme. If he hears his name called in the 2023 NFL Draft, he will be just the second Fiji-born player to be drafted (linebacker Freddy Keiaho, who was drafted in the 2006 NFL Draft, was the first). Bainivalu wants to be a power blocker and unload on defenders, but he doesn’t consistently displace or overwhelm his man because of fundamental inconsistences. Although he doesn’t offer much position flexibility, he offers proven durability — no other Husky played more snaps (1,892) than he did over the last three seasons. Overall, Bainivalu looks the part with his size and length, but he ends up on the ground way too often because of balance and technique issues that must be cleaned up to survive NFL roster cuts.
beast_strengths: Outstanding size, length and hands for the position … uses his long arms to fit into the chests of defenders … doesn’t often get bullied into the pocket, because of his ability to sink his weight and anchor … uses his girth to stubbornly get into position to wall off run lanes … functional mobility on short-side pulls … committed only four penalties (two holding calls, one false start, one unnecessary roughness) in his 31 career starts … worked his way into the starting lineup at right guard in the final few games of 2019 and didn’t give up his spot, finishing with 31 straight starts.
beast_weaknesses: Not an explosive blocker … aggressive puncher, but he often throws his hands too early or off target, allowing the defender to avoid him … needs to keep his feet underneath him to avoid being tossed … spends too much time on the ground … inefficient movement skills and looks like a fish out of water when asked to execute out in space … late reaching second-level targets and struggles to break down in space versus athletic linebackers … inconsistent communication and awareness on blitz pickup and delayed pressures can fool him … served a three-game suspension to start the 2019 season … will turn 25 late in his NFL rookie season … played left tackle in high school but was a right guard only in college.

beast_summary: A four-year starter at Rutgers, Izien was the strong safety in defensive coordinator Joe Harasymiak’s 4-2-5 scheme. He entered the starting lineup midway through his redshirt freshman season and started every game since (41), becoming just the 14th player in school history to reach 300 tackles. Izien is an explosive mover with rabbit feet and the physicality to operate near the line of scrimmage. He needs to do a better job allowing the game to come to him with not enough ball production to justify his overaggressive nature. Overall, Izien’s shorter stature will remove him from consideration for several teams, but he has the toughness, speed and quick-twitch reflexes to be a core special-teamer and backup. His impressive pro-day performance will earn him a secondary look by evaluators.
beast_strengths: Rocked-up, muscular build with decent length considering his height … explosive athlete with immediate acceleration once he triggers … appears smooth in his cover transitions and quickly closes ground … feisty and tough in man coverage versus slots (tight ends and receivers) … has rabbit feet for leaping opportunities at the catch point … aggressive in run support, striking with hip snap and finishing with hand strength … made a concerted effort to minimize missed tackles on 2022 tape compared to 2021 … extensive special teams resume (572 snaps) with a blocked punt as a senior … maniacal worker in the weight room to maintain his body at peak condition … durable and played in every game the past four years …
beast_weaknesses: Short with a maxed-out frame … quickly makes up ground, but will lose phase too easily at the top of routes because of his guessing … can be drawn out from his spot by the eyes of the quarterback … bites on initial route movements and late to sort through combinations … subpar ball instincts and struggles with his back to the quarterback … massive size differences between him and NFL tight ends will be tough to overcome … play strong, but can be too easily held up by blockers … zero interceptions and only eight pass breakups over his final 25 college games.

beast_summary: Devonnsha (duh-VAWN-shay) Maxwell, who is one of five children, prepped at Valdosta High where he was a defensive end and tight end. He led the program to a 14-2 record and a state title in 2016, finishing his senior year with 69 tackles, 10 tackles for loss and 5.5 sacks. He also threw the shot put and discus. He signed with FCS Chattanooga and became a five-year starter, setting school and SoCon records for career sacks (37.5). Maxwell showed his disruptive nature from various alignments (everywhere 4i to nose), generating pressure with his quickness off the ball and nimble feet to feel his way through gaps (55.5 tackles for loss in 47 career games). He was asked to play a lot of snaps and would coast on some plays but played well versus top competition (two sacks on 2022 Illinois tape). Overall, Maxwell will struggle to control blocks and maintain his base laterally, but his first step burst and power create havoc, projecting best as a rotational one-gapper.

Derek Parish grew up outside of Houston and attended Pearland High, where he was a standout pass rusher, earning All-District honors as a senior with 12.0 sacks. A three-star recruit, he was recruited to Houston as a linebacker before moving to edge rusher, where he spent the majority of his college career. He was on pace for a record-setting senior year before a torn bicep injury. But he returned in time for the East-West Shrine Bowl, where he transitioned to fullback (played only eight offensive snaps in his six college seasons). His tape is a balanced mix of unrelenting play speed and urgency. He has a muscular frame and caught the ball well during Shrine practices but is understandably raw as a route runner and blocker. Overall, Parish has a limited body of work on offense, but he is passionate about football with elite competitive toughness, which will make it extremely difficult for a coaching staff to cut him. He has the makeup of a special teams ace.

Isaiah “Zay” Bolden was a receiver and defensive back at Bartram Trail High before transferring to Wesley Chapel (though he was temporarily dismissed from the team in 2017). He was also a standout track athlete, winning conference titles in the 100 (10.54) and 200 meters (21.74). A four-star recruit, he flipped from Florida State to Willie Taggart and Oregon, then flipped back to FSU after Taggart was hired there as head coach. After two seasons, he left the team early in the 2020 season and transferred to Jackson State to play for Deion Sanders. Bolden led the FCS in kick return yards (36.9 average) in 2021 and became a starting cornerback in 2022. Although his technique and play recognition are underdeveloped, he moves differently than most his size. As a return specialist, he has special acceleration. Overall, Bolden isn’t a squeaky-clean prospect and is unproven in several areas, but his rare mix of speed, length and explosive traits is ready to be cultivated.

A four-year starter at Arkansas, Wagner was entrenched at right tackle in former offensive coordinator Kendal Briles’ zone-based scheme. He returned as a super senior and team captain in 2022 and had his best season, also signing an NIL deal with WWE (with his long hair and size, professional wrestling could be in his future). Wagner is a long positional blocker with the strength in his hands to latch and drive or get into the chest of defenders before they can enter their rush. However, his sustain skills are shaky and he can too easily get off schedule in space. Overall, Wagner is an experienced, well-schooled, strong blocker, but his upright pads and below-average athleticism will create balance issues against NFL talent. He projects as a potential backup right tackle in the NFL for a power-run scheme.
beast_strengths: A large human with his taller stature and long arms … flashes strength in his hand presence to strike with pop in his pass sets and grip and rip in the run game … physical at contact to mash and move bodies from the lane … able to settle down against the power rush to create a solid base … stays on his schedule in pass protection to meet and mirror initial movements … his coaches speak highly of his mental and physical toughness (head coach Sam Pittman: “He’s tougher than an ol’ billy goat.”) … voted a 2022 team captain … was a veteran presence in the Arkansas locker room and someone that his teammates relied on … played in 53 games in college, including 40 starts versus SEC competition.
beast_weaknesses: Doesn’t have ideal body coordination and lower-body flexibility … struggles to stay centered versus shifty counters in space … his feet get clunky and his base narrows when on the move … will panic at times in space and gets too far out in front of his feet … his upright style will make it tougher to anchor versus NFL rushers … doesn’t stray too far from the line of scrimmage as a downfield blocker … missed three games as junior because of a broken finger that required surgery (October 2011); was limited during 2022 spring practices with a back injury.

beast_summary: Bumper Pool, who legally changed his first name from James to Bumper at the age of 16, grew up in Lucas and started playing at the pee-wee level. He was a four-year letterman at Lovejoy High and combined for 424 tackles over his final three seasons. A four-star recruit, he grew up an Arkansas fan and passed on offers from Alabama, Michigan and others. Pool recorded 90-plus tackles in each of the last four seasons and departs as the school’s all-time leading tackler (441). He injured his hip in November 2022 and required bilateral labral surgery, which sidelined him for the pre-draft process. Pool does a terrific job with his run fits, plugging gaps or containing outside. He’s not explosive, but he thumps at contact and moves with passable change-of-direction skills to chase down runners in pursuit. Overall, Pool has only average speed and can be late recognizing things in coverage, but he is a tackling machine who knows how to leverage the run.
br_positives: – Solid athlete with solid movement skills to help defend against outside runs and in coverage. | – Knows when to pick his spots to shoot an open gap versus the run and get unblocked tackles for a short gain. | – Takes on blocks with his hands which, combined with his lateral movement skills, allows him to escape against outside runs. | – Good at reading the running back's path versus zone runs to put himself in a position to make plays. | – Hustle player.
br_negatives: – Instincts in coverage are a work in progress. Late to read pass versus play action, struggles to locate threats in zone and will lose his man when playing man coverage, ending up covering grass far too often. | – Lacks strength to hold his ground against inside runs when blocked by offensive linemen. Occasionally ends up on the ground. | – Tries to work around blocks and will take himself out of his gap. | – Dives and leaves his feet when making open-field tackles, leading to misses. | 2022 STATS | – 11 G, 92 TOT (37 SOLO), 4.5 TFL, 2 SK, 3 PD

beast_summary: A two-year starter at Louisiana, Jefferson was an outside wide receiver in offensive coordinator Tim Leger’s balanced scheme. After three years at Alabama State, he continued to mature on the field for the Ragin’ Cajuns and was one of the team’s go-to weapons (averaged one touchdown every 5.4 receptions over his five college seasons). Jefferson has better on-field speed (21.63 mph) than what his 40-yard dash would indicate, using his long, swift strides to win on vertical tracks. His size and leaping skills help him attack the catch point, but he needs to be more of a presence in the red zone (only one of his 11 touchdowns at Louisiana was a red-zone catch). Overall, Jefferson is a role-specific pass catcher, but he has the acceleration, body control and vertical tracking skills to compete for a fourth or fifth receiver spot on an NFL depth chart. His skills as a gunner will boost his chances of staying off the cut list.
beast_strengths: Tall, limber athlete … builds up his speed with long strides to eat up cushion and put corners on their heels … productive vertical threat, getting behind coverage with his straight-line speed … attacks defenders at the top of the stem, allowing him to work to open space … solid ball tracking and frames his hands well to attack (sometimes at the highest point, other times not) … strong leaper to adjust mid-air and win on jump-ball opportunities … body control allows him to sidestep the first defender for extra yardage … rigorous and fundamentally sound perimeter blocker … was forced to grow up at an early age because of his father’s cancer battles … became a gunner on punt coverages as a super senior in 2022 and totaled three tackles.
beast_weaknesses: Very lean-muscled and lacks ideal bulk on his body … average play strength will be fiercely challenged by NFL defenders … not a true burner and won’t simply out-race NFL coverage … can be mugged by press corners, delaying his routes … needs to use better sink in and out of breaks to efficiently unfurl his long legs … inconsistent route awareness and can be late making adjustments … needs to better use his body positioning, especially at the first down sticks and in the red zone … fumbled twice in 2022.

beast_summary: Sean Clifford, who has a younger brother (Liam) on the Penn State roster, was a three-year starter at St. Xavier High School and led the Bombers to the Division I state championship in 2016. A four-star recruit, he committed to Penn State over several SEC offers and became the Nittany Lions’ all-time leader in passing yards, passing touchdowns and completion percentage. Clifford was the first player in his high school’s history to be a two-time captain and was only the second four- time captain in Penn State history. He was effective in a college RPO-based system, and his willingness to hang tough in the pocket or utilize his mobility helped keep drives alive. However, he needs to get through his progressions quicker and make things easier on his receivers to finish catches. Overall, Clifford throws well on the move and NFL teams love his toughness and smarts, but his current decision-making and ball placement are too inconsistent for what is required at the next level.

Arther “Art” Green grew up in the St. Louis area and played safety and receiver at Parkway Central High. He also set the school record in the 100 meters (11.04 seconds) and placed top 10 in the state in relays. Because of academics, he went the juco route, and he moved to cornerback full-time in 2018. A three-star juco recruit, he signed with Houston (over SEC offers) in 2020 and became a full-time starter in 2022, leading the team with 10 passes defended). Green has press- man size, but has also shown considerable growth understanding zone concepts and route recognition to better know when to stay patient and when to swoop in for plays on the ball. His footwork lacks desired fluidity and technical grace, which hurts his ability to stay connected. His look-and-lean and ball skills flashed during East- West Shrine Bowl practices. Overall, some NFL teams follow a simple formula at corner: They want tall, long athletes who can run. Green falls in that category.

A three-year starter at Cincinnati, Taylor was a Y tight end (mostly inline) and part of a rotation in former offensive coordinator Gino Guidugli’s spread RPO offense. A highly sought-after recruit out of high school, he wasn’t a high-volume target for the Bearcats with only 69 catches in 60 games played (and only one catch of 20-plus yards in 2022). Taylor is a good-sized athlete and maximizes his catch radius to pull down throws away from his eyeline. He battles as a blocker and creates solid fits with his pad level, but he will have a tough time matching up at the point of attack in the NFL. Overall, Taylor has a very average skill set and doesn’t have the resume of a playmaker, but his basketball background is evident with the way he moves and catches the football, giving evaluators optimism about his developmental upside. He might be able to fend for a rotational No. 3 tight end role.
beast_strengths: Sturdy frame and worked his tail off to rework his body composition (didn’t start lifting weights until college) … catches the ball well with his hands … able to create a step of separation when he gets rolling vertically … effectively uses shoulder/body moves before making 90-degree cuts at the top of routes … keeps his legs pumping to finish forward as a ball carrier … competitive blocker and has the lower-body flexibility to create leverage at contact … applies sound techniques and stays after the block … his coaches speak highly of his maturation since high school … was a regular on punt coverages his final three seasons at Cincinnati.
beast_weaknesses: Builds to speed and not a one-step explosive mover … his patterns lack polish and breaks lack suddenness … needs a moment to get his route back on path after he meets early resistance from defenders … non-threatening after the catch and won’t make defenders miss in space … inconsistent sustain skills and gets caught trying to overwhelm targets instead of controlling them … long defenders can get into his frame … wasn’t highly targeted in college with an unimpressive receiving resume … missed one game as a senior.

beast_summary: Alex Palczewski (pal-CHESS-key), who is one of three boys, is the son of Polish immigrants who came to the U.S. in the mid-1980s. At Prospect, he was a four-sport letterman (football, track, water polo, wrestling), although he missed most of his junior season with a fractured vertebra. He was a starting senior right guard in Prospect’s option offense. A three-star recruit, Palczewski committed to Illinois where he set a Big Ten record with 65 career starts across three different positions (finished his career with 4,390 offensive snaps). He has physical, insistent hands at the point of attack and stays after his blocks to spring runs. Although he plays with quickness, his footwork gets sloppy in his pass sets and he finds himself out of control at the second level. His wide hands invite rushers to bully him. Overall, Palczewski has played a lot of football with experience at both tackle and guard, but he can too easily be knocked off balance and struggles to sustain.

Xavier Gipson was born and raised in Dallas and was a standout four-year cornerback at Woodrow Wilson High. He also played receiver as a senior and had 24 catches for 383 yards and five scores. He also ran track, posting a 10.55 100 meters. A three-star recruit, he committed to SMU (as a cornerback) but grades were an obstacle and he decided to go the FCS route, signing with Stephen F. Austin (as a wide receiver). He led SFA in receiving each of his four seasons and was responsible for four punt return scores. A slot-only receiver in college, Gipson is a speed demon with or without the football, using natural burst to quickly outflank pursuit. He is shifty in his routes, but his timing, tempo and footwork need to be sharper against NFL coverage. Despite smaller hands, he is dependable tracking and securing grabs away from his frame. Overall, Gipson is an undersized slot target, but his explosiveness allows him to make big plays on offense and special teams.

Ben Sims grew up in San Antonio and lived with his mother (Julie Sims-Louden) after his parents divorced when he was young. He attended Tom C. Clark High, where he led the team in receiving as a junior and senior. A three-star recruit, he committed to Matt Rhule and Baylor over Auburn and UTSA, his hometown school. Sims became the starter over his final three seasons and finished his career with the school record for touchdowns catches by a tight end (12). Although he builds his speed and lacks dynamic separation qualities, Sims is controlled within his routes to leverage in-breakers and make himself available to his quarterback. He has a sturdy base in pass protection but struggles to uncoil inline, and he is still learning how to properly use his hands/reach to fit and control his man in the run game. Overall, Sims is a balanced athlete with steady hands, but he isn’t a threat after the catch and needs to turn his losses into stalemates as an NFL blocker.

Tavion Thomas had a tough upbringing in Dayton and attended Dunbar High, where he combined for 2,670 rushing yards during his final two seasons. A three-star recruit, he had offers from Alabama, Ohio State and others, but academic issues forced him to Cincinnati. Thomas butted heads with the coaches and went the junior-college route for the 2020 season. He was sent home and was temporarily homeless back in Dayton, living out of his car with his one-year-old son. He found a home at Utah and led the team in rushing in both 2021 and 2022. A smooth, good-sized athlete, Thomas is a chore to bring down and consistently falls forward with his body strength. But his spotty vision and patience lead him into his own blockers at the line, and his ball security and pass-catching are suspect. Overall, Thomas needs to answer accountability questions with NFL teams, but he is a big-bodied runner with contact balance, power and pass-blocking skills.

br_positives: —Good size and length. | —Strong play-recognition skills.
br_negatives: —Tentative at point of contact, does not strike ball-carriers. | —Body control and change of direction is erratic. | —Lacks ideal athletic profile, a tad of a liability in coverage.

beast_summary: Griffin Hebert was a standout receiver at St. Thomas More High, helping the program to its first state title his senior year. He finished his prep career with more than 1,000 receiving yards and 24 touchdowns while also earning All-District honors in basketball. A two-star recruit, Hebert committed to Louisiana Tech, where he moved to tight end on the depth chart. As a super senior in 2022, he led all FBS tight ends in yards per catch (18.7) and lived beyond the sticks (78.3 percent of his grabs resulted in a first down or touchdown). Hebert has fantastic route-running athleticism with an explosive lower body to shake free underneath, win on vertical patterns or gash defenses as a RAC weapon. He is a try-hard blocker who gets in the way, but he doesn’t have the play strength to control or neutralize his man. Overall, Hebert’s remarkable testing numbers match his on-field athleticism before and after the catch. He can be a fun H-back for a creative NFL play caller.

Ronnie Brown grew up outside of Baltimore and played running back and defensive back at Sparrows Point High. He transferred to Dundalk High for his senior season and earned All-State honors with more than 1,500 yards rushing. A no-star recruit, he didn’t receive many looks from FBS programs and signed with Shepherd in Division II. He shared the backfield duties as a junior and had a breakout senior season, ranking No. 3 in the NCAA (all-divisions) with 199.9 all-purpose yards per game. Brown is a quick-footed ball carrier with lateral agility and vision to pick his way through traffic at the line. He is thin-boned and lacks the run strength or build desired for inside work. With soft hands and speed, he is a weapon as a returner and in space as a pass target (14.3 yards per catch). Overall, there might be a new “Ronnie Brown” at running back in the NFL, thanks to the Shepherd product’s play speed and pass-catching traits. Some scouts view him as a wide receiver.

br_positives: — Athletic player with quick feet and very good short-area quickness. Good deep speed with ability to recover downfield. | — Active in run support, aggressive tackler who doesn't shy from contact. | — Great ball skills. Has a knack for finding the ball.
br_negatives: — Undersized player who lacks overall length and size. | — Can lack coverage awareness at times. Below-average route recognition. | — Lacks strength in the run game, relies on quickness and struggles to set the edge. Tends to dive at ball-carrier's ankles at times.

beast_summary: Kaleb Hayes was born in Pasadena, Calif., and was primarily a quarterback at San Gorgonio High. He led the program to its first state title in 2016, combining for 5,749 yards (3,139 passing, 2,610 rushing) his junior and senior seasons. A three-star recruit, he signed with Oregon State (over BYU) as a cornerback and led the team in passes defended in 2019. He entered the transfer portal after the 2020 season but considered only BYU. He led the Cougars in passes defended both years in Provo. Hayes is a twitchy, urgent athlete with top-end speed and short-area burst to match up with NFL receivers. He needs to display more consistent composure to maintain phase and avoid penalties. He has great length to obstruct windows when he locates the ball, but he is still searching for his first interception. Overall, Hayes’ route processing and physicality need work, but he has the athletic traits to play sticky coverage. His elite pro day showing might get him drafted.

Durell Nchami (CHAM-ee) was a three-year starter at Paint Branch High and earned Conference Defensive Player of the Year honors as a senior with 10 tackles for loss and seven sacks. A three-star recruit, he grew up 15 minutes from College Park and committed to Maryland over Pitt, Syracuse and others. He showed immense promise when on the field, but he missed all of 2019 and most of 2021 with injuries. He totaled only 49 tackles in 32 career games, but a high percentage of those came in the backfield. Nchami looks the part of a pass rusher with his athletic build and long arms. He flashes speed to the edge and speed to power as a bull rusher, but he needs to develop a more coordinated attack with his hands to beat NFL blockers. He put too many missed tackles on tape and must stay under control. Overall, Nchami needs to prove he can stay healthy in the NFL, but he has disruptive burst when on the field to win the corner, dip and flatten to the quarterback.

Lance Boykin grew up playing football with his older brother, Ridge, who was a defensive end at Campbell (2015-2021). He attended High Point Christian Academy, where he combined for 1,560 rushing yards on offense and 14 interceptions on defense. A two-star “athlete” recruit, Boykin played corner at Old Dominion for three years before deciding to transfer to Coastal Carolina because of the coaching turnover. As a senior, he led the team in passes defended and interceptions. Boykin has long limbs and smartly uses his body length to smother receivers in press and get his hands on the football downfield. His confidence and route awareness are strengths of his game, but his lower-body burst doesn’t match his eyes, and his tight transitions leave him in recovery mode. He’s a strong tackler in the run game. Overall, Boykin lacks desired speed and twitch for the position, but he is long, physical and mentally tough — essential ingredients for an NFL press-man corner.
beast_strengths: of his game, but his lower-body burst doesn’t match his eyes, and his tight transitions leave him in recovery mode. He’s a strong tackler in the run game. Overall, Boykin lacks desired speed and twitch for the position, but he is long, physical and mentally tough — essential ingredients for an NFL press-man corner. GRADE: Priority Free Agent
br_positives: — Excellent length and size. Ideal for cornerback in the NFL. | — Very good ball skills and hands to catch the ball away from his body. | — Great vision in zone. Has a good feel for his threats and has the ability to bait the quarterback into throws. | — Triggers quickly to the run and quick game. Uses his quickness to dip and rip past blocks.
br_negatives: — Plays high in his backpedal, which can affect him sinking his hips and redirecting. | — Long strider with above-average speed and lack of recovery speed when beat. Has trouble with stop-and-go routes.

beast_summary: Keidron (KEE-drun) Smith comes from a family of athletes: Both of his parents played college basketball, and his sister (Kaylon) plays for Vanderbilt’s women’s basketball team. He starred in basketball (surpassed 1,000 points) and football (seven career interceptions) at Oxbridge Academy. A three-star recruit, he was a four-year starter at Ole Miss before transferring to Kentucky for his super-senior season, leading the Wildcats with a pair of interceptions in 2022. Smith has an extensive resume (60 games played in the SEC) and was dependable in coverage on tape (didn’t allow a completion over 25 yards in 2022). He uses his size and physicality to make receivers uncomfortable mid-route. That aggressiveness also carries over to the run game with his ability to trigger and finish downhill. Overall, Smith can be tied up against savvy route runners, but he is a good-sized athlete with length, ball skills and cover awareness, projecting best in a Cover-3 scheme.

Taron Vincent grew up around the game as the son of an All-Pro cornerback. His father (Troy) currently serves as the Executive Vice President of Football Operations for the NFL. Taron started his prep career at Gilman School in Baltimore before transferring to IMG Academy where he was named the 2017 National High School Defensive Player of the Year. A five-star recruit, he signed with the Buckeyes to play for legendary defensive line coach Larry Johnson. His career production doesn’t jump off the page, but he would often do the dirty work, eating up blocks and allowing the linebackers to flow to the football. He allows himself to get high at times and can be moved from his spot (see 2022 Rutgers tape), but with proper leverage and gap discipline, he anchors and controls the point of attack. Overall, Vincent isn’t a disruptive pass rusher, but he is assignment sound with a consistent motor and could find a rotation in the NFL as a run-plugging three-technique.

Malik Knowles was born in Lynwood, Calif. before moving in with his aunt and uncle in Mansfield at age 9. He was originally a running back, until a growth spurt moved him to receiver at Lake Ridge High, where he collected 15 receiving touchdowns as a senior. A three-star recruit, he signed with Kansas State and now leaves ranked top five in program history in all-purpose yards (3,998). He averaged 27.7 yards per kick return with three scores and posted consistent receiving production. Knowles has quick, steady hands and shows quickness out of breaks to create pockets of separation for his quarterback. He can win deep with his speed, but his routes can be easily affected by defenders, and he must continue working to get open. He was unable to work out for NFL teams pre-draft because of a PCL repair (February 2023). Overall, Knowles has NFL talent as a receiver and kick returner, but he must become more consistent with the details of the position.

A two-year starter at Central Michigan, Nichols was the bell-cow back in offensive coordinator Paul Petrino’s multiple run scheme. He earned MAC Offensive Player of the Year honors in 2021 with an FBS-best 2,186 all-purpose yards and 1,848 rushing yards, but his rushing yards per game dropped from 142.2 to only 68.4 in 2022 as he battled injury. With his blend of quickness and power, Nichols can be a tackle breaker and won’t need gaping holes to reach the second level. But he can be methodical at times as he follows his blocks and needs to better anticipate openings before they present themselves. Overall, Nichols is a productive, determined runner with solid feel between the tackles, but his next-level potential will be capped by a lack of creativity with the ball in his hands and inconsistent passing-down skills. His workhorse approach could get him on the field in the right situation.
beast_strengths: Fills out his uniform well and built like an NFL back … patient, coordinated footwork at the line of scrimmage … able to read, press and make sound decisions on zone runs … squares his pads and runs with physicality and strength to force his way through narrow holes … not shy breaking out a stiff-arm … has the mentality of a workhorse back (averaged 29.3 offensive touches during his 2021 season) … soft hands to secure throws away from his frame … led CMU in rushing each of the past three seasons … his 1,848 rushing yards in 2021 were the second-most in a single-season in school history.
beast_weaknesses: Runs big, but inconsistent pad level makes himself too much of a target for tacklers … not a sudden ball carrier with limited wiggle in confined spaces … average acceleration through the hole and doesn’t have breakaway speed … can run with power or finesse but tends to be inconsistent when choosing which avenue to use … willing in pass protection, but his technique and execution are below average … too many focus drops on his tape (five in 2022) … missed chunks of his final season because of a toe injury (October 2022), sitting out three full games and parts of others.

br_positives: — Feisty player who is ultra competitive. Didn't back down to any of the competition from the 2022 season. | — Quick feet with very good body control. Keeps a good base and plays with good balance. | — Aggressive against the run. Triggers quickly to what he sees.
br_negatives: — Undersized player who lacks both ideal height and size. | — Poor eye discipline at times. Eyes can get locked onto the quarterback for too long.

beast_summary: A three-year starter at LSU, Baskerville played SAM linebacker in defensive coordinator Matt House’s scheme (his fourth defensive coordinator in his five seasons in Baton Rouge). After struggling with academics as an underclassman, he returned as a fifth-year senior (led the team in tackles) and did everything that was asked of the coaches and support staff to get his grades back on track to graduate. Baskerville diagnoses well downhill to flow with leverage, diagnose pullers and finish at the ball carrier. However, his range and instincts are much better vs. the run than the pass. Overall, Baskerville is football smart and triggers without wasting steps, but his athletic and strength profiles are very average and tougher to overcome at the NFL level. His special teams background and coachability will help his chances of earning a roster spot.
beast_strengths: Patient diagnose skills vs. the run and reacts quickly to play development … scrapes well laterally to mirror runs and stay ahead of pullers … works to keep his pads square while avoiding climbers and filling gaps … knows when to take on blocks or when to sidestep them … strong wrap and drag-down tackler and is a consistent finisher (see 2022 Tennessee tape) … follows the quarterback’s eyes to passing lanes (led team in passes defended in 2022) … communicates with his teammates well pre-snap … showed focus and determination to change the narrative about his academics and earn his degree (head coach Brian Kelly: “He has been inspirational in everything he has done.”) … saw a lot of special teams action (567 career snaps) with a pair of punt blocks.
beast_weaknesses: Lacks ideal size and length by NFL standards … can be neutralized in the hole and struggles to escape once engulfed by blockers … doesn’t have ideal play strength in his upper or lower bodies … average speed, and doesn’t consistently close the gap … his hip tightness shows with quick direction changes in the open field … loses track of backs and tight ends in man coverage … better box tackler than in the open field, which also shows on special teams (more missed tackles than tackles on special teams coverages) … was suspended from school because of grades and didn’t participate with the team in spring 2021.

beast_summary: Tim DeMorat, the youngest of four kids, grew up on the Atlantic coast in Florida. He played baseball and football at Viera High School, passing for 4,518 yards and 45 touchdowns his final two seasons. A no-star recruit, DeMorat received four FCS-level offers and committed to Fordham, becoming the starter as a true freshman in 2018. As a senior, he led the FCS in passing yards and leaves as one of the top passers in FCS and Patriot League history, having set the league records for passing yards and touchdowns (career and single-season), while playing in a wide-split offense, DeMorat has a strong arm and shows a natural feel for recognizing coverages and layering throws in between defenders. He tends to linger on his preferred read and will lead defenders to the football. Overall, DeMorat must develop his eye discipline to be a consistent small-window thrower in the NFL, but he is a functional athlete with the arm and intangibles to be a developmental option.

A one-year starter at Penn State, Tinsley was primarily an outside receiver in offensive coordinator Mike Yurcich’s RPO-based scheme. He had to learn five different offenses (at three different stops) in his five years in college, but he quickly digested the Penn State playbook and connected with quarterback Sean Clifford, who was also his roommate. What Tinsley doesn’t offer as a deep threat, he makes up with his crisp quickness underneath and finishing skills at the catch point. However, the absence of high-end explosiveness limits his special teams value and ability to be more than a possession target. Overall, Tinsley is well-liked by evaluators because of his fluid movements, ball skills and football smarts, but the lack of game-breaking athleticism puts a cap on his pro ceiling. He projects as a reliable slot option.
beast_strengths: Average height, but well-strapped together with length and hand size … above-average short-area quickness … route precision allows him to snap off his breaks … eyes quickly locate the football, and his body stays balanced adjusting to it … efficient pluck-and-put away technique … rescues throws off his shoulder or down by his cleats … crowded catch points didn’t seem to faze his focus on tape … dependable character and made an impact in Happy Valley despite only one year there (offensive coordinator Mike Yurcich: “He’s a team guy. He loves to compete … love that kid.”) … comfortable working inside and outside … led Penn State in receptions in 2022.
beast_weaknesses: Lacks desired top-end speed … doesn’t have a secondary burst to easily create vertical separation (only four of his 51 catches in 2022 came on throws of 20-plus yards) … footwork lags if his body rhythm isn’t on point in his stem work … can do more to effectively sell his patterns … needs to improve his physicality vs. rugged press corners … doesn’t consistently play above the rim or use body position to box out defenders … not a dynamic make-you-miss threat, regardless of the space … had only one game with 70-plus receiving yards in 2022 … marginal special teams experience and potential in the NFL. CONTENTS [77]

beast_summary: Durrell Johnson was a safety and linebacker at Overlea High in Baltimore, earning All-Conference honors as a senior. He went the juco route after high school and signed with Asa College in Brooklyn, where he moved to defensive end. A two-star juco recruit, he was just 225 pounds, but Liberty saw his potential. He led the team in sacks in his first season but battled a knee injury in 2021. He had an All-American 2022 season with an FBS-best 27.5 tackles for loss (5.5 more than Tuli Tuipulotu at No. 2). Johnson is a long, thinly-built edge rusher with small hands, but he has the first-step quickness to get the drop on blockers at the snap. He has an instinctive ability to unwind from blocks and stay locked on the football, but the lack of power in his body shows up in the run game. Overall, Johnson is overly reliant on his initial step as a rusher and needs to continue getting stronger, but he has developmental traits in a 3-4 scheme with closing burst for a superpower.

Allister “AJ” Finley Jr. grew up in Mobile and started playing football (quarterback) at age 4. He was a cornerback and running back at St. Paul’s Episcopal School and helped the program to state titles his first three years (led the team in rushing as a junior). As a senior, he posted six interceptions. A three-star recruit, he committed to Ole Miss (over Iowa and Tennessee) and moved to safety full time. He married his college sweetheart (Ruby Draayer) in May 2022. Finley is a long, slender athlete with below-average play strength. He displays adequate speed and instincts from the hash or single-high to cover the sideline and deep third of the field. His inconsistent physicality is a concern when working downhill, and he doesn’t have the quick twitch directional change to pattern match NFL receivers. Overall, Finley has a chance to make a pro roster because of his functional range and athletic ball skills, but he must become a more secure tackler to earn his way.

Daniel Barker bounced around high schools and transferred to Boyd Anderson High as a junior, before he wound up at Deerfield Beach and earned All- County as a senior tight end. A three-star recruit, Barker committed to Illinois (over Kentucky) and became the school’s all-time record holder for touchdown grabs by a tight end (11). He pulled his name out of the 2022 NFL Draft and transferred to Michigan State for his “super senior” season, then set a career high in catches. A long, solidly built athlete, Barker works towards open space with tracking skills, but his speed and separation abilities are average at best. While he blocks with a competitive edge to remove defenders from their feet, his subpar technique and positioning will be quickly exposed versus NFL defenders. Overall, Barker is a coordinated route runner and flashes athletic pass-catching ability, but he is a below-average blocker and faces a steep uphill climb to make an NFL roster.

A two-year starter at West Florida, Durden was an outside receiver in the Argos’ balanced offense. After a short-lived pro baseball career, he returned to the football field was immediately productive, initially at Mercer and then West Florida where his 23 receiving touchdowns matched the program record. An impressive athlete for his size, Durden has a smooth accelerator before and after the catch and displays natural pass-catching skills thanks to his steady hand-eye coordination (averaged 19.7 yards per catch in his career). He shifts his gears well as a route runner but could use more polish to consistently create separation out of his stem turns. Overall, Durden will need to prove he can match up vs. NFL speed and strength, but he has the athletic profile and instincts (as a receiver and ball carrier) to earn an NFL roster spot in camp. His value on special teams (as a return man and gunner) could give the edge.
beast_strengths: Good-sized athlete with functional strength to beat the jam … explosive timed speed and play speed … displays the acceleration to consistently gain vertical separation against Division II corners … graceful in mid-air with natural ball-tracking skills … takes sharp angles out of his breaks … mixes his gears as a route runner and not shy attacking the middle of the field … can turn short gains into big plays, displaying outstanding vision, competitive toughness and contact balance with the ball in his hands … productive on special teams as a returner and gunner (10 special teams tackles) … averaged 17.7 yards per punt return in 2022, including a 64-yard touchdown (14/248/1) … averaged 24.6 yards per kick return (43/1,058/1) … receiving production increased each season in college … NFL scouts say his pro day workout (in 33-degree weather) was “outstanding.”
beast_weaknesses: Doesn’t have a body of work against top-tier competition … routes can be overly deliberate at times, drawing sticky coverage … shorter arms and might struggle to fight through the physical coverage of longer corners … inconsistent high-pointer and too content using his body/wrists to finish … contested windows disrupt his focus … guilty of bracing himself for contact at the catch point, making grabs tougher than they need to be … patient with the ball in his hands to follow his blocks but will need to make quicker decisions vs. NFL pursuit … will turn 25 during his NFL rookie season … suffered a left wrist injury that required postseason surgery (December 2022).

beast_summary: Tyler “Ty” Okada grew up playing football outside of Minneapolis and was coached by his father (Chris). He played quarterback at East Ridge High and was also a standout baseball player and wrestler. Without any Division-I scholarship offers, he jumped at the preferred walk-on offer from FCS-level Montana State. He moved to defensive back and battled injuries his first few seasons before emerging as a playmaking nickel back as a junior and senior. Okada played corner, safety and nickel and learned how to play defense from various alignments. He is occasionally out-flanked as a run defender, but he is a strong tackler when his angles are right. In coverage, he is fast and fluid with terrific reactive quickness. His coaches say his discipline and football character are “outstanding.” Overall, Okada masks his average size with athletic versatility and football IQ plus the makeup for special teams. After his pro-day performance, he has a decent chance to be drafted.

Thomas “Tommy” DeVito was born in Livingston, N.J. and was a two-year starting quarterback at Don Bosco Prep. As a senior captain, he passed for 2,005 yards and 16 touchdowns. A four-star recruit, DeVito was the top-ranked player in Syracuse’s 2017 class and became the starter in 2019. He battled injuries and decided to transfer after losing his starting job. DeVito joined Illinois in 2022 and posted career bests across the board, leading the Illini to an 8-5 record. Although he takes too many hits on his body, he competes with admirable toughness to stand tall in the pocket and play through pain. He is timely in his reads and puts the ball out in front of receivers to let them make plays away from defenders. His footwork and arm slots become unglued when pressure forces platform changes. Overall, DeVito showed improved pocket feel and downfield touch in 2022, but an NFL career requires more consistency than what he has put on tape thus far.

Emari (ee-MAR-ee) Demercado (dee-mer-KAH-doe) was born and raised in Inglewood. He started his prep career at Carson High before transferring to Downey, where he rushed for nearly 1,000 yards as a senior. With just two FBS offers (Army and Navy), he enrolled at Saddleback College for one season to boost his recruitment. He signed with TCU, where he was buried on the depth chart. When Kendre Miller was injured in the playoff semifinal, though, Demercado stepped up with 150 rushing yards, helping TCU advance to the title game (which was five minutes from his home in Inglewood). Demercado is a strong, well-built back with okay vision, although he needs to stay tighter with his run angles. He had only 378 touches in five years at TCU, so there is plenty of tread left on those tires. Overall, Demercado didn’t have a college career full of highlights, but he shined when it mattered. He is a run-to-daylight runner who knows how to maximize each touch.

Demontrey “Trey” Jacobs played multiple sports growing up, and his mother (Venessa) has been the head volleyball coach at Southern the last 10 years. He played both ways as a senior at East Ascension High, but at 250 pounds, he was primarily known as a pass rusher. He signed with FCS Grambling and transitioned to offensive line. Once the pandemic hit, he transferred up to South Florida and the FBS level prior to the 2020 season. He started at both left and right tackle over his final two seasons and combined for only two penalties. Jacobs has elite arm length and hand size with adequate strength once in position. However, he struggles to maintain knee bend in his pass sets, which leads to immediate balance and control issues. He will need to shed multiple bad habits to stick in the NFL. Overall, Jacobs has a tough time keeping his upper and lower halves on the same page, but his movement potential and size/length could land him on an NFL practice squad.

Princeton Fant, who is the cousin of Seattle Seahawks’ tight end Noah Fant, was a four-year starting wide receiver at LaVergne High. A three-star wide receiver recruit, he committed to in-state Tennessee (over LSU and Ole Miss) and moved to running back for two years before transitioning to tight end for his final four seasons. Fant had his most productive season as a senior with nine total touchdowns, including five rushing scores, mostly as the upback in goal-line situations. Fant, who has a three-year-old daughter (Aaliyah), doesn’t offer ideal size or strength through contact, and his unpolished routes lead defenders to his targets. His special teams resume is also underwhelming. However, he plays with loose movements and focused ball skills as a pass catcher with shiftiness after the catch. Overall, Fant is strength- and technique-deficient as a blocker, but his athletic upside as a utility H-back and special teamer will be his ticket to an NFL camp.

Truman Jones grew up in the Atlanta area and helped lead Westminster School to a state championship in football (2015) and lacrosse (2017), earning All-State honors in both sports. A no-star linebacker recruit at 190 pounds, he had an FBS offer from Maryland but followed in the footsteps of his father (Archie) and signed with Harvard. He moved to edge rusher prior to the 2019 season and had an All-American senior year (as a captain) with a league-best 13.0 tackles for loss (also finished his career with four blocked kicks). Jones plays with the initial quickness out of his stance to attack gaps or create a speed-to-power push. He competes with controlled aggression, but NFL blockers will quickly neutralize him at the point of attack and his pass-rush toolbox isn’t very deep. Overall, Jones needs to expand his hand usage and learn how to string moves together for the next level, but his athletic tools and energy are a nice play to start for a developmental guy.

A four-year starter at Purdue, Graham played a nickel linebacker role in former co-defensive coordinator Ron English’s hybrid back-seven. A quarterback and safety in high school, he was a movable chess piece for the Boilermakers’ defense and played most of his snaps in the box, but he also lined up as a slot defender and edge player. Graham is long and physical with a downhill appetite that keeps his pursuit alive through contact. However, he needs to improve his pad level at the point of attack and his freelancing leads to missed run fits. Overall, Graham is alert, well-built and driven to make plays, which might fit as a SAM linebacker, but his pursuit speed is average and his tight transitions will be tough to overcome vs. NFL skill athletes. His versatile background and special teams potential could be his saving grace.
beast_strengths: Passes the eye test with his athletic, muscular build … long-limbed and physical … processes quickly, and his itchy trigger finger helps drive on plays downhill … the coaches trusted him to wear multiple hats depending on personnel groupings … runs the alley with conviction … faces up the ball carrier and brings his feet … casts a wide net as a tackler … doesn’t waste his length when working off blockers … stays square in his drops and feels routes coming … brings “buckets of energy” to both practice and games, according to NFL scouts … his junior tape shows a productive teams player on kickoff coverage.
beast_weaknesses: Speed is mediocre at best … upright play style and labors in his transitions … hip and lower body tightness hinders his explosiveness in the open field … needs to use more consistent pad level to leverage blockers for quicker disengagement … runs himself out of plays when he opts to freelance … unrefined blitzer and needs to improve his timing as a gap slicer … will struggle to match the quickness of NFL tight ends in man coverage … suffered a tibia injury in the 2022 season opener and missed the next four games.

beast_summary: Zaire Cordero-Barnes, who has an older brother (Zavier) who played linebacker at Saginaw Valley State, prepped at Carmel Catholic where he earned All- State honors as a running back and safety as a senior, finishing with 77 tackles and six touchdowns. A three-star athlete recruit, he had a host of MAC offers and committed to Western Michigan. After a torn ACL sidelined him in 2020, he became a full-time starter at “sam” linebacker in 2021 and had a career year as a senior with a team-best 93 tackles and nine passes defended. A high school safety, Barnes looks comfortable pedaling in reverse with the footwork to quickly gather and go. His read-react skills have gotten better as he has played more football. He would benefit with improved wrap technique but is generally a consistent tackler. Overall, Barnes is constantly around the football because of his key reads and play speed, and his special teams contributions could be his ticket to an NFL roster spot.

Kyle Patterson, the youngest of four children, is the son of Shawn Patterson, who was a second-round pick in 1988 by the Green Bay Packers. Kyle played football and basketball at Perry (and a high school teammate of Brock Purdy). A three-star recruit, Patterson passed on offers from Alabama, Georgia and others to sign with Air Force. However, his college career was disrupted by a torn ACL and MCL in his knee (September 2021) followed by a clean-up procedure (July 2022) and another knee injury (October 2022). He has another knee surgery scheduled for April 2023. Patterson is a stout, balanced blocker who can seal the edge and be an asset in the run game. He wasn’t a high-volume receiver but was productive when targeted (16 of his 18 career catches resulted in a first down or touchdown). Overall, Patterson has the blocking talent and development upside to warrant a draft pick, but the health of his knee might force him to go the undrafted route.

Tyreque Jones grew up outside of Los Angeles and started his prep career as a quarterback at Kaiser High. He transferred to San Gorgonio High for his senior season and caught 52 passes for 1,128 yards and 16 touchdowns, adding 77 tackles and two interceptions. A three-star recruit, Jones signed with Boise State, and he quickly became part of the safety rotation, setting career-bests in 2021. He moved to nickelback in 2022 as a super senior with mixed results. Jones offers above-average straight-line speed in coverage and when giving chase in the run game. With his physicality, he looks to run through ball carriers, but cares more about striking than wrap-tackling. Against the pass, he sees plays develop, but he lacks the short area balance and burst to stay connected to routes. Overall, Jones has impressive length and zone instincts, but his low batting average as a tackler and tight coverage transitions will be high hurdles to clear in the NFL.

A one-year starter at Kentucky, Manning locked down the right guard spot in former offensive coordinator Rich Scangarello’s zone-heavy run scheme. His journey since his senior year of high school has included overcoming leukemia, moving from defense to offense and reigniting his NFL chances as a super senior in Lexington. Manning plays wide in pass protection and stays vigilant, always looking to put his heavy hands to good use. However, his pad level and body control leave him in compromised positions and his hand technique lacks the consistency to bail him out. Overall, Manning has the size and makeup that will appeal to NFL teams, but his below-average athleticism and consistency will be tough hurdles to clear versus NFL skill. He projects as a potential swing guard in the NFL.
beast_strengths: Looks the part of an NFL guard with his wide frame and long arms … stout body type and doesn’t easily give ground (see: 2022 Georgia tape) … able to drive/uproot from his inline steps in the run game … rugged play style and leans into his hands for maximum power at contact … finishes his blocks to the ground when he can … plays with strong hands to secure his fitting … not a rangy player but showed adequate foot speed on short-area pulls … mature and tough-minded and has already overcome cancer at a young age … started double-digit games at both guard spots in college.
beast_weaknesses: Marginal overall athleticism … inconsistent knee bend and plays with his head past his feet too often … average in his initial setup and sluggish when attempting to react to pass-rush quickness … limited redirect skills and can be crossed up easily … too much wasted motion with his hands, which causes his punch to be late into contact … upright on the move with subpar body control … committed two false starts within three plays on the 2022 South Carolina tape … doesn’t have desired range for outside pulls or screen-game work.

beast_summary: Alan (uh-LAWN) Ali (ah-LEE) grew up in Fort Worth and was a three-year starter at Timber Creek. He was an All-District left tackle as a senior. A three-star recruit, Ali hoped to stay close to home at TCU, but settled for SMU instead. After four seasons as a starter for the Mustangs, he transferred to the Horned Frogs (his childhood favorite team) for his sixth and final season. Ali’s addition at center stabilized TCU’s offensive line (allowed Steve Avila to move to guard) and was an unsung reason for its 2022 success. While fundamentally sound and smart, he has an average physical profile with limited displacement in the run game and struggles to recover versus shifty rushers. He has rare experience, with 60 career games played, and at least one start at each of the five offensive line positions. Overall, Ali is an effective positional blocker and attacks his job with a technical mind, but his average length, athleticism and power could make it tough for him to stand out.

A three-year starter at Minnesota-Duluth, Laing lined up at right tackle in head coach Curt Wiese’s RPO spread scheme. After his All-American junior season, he considered jumping to Division I via the transfer portal but returned to Duluth in 2022 because he wanted to be a team captain, and he produced another All-American season (zero sacks allowed in 2022). Laing does a nice job in his setup to immediately achieve a low, balanced position with efficient hand strikes to stay after defenders from snap to whistle. However, he struggles to regain control of the rep when he can’t stay centered, which will show up against the explosive speed and power awaiting him at the next level. Overall, Laing faces a substantial jump in competition going from Division II to the NFL, but he has a chance to become Duluth’s first NFL Draft pick since 1990 because of his athletic versatility on the interior and competitive profile. After some time on a practice squad, he has the ability to carve out a career similar to Hjalte Froholdt.
beast_strengths: Athletic off the ball and quick into his blocks … moves with the controlled mirroring speed to cut off rush angles … redirects well to respond and pick up inside counters … plays with enough functional strength to slow interior rushers when he stays centered … comfortably climbs to the second level and can fit linebackers in space … pleasant and thoughtful off the field, mean block finisher on the field … added 65 pounds since high school (515-pound squat) … stayed loyal to his teammates and coaches instead of leaving for greener pastures in the transfer portal … practiced at guard as a redshirt freshman before moving out to right tackle for his final three seasons (took snaps at center and guard during East-West Shrine Bowl week).
beast_weaknesses: Unimpressive frame with short arms and average bulk … doesn’t have a ton of power in his lower body and doesn’t drive defenders off the ball as a run blocker … tends to wear down after first contact … sitting down and halting NFL bull rushers won’t be a smooth transition for him … punctual hands, but his placement and reset skills will need time to catch up to NFL speed … his feet will panic at times and lead to undisciplined steps … will be a 24-year-old rookie … practiced at guard in college, but his starts came at right tackle and he lacks true experience at center … faces a substantial jump in competition after playing at the Division II level the past six years.

br_positives: – Named team captain at the beginning of the season. | – Good athlete with springy legs; moves really well for the position. | – Has the speed to carry running backs and tight ends down the field and take away posts/the seam when playing Tampa 2. | – Should have few to no issues mirroring and matching tight ends in man coverage. | – Uses his hands and athleticism to avoid blocks/make offensive linemen miss when moving laterally versus outside zone. | – Solid at working the hands as a pass-rusher when blitzing and has fluid hips to clear his lower half and get a clean win. | – Experience playing special teams.
br_negatives: – Instincts versus the run are a mess; often looks like he's guessing. | – Against inside runs, he drops his hands and tries to go chest-to-chest with blockers. | – Lacks the strength to get extension; he concedes ground to create space, and he will get pushed around by tight ends in the running game. | – Angles as a run defender are poor/too shallow. | – Doesn't have much power behind his pads; offensive linemen will be able to catch and control him when he blitzes, and he's not going to knock running backs backward when tackling. | – Can get caught staring in the backfield when playing zone coverage. | – Seemingly fell out of favor with LSU's new coaching staff last season; his playing time was significantly reduced after the first half of the season.

beast_summary: Amari Burney was a two-way starter at Calvary Christian High in Clearwater, playing all four seasons on varsity. He finished his prep career with 992 receiving yards and 12 touchdowns plus 182 tackles at safety. A four-star recruit, he committed to Florida (as a safety) over Ohio State and others. He moved to linebacker in 2019 and was a part-time player until his senior year, when he earned a starting weakside role and posted career highs across the board. Burney has done a nice job strengthening his body and honing his break-down and tackling skills. He will struggle to keep himself clean and doesn’t have the length to easily press blockers off him in the run game. Although his zone instincts let him down at times, Burney has the fluidity to transition and stay attached to backs and tight ends. Overall, Burney is caught in between safety and linebacker, but his speed and matchup skills in coverage are why NFL teams are taking a long look at him.

Joseph “Jo” Ngata (enn-GOT-uh), who is the middle son of three boys, was born in Reno, Nev., and raised in nearby Sparks by his Cameroon-born parents. The family moved to Folsom so their boys could play football, and Ngata led Folsom High to back-to-back state titles in 2017 and 2018. A four-star recruit, he chose Clemson over Alabama, Ohio State and many others. However, he battled several injuries and struggled to find the end zone (didn’t lead the team in receiving in any of his four seasons). Ngata has a long, angular frame with acceleration out of his stutter-step release to challenge cornerbacks on the outside. Though his catch radius belongs on the NFL level, his lack of runaway speed or short-area burst hinders the snap out of breaks. Staying healthy is the key question mark. Overall, Ngata naturally uses his body length to make full-extension grabs over defenders, but his struggles to create his own separation will be a challenging mountain to climb.

A four-year starter at Texas Tech, Thompson was a committee back in offensive coordinator Zach Kittley’s version of his spread, Air-Raid attack. After rushing for 765 yards as a redshirt freshman, he didn’t reach 700 rushing yards the next three seasons, but he consistently found the end zone as just the third player in Texas Tech history to reach 40 career touchdown runs. Thompson patiently reads and sets up blockers with the footwork to maneuver through narrow gaps. Although he doesn’t have push-the-pile power, he runs with purposeful toughness (he just needs to stay healthy). Overall, Thompson doesn’t have the explosive traits that will easily set him apart in the NFL, but he is savvy one-cut runner thanks to his press, sort and drive skills. His development on third downs and special teams will be key factors for him to make a 53-man roster.
beast_strengths: Patient runner with a strong feel for cutback timing … settles his feet for controlled plant-and-go movements to daylight … able to drop his hips and move laterally to toy with linebackers … has a frame to comfortably carry 205 pounds or 220 pounds … skillfully dishes a stiff-arm and steps out of diving tackle attempts … coaches say he has come a “long way” with his steadiness as a pass catcher … has a nose for the end zone (40 career rushing touchdowns) … three-time team captain and very well-liked in the locker room … production doesn’t jump off the page but it was consistent (finished his career No. 8 on the school’s all-time rushing yards list).
beast_weaknesses: Doesn’t have a home run gear (only one carry of 25-plus yards in 2022) … more quick than sudden in his cuts with limited juice around the corner … too patient at times and needs to be more aggressive with his decision-making … not a hammer or pile-mover … more of a screen receiver than true route runner, and his pass blocking is best described as inconsistent … limited special teams résumé … underwent surgery on his shoulder (April 2021) and missed the first two games of the season; missed time late in his senior season (November 2022) with a sprained ankle … arrested on a warrant for reckless driving (September 2020), a misdemeanor charge from racing a fellow teammate on the highway.

beast_summary: Shaquan “Shaq” Davis was a basketball-focused athlete most of his life and didn’t take football seriously until his junior year at Summerville (alma mater of several pros, including AJ Green). He had more scholarship offers for basketball but decided to pursue football. However, he didn’t have the grades for the FBS teams looking at him. FCS-level South Carolina State took a chance, and he missed 2018 to get his grades on track. He quickly became a key playmaker and led the team in receiving the past three years. Davis looks like a basketball player with his tall, long frame and stringy muscle tone. He accelerates to top speed quickly with his expansive strides and shows upper body flexibility to win deep (20.5 yard/catch average). However, his ball skills are troublesome, and he doesn’t always play up to his size. Overall, Davis’ game lacks attention to detail, but he has Martavis Bryant-like developmental upside, making him worthy of bringing to NFL camp.

Noah Taylor was born in the Bronx and attended Avalon School (north of Washington, D.C.) where he was a four-year varsity starter at receiver and linebacker. A three-star recruit, he committed to Virginia to play defense under Bronco Mendenhall. He started for three seasons but entered the transfer portal after Mendenhall left the program. He transferred to North Carolina and played the “jack” linebacker role, but a right knee injury in October 2022 and subsequent surgery cut short his final season. He is expected to be cleared by August 2023 but was unable to work out for NFL teams before the draft. Taylor has a long, slender frame with stringy muscle tone and average strength. He looks good on his feet to handle space or blitz but needs to be more aggressive in the run game. Overall, Taylor won’t be a natural fit more most schemes, but he plays with twitch, quickness and bend to be a nickel hybrid linebacker who can drop and rush.

br_positives: — Excellent size and length for the position. | —Versatile player who can play at multiple levels of the defense. Best when playing close to the line of scrimmage. | — Aggressive player against the run. Triggers quickly.
br_negatives: — Below-average man cover skills. Lacks ideal twitch and movement skills. Heavy-footed at times and can be handsy. | — Lacks physicality for his size when tacking. Takes on blocks, but does not control them. Below-average strength.

beast_summary: Titus Leo, one of four children, grew up in Brooklyn and was a multi-sport standout at Sheepshead Bay High, playing both ways as a wide receiver and safety. He signed with Wagner of the FCS in nearby Staten Island and quickly announced himself as a playmaker, despite the program winning only two of 36 games the last four years. Transitioning to edge rusher and linebacker, he learned under current NFL players Cam Gill and Chris Williams and played in three different schemes in five seasons. A two-time captain, Leo earned a spot on Bruce Feldman’s “Freaks List” with his ability to pounce out of his stance and chase down the ball. He plays with active hands that stay out in front but tends to get crazed in his rush and needs to rely more on punctuality and planning. Overall, Leo is an NFL-caliber athlete with a red-hot motor, but he needs to develop his skill for a more efficient attack plan. He is a work in progress as a pass rusher with special-teams value.

Kilian Zierer (ZEER-rer), who is one of three children, grew up in Munich, Germany, and played soccer throughout childhood. At age 16, he tried football and played mostly wide receiver and tight end. He received one scholarship offer and moved to the offensive line at the College of Canyons. A three-star juco recruit, he committed to Auburn (over Florida, TCU and USC) but missed 2020 as he rehabbed a torn ACL. After he was a part-time player in 2021, he became the full-time starting left tackle as a senior. Zierer looks the part in pads but is still piecing everything together. He has the range to reach his landmarks and close space on rushers, but he tends to forget his feet and lose control through engagement. He must strengthen his core and anchor to match up in the NFL. Overall, Zierer has inconsistent tape full of youthful, inexperienced mistakes, but he is a fluid mover with the foot quickness and functional length worth developing on the practice squad.

Deslin Alexandre was born in Haiti and came to the United States in 2002 with his family. He was a basketball-focused athlete most of his life, until he started playing football as a junior at Deerfield Beach High. He was named All-County honors as a senior. A three-star recruit, he committed to Pitt over NC State and was part of the Panthers’ defensive end rotation for the last five seasons. A two-time team captain, he was named the 2023 Jason Witten Collegiate Man of the Year. Alexandre has a strong, filled-out build with active hands to tilt the field, barrel through soft edges and work half a man as a rusher (his 2022 Syracuse tape showed CONTENTS [192] his disruptive skills). He can stack and play off lateral blocks in the run game, although his lack of explosiveness often leaves him a step behind. Overall, Alexandre lacks creativity or high-end athleticism for an edge defender, but he is a grinder with outstanding smarts and intangibles to round out a defensive end depth chart.

Jack Colletto moved to Camas (just outside of Portland) from Seattle as a sophomore in high school. After playing safety as a junior, he became the starting quarterback as a senior and was the Gatorade Player of the Year, leading Camas to the 2016 state title. A two-star recruit, he went to Arizona Western College for a year and then signed with Oregon State over Vanderbilt. He arrived as a quarterback before moving to linebacker and short-yardage running back, doing whatever he could to get on the field (won the 2022 Hornung Award as the most versatile player in college football). Colletto is a hard-nosed player with the physicality needed for blocking duties. He has only average speed but appears smooth in his routes with succinct footwork and tracking hands to finish catches. Overall, Colletto might be a jack-of-all-trades, master-of-none player, but his athleticism, competitive toughness and versatility will speak to NFL coaches.
