beast_summary: A four-year starter at Memphis, Henigan operated well in offensive coordinator Tim Cramsey's multiple-based scheme. He became the ﬁrst true freshman to start a season opener at Memphis and ﬁnished his career ranked No. 1 in both school and AAC history in passing yards (14,266) and passing touchdowns (104). Henigan does an efficient job keeping his progressions on schedule — the ball often comes out before the receiver is out of his break. He was a model of consistency, regardless of the opponent, a trait best illustrated by his 41-game passing touchdown streak (tied with Marcus Mariota for second longest in FBS history). Though he has an innate feel for shuffling in the pocket to buy time, he doesn't have the escapability to easily access different throwing platforms. Overall, Henigan will have a chance at a pro career, because he can play on time and deliver with touch, but his movements and arm power won't stand out. He will have a chance at a career as a backup in the right situation.

beast_summary: Thomas Perry grew up in a football family — both his father (Scott) and uncle (Bill) played the sport. Thomas Perry played guard and defensive tackle at Haddam-Killingworth High, where he was also a state-champion wrestler. Undersized at 6-foot-1 and 260 pounds, he didn't receive any Division I looks and committed to Division III Middlebury, which also offered his major (3.92 GPA in molecular biology and biochemistry). He broke into the starting lineup as a freshman and became an All-American as a senior left guard. Nicknamed "Thomas the Tank," Perry was dominant against inferior competition on tape and didn't look out of place during East-West Shrine Bowl practices. He is a tireless worker who enjoys the grind — and that translates to his on-ﬁeld play strength. He is very controlled out of his stance, with spice in his hands to pepper defenders. He is also one of the most competitive ﬁnishers in this class. Overall, Perry is undersized and will require development time as he transitions to center (and faces better competition). But he is wired the right way with the intelligence, athleticism and power worth the investment.

A two-year starter at Georgia, Lovett worked mostly out of the slot in offensive coordinator Mike Bobo's scheme (86.5 percent of snaps in the slot in 2024). Although his production was average, he was a reliable target for quarterback Carson Beck the past two seasons and developed under former wide receiver coach Bryan McClendon (now the Tampa Bay Buccaneers' wide receivers coach). With synchronized shake in his routes, Lovett created quick windows underneath for catch-and-go plays. But he struggled to expand beyond being a singles and doubles hitter, and his average size will be more of an issue working against NFL coverage. Overall, Lovett presents a small-throwing target and likely will be limited to the slot, but he has a ﬂuid stride with solid ball skills to make plays — if given the chance. His speed can be used on special teams, as well.

His upside as a third-level threat will have NFL teams interested.

He looked like a top-100 NFL prospect following the 2022 season at South Carolina, but injuries sidetracked his trajectory and he struggled to sustain a high level of play for Ole Miss. A good-sized target, Wells is a coordinated athlete who can make natural adjustments on the ball and be a threat after the catch. However, he isn't much of a route technician, wasn't reliable as a ﬁnisher and doesn't have a special teams background. Overall, Wells is a confounding prospect, because he looks like a shell of the promising player studied in 2022. There is talent there, but his lack of consistency getting open and ﬁnishing catches were a problem in 2024 — and it is hard to see that changing in the NFL.

With Kenny Pickett at his quarterback in 2021, he put himself on the NFL radar as a freshman, although he struggled to build on that early success over the past three years (never reached 350 receiving yards in a season). Bartholomew plays with promising speed and toughness over the middle and can chew up yards versus zone, but he lacks the explosive traits to effortlessly separate from man coverage. His blocking improved incrementally each season, turning from a glaring weakness to a serviceable piece of his game — a reﬂection of his hard work and tenacious attitude. Overall, Bartholomew needs to continue getting stronger and sharpening his routes to ﬁnd a permanent home in the NFL, but he has better pass-catching traits than his stat line would suggest. His intangibles will make it tough for a coaching staff to cut him.

beast_summary: Gerad Christian-Lichtenhan grew up in Vacaville, Calif., with his parents (Tabitha and Teri). He started playing football at age 6 and competed up an age group throughout Pop Warner because of his size (also played soccer and was a swimmer). After relocating to Davis, Calif., he played both ways (offensive tackle and defensive line) in high school and helped his team orchestrate a turnaround from 0-10 his sophomore year to 10-2 his senior season. A three-star recruit, his goal was to play in the Pac-12 — Colorado gave him that chance. After starting for two seasons in Boulder (including blocking on Shedeur Sanders' blindside in 2023), he transferred to Oregon State for his ﬁnal season. Christian-Lichtenhan lives up to his nickname, "Tank," with his massive size and the wingspan of a pterodactyl. His feet are on the heavier side, but he plays controlled in pass protection, using his length and base to slow rushers. Although inconsistent leverage hurts his effectiveness in the run game, his clench strength helps him stay connected through the ﬁnish. Overall, Christian-Lichtenhan will have a tough time overcoming some of his athletic limitations, but his size and improvements each season will earn him plenty of chances at the next level.

A two-year starter at Miami, Mauigoa played Mike linebacker in then-defensive coordinator Lance Guidry's 4-2-5 base scheme. After two seasons at Washington State (he was teammates with Cam Ward at two different programs), Mauigoa transferred to Coral Gables, where he led the Hurricanes in tackles and tackles for loss as both a junior and senior. Miami's green-dot player on defense, Mauigoa reads well pre- and post-snap and is at his best working downhill angles to skim blocks and make stops at (or behind) the line — he had 29 tackles for loss in 26 starts at Miami. His awareness carries over to coverage, although his reaction quickness isn't as sharp and offenses can ﬁnd success targeting him. Overall, Mauigoa needs to clean up his missed tackles and coverage missteps to earn defensive snaps, but his instincts, chase speed and mentality are draftable traits that will endear him to NFL coaching. Special teams will help him make a roster.

beast_summary: A one-year starter at Cal, Harris lined up primarily at left cornerback in head coach Justin Wilcox's scheme. A former preferred walk-on at Oregon State, he made a name for himself at Idaho (school-record 35 passes defended) and ﬁt in well at Cal opposite Nohl Williams in 2024. Capable of playing a mix of press and off, Harris moves fairly effortlessly in all areas of the ﬁeld to turn and run with receivers or work down and get physical against the run. Though he looks natural making plays on the football, he needs to clean up his route-mirroring mechanics early and at the top of routes. Overall, Harris needs to improve some of his spacing issues in coverage, but he has legit speed and ball skills that will serve him well in the NFL. He falls in the "there is something promising here" category of prospects.

Primarily a quarterback in high school, he battled injuries over his last three seasons, but his impact and tackle production still increased each year. Verdon has the body length and smooth athleticism to match up in man and zone coverage, although he tends to be more reactive than proactive. Though not an intimidating or forceful tackler, he stays disciplined with his keys and does a nice job lassoing ball carriers. A four-star recruit, he committed to Texas as a quarterback and redshirted in 2020 while recovering from that knee injury. He later transferred to Utah, where he transitioned to running back before transferring again in 2024, this time to Arkansas. Overall, Jackson isn't a dynamic athlete, but he runs with tempo, vision and physicality. He'll stick around, if he lands in the right situation/role.

A two-year starter at Auburn, McLeod played the "Buck" position as a hybrid linebacker in defensive coordinator D.J. Durkin's 4-2-5 scheme, lining up off the ball on early downs and putting his hand on the ground in sub-packages. He showed promise at Appalachian State before transferring to Auburn, where he posted 24 tackles for loss in his 24 games played. With his assignment-based approach, McLeod shows very little lag in his read-react and plays with well-channeled aggressiveness to create pursuit lanes, both as a run defender and pass rusher. Overall, McLeod is the type of prospect that grows on you, because of the different ways he can align and make an impact. It will be critical for him to ﬁnd the right role, though. He projects best as a hybrid outside linebacker in a 3-4 scheme.

He didn't look the same down the stretch in 2024, and his ability to stay healthy and effective will be crucial if he is going to make it at the next level. Overall, Tate has an NFL frame with functional mobility and technique but must show he can overcome his questionable balance and body control in the run game. He will boost his chances if he can prove to coaches that he has versatility across the interior. He is expected to be full-go by training camp after January knee surgery.

beast_summary: O'Donnell Fortune started playing football in ﬁfth grade for the Chargers at Dillon Park in Sumter, S.C. His junior year at Sumter High put him on the recruiting map (ﬁve interceptions — he had three more as a senior and received all-state honors). Fortune was a three-star recruit as a safety and corner and grew up a Gamecocks fan. After a 100-yard pick six in South Carolina's 2022 bowl game, he became a starter as a junior and played his best ball as a senior. Fortune is a tall, slender athlete with length that he uses to disrupt route timing and obstruct passing windows. He isn't shy about trusting his instincts and tracking the eyes of the quarterback to make plays. His tackling was ﬁne on some tapes but atrocious on others (LSU, Illinois, Kentucky), especially when he tried to hit too high. Overall, Fortune needs to play with improved discipline, both in coverage and run support, but his ball awareness and ﬂuidity will translate well to the pro game.

Reid plays with a quick trigger and little wasted movements when keying or scraping across the line as a blitzer and run defender. beast_summary: Johnny Walker Jr. grew up in Tampa, Fla., with his parents (April and Johnny Walker Sr.). At Chamberlain High, he combined for 41 tackles for loss and 25 sacks over his junior and senior seasons, despite battling a knee issue in 2019. A three-star recruit, he initially committed to Washington State before ﬂipping to Missouri late in the process. Walker bided his time before becoming a starter as a junior and earning second-team All-SEC honors as a senior captain. After recording just one sack over the ﬁrst six games of 2024, he ripped off 8.5 sacks in the ﬁnal seven. Walker has improved year over year as he's learned how to maximize his skill set. He doesn't have top-tier burst or redirect skills for a 250-pound edge rusher, but he is a better football player than a high-end athlete. He keeps his hands and feet in sync and understands how to leverage his pass-rush angles. His run-game awareness also showed improvement from his junior tape. Overall, Walker doesn't play with consistent explosion or bend, but he can dip and rip to affect the quarterback when he times up the snap. He is a potential sub-package rusher in the NFL.

Kyonte Hamilton grew up outside of Washington, D.C., and was introduced to football and wrestling by his father at age 5. He starred in both sports throughout middle school and at Georgetown Prep, playing both quarterback and linebacker on varsity. As a senior in 2020, he won a state and national championship wrestling in the 220-pound category. A three-star recruit in football, he was also one of the top wrestling recruits in the country and committed to Rutgers for both sports (gave up wrestling after the 2021 season). Hamilton played in every game the past four seasons and saved his best for his senior year (second on the team with 27 pressures). You can see his wrestling background in his bend and hand strength, especially when he gets underneath blocks and imposes his will. He ﬂashes twitch and fast hands off the snap, but his block recognition to be more of a playmaker in the run game is still developing. Overall, Hamilton is strong, explosive and durable. He's viewed as an ascending prospect by NFL teams.

Chandler Martin grew up outside of Atlanta, with his parents (Jeff and Sherlonda). His older sister (Jaya) played volleyball at Hiram College. Martin started playing linebacker at age 6 and continued on to Arabia Mountain High, where he posted 108 tackles as a senior in 2019. A two-star recruit, he went overlooked because of his size and signed with FCS East Tennessee State (enrolled at just 16). After three seasons, he entered the portal and transferred to Memphis for his ﬁnal two seasons. He led the Tigers in tackles, tackles for loss and sacks as both a junior and senior. Martin is extremely active and plays with his feet on ﬁre. He can read and react in a blink to make plays at or behind the line (33.0 combined tackles for loss the past two seasons). He will run himself out of plays or into blockers at times, because of his eagerness to make plays. Although his coverage awareness is up and down, he showed improved conﬁdence in his drops as a senior. Overall, Martin is a tad undisciplined, but he is an explosive athlete with the closing speed to be a useful run-and-hit linebacker on defense and special teams.

A two-year starter at Miami, George was an outside receiver in offensive coordinator Shannon Dawson's RPO-based version of the Air Raid. He earned All-ACC honors as a junior and senior, although he produced both highs and lows as part of the Hurricanes' receiving rotation. Overall, George has shown improved route polish and ball tracking, which will give him a chance to stick in the NFL. His undisciplined tendencies and lack of size, however, will make it an uphill climb. Proving himself on special teams could help him stand out in camp.

Overall, Walker is shot out of a cannon when he trusts his vision, and his 2024 jump in production against better competition is encouraging. As conﬁrmed by his testing numbers, he has the speed and wiring to shine on special teams while adding depth on defense.

Marcus Wehr grew up in Billings, Mont., with his parents (Dave and Teresa). At Billings Central High, he played both ways as a 225-pound blocker in the team's Wing-T offense. As a senior, he helped the team to an undefeated 12-0 record and the 2018 state title. He was recruited as a defensive end and signed with Montana State. He moved to defensive tackle in 2021 but was buried on the depth chart, so the coaches asked him to add weight and transition to the offensive line before the 2022 season. He had his best season as a senior in 2024, helping Montana State to the FCS title game. Described as a "student of the game" by his coaches, Wehr uses ﬁrm, independent hand usage to keep his target occupied and maintain the depth of the pocket. His leg drive helps him create movement in the run game, and he consistently strains to ﬁnish. Overall, Wehr is still learning how to maximize his abilities at guard, but he showed consistent improvements and handled himself well against better competition at East-West Shrine Bowl practices. He will help his chances of sticking on an NFL roster if he also can prove himself at center.

A four-star recruit, he was the top-ranked recruit in Wisconsin and picked the Badgers over Georgia, Michigan and others. In his pass sets, Wedig works from a stabilized base and uses independent hands to protect the corner. He plays with more conﬁdence in the run game when he maintains his pad level. Overall, Wedig's consistency in pass pro should improve with more reps. If it does, he has the tools to develop into an NFL swing tackle.

Holden gives his quarterback a large target and is at his best on digs and crossers, attacking the teeth of the defense. He stays coordinated in his releases and route entrance but lacks the speed or suddenness to easily separate, especially on the ﬁrst and second levels. Overall, Holden will have a tough time detaching from NFL corners, but he produces when he plays to his play strength and physicality. The interview vetting process will be pivotal for him.

His production and impact improved each season in the SEC, including career bests as a senior leader of the Razorbacks' defensive line. Gregory is a player who understands his role as a force player who can occupy space, ﬁght through a crowd and pick away at the scraps. He occasionally shows life as a pass rusher (see 2024 Tennessee tape), but he needs to develop more of a plan, rather than simply overwhelming blockers. Overall, Gregory is an athletic-looking 320-pounder who has enough power to control the block in front of him, but he is more likely to be on the clean-up crew (rather than the defender creating disruption). He has the foundation of an early-down backup in the NFL.

beast_summary: Jacob Bayer, one of four kids, grew up south of Fort Worth, Texas, with his father (Jacob) and mother (Mary Boggess), who played college softball at Howard Payne. His younger brother (Caleb) is an offensive lineman at Division III Trinity. Bayer was an all-state left tackle as a senior at Grandview High. A two-star recruit, he committed to FCS Lamar (over Air Force and Wyoming) and started all 22 games at center his ﬁrst two seasons. He entered the transfer portal after the 2022 season and signed with Arkansas State, where he was an All-Sun Belt center both of his seasons in the program. One of the top-ranked powerlifters in Texas while in high school, Bayer has outstanding grip strength to control his man when he keeps his blocks centered. He does a nice job working himself into lateral positioning, although his recovery skills need work. His run-blocking leverage improved throughout the 2024 season, which makes sense, considering that he returned to the starting lineup just ﬁve months after ACL surgery last spring (his quick recovery reﬂects his work ethic). Overall, Bayer was a center-only lineman in college, but he plays with strong, stubborn hands to get the job done and compete for a roster spot.

A three-year starter at Oklahoma, Downs lined up at defensive end in defensive coordinator Zac Alley's 4-2-5 base scheme. A diehard Sooner for as long as he can remember, he put himself on the NFL radar as a sophomore. Although his production dipped slightly the past two seasons, his impact showed on each tape studied. Downs is gap sound, alert and disciplined in the run game and stacks a ton of effort plays. His tape doesn't show a consistent pass-rush threat, mostly because of his lack of bend and length, but he has the quickness to work half-a-man and his physical hands help him work off blocks. Overall, Downs has some tweener traits and will be caught in between positions for several schemes, but he is a high-motor, blue-collar base end, and coaches will appreciate that they'll know exactly what they are getting every down. His experience on special teams (382 snaps in college) can help him earn a backup role

beast_summary: Melvin Smith Jr. grew up in northwest Louisiana and started playing football in elementary school. He was an all-league defensive back as a senior at Airline High in Bossier City, leading the program to a 10-win season and the 2019 district title. A no-star recruit, he signed with Division II Southern Arkansas, where he became a four-year starter. He had proliﬁc junior and senior seasons, registering a combined 35 passes defended and nine interceptions. Smith has production that jumps off the page — and it came both in off coverage, where he could drive on throws, and press man, where he pinned receivers to the sideline and found the football. He is only average in his hip turn and can get stuck at times in his transitions, but he plays with heart. I also don't question his compete skills, although his tackling was average, even by Division II standards, and must improve for him to get NFL athletes on the ground. Overall, Smith had the pre-draft process he needed to earn a shot — he didn't appear out of his element against better competition at the Senior Bowl, and his testing veriﬁed that he has NFL-level athleticism.

Josiah "J.J." Roberts, one of ﬁve children, grew up near Huntington, W. Va., with his parents (B.J. and Tosha). Two of his younger brothers (Nemo and Zaky) currently play college football at Division II Fairmont State. Roberts was Gatorade Player of the Year in West Virginia as a senior at Cabell Midland High, playing quarterback (in an option offense) and defensive back. A three-star recruit, Roberts was the fourth-ranked player in West Virginia (two spots behind 2024 Steelers second-round pick Zach Frazier), but he was overlooked by the Mountaineers and signed with Wake Forest. After three years, he transferred closer to home and joined Marshall for his ﬁnal two seasons. Roberts has the body type of a cornerback but the mentality of a safety with the way he runs the alley with speed and conviction (led the team in solo tackles in 2024). He explodes into ball carriers, although he often opts for the big hit instead of relying on tackling fundamentals. He plays with impressive range in coverage (led the Sun Belt in passes defended in 2024), although the speed he faced against Ohio State gave him some trouble. Overall, Roberts has the athletic proﬁle, production and playing temperament that could make him a draft pick.

Isas (ice-iss) "Ice" Waxter II grew up in the Newark, N.J., area with his mother (Glenda). He started playing football and running track at age 8. He attended Immaculate Conception High and played both ways (cornerback and wide receiver). A no-star recruit, Waxter received seven FCS offers and committed to Villanova. After missing the 2022 season because of a knee injury, he became a full-time starter the past two seasons and led the CAA with three forced fumbles in 2024. Waxter is a good-sized athlete who looks to disrupt routes early. He works hard to stay on top of the route, although his handsy approach won't ﬂy against NFL athletes. He doesn't shy from the physicality in the run game, but he must ﬁnd better control to cut down on missed tackles. Overall, Waxter needs to polish his footwork and technique, but he passes the eye test, runs well enough and battles on every snap. Some NFL teams have him tagged as a future safety.

Jackson Meeks, the nephew of NFL defensive end Za'Darius Smith, grew up with his mother (Genniefer) in Phenix City, Ala. He posted moderate receiving production at Central High but went overlooked by instate powers Alabama and Auburn. A three-star recruit, he was hoping to play in the SEC and committed to Georgia within a week of being offered his senior season. After three years (and two national championships) as a backup, Meeks entered the transfer portal and found a friendly face in former Georgia assistant Fran Brown, who took over as the Syracuse head coach in 2024. With fellow transfer Kyle McCord at quarterback, Meeks eclipsed 1,000 yards receiving in THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 138 2024. He isn't a polished separator in his routes, but he is physical to the football to pluck and ﬁnish (No. 2 in the FBS in 2024 with 21 contested catches). His body strength shows mid-route, over the middle and after the catch (Brown: "He's a dog."). Overall, Meeks isn't a burner, which will limit his role at the next level, but he plays with the competitive juices, decisive movements and ball skills to be a chain-moving option.

A three-year starter at Rutgers, Powell was the Mike linebacker in then-defensive coordinator Joe Harasymiak's 4-2-5 base scheme. He put himself on the NFL radar in 2022 and was trending toward being a top-100 pick until injuries sidetracked his trajectory. A big athlete, Powell is a smooth mover with functional range, although he didn't look quite the same on the 2024 tape while working his way back from an Achilles injury. He offers rare length and admirable physicality to work near the line of scrimmage, but he needs to stay disciplined with his keys and timing to remain a factor in the play. Overall, if Powell stays healthy and returns to form, he has the frame and tools worth developing on an NFL practice squad.

beast_summary: Nash Hutmacher grew up in South Dakota, with his parents (Joe and Laura). He was a multisport star at Chamberlain High School, winning the state title in the shot put and discus, earning all-state on the defensive line and ﬁnishing as a four-time state champion wrestler with a 166-0 record (started practicing with the varsity team in sixth grade). A three-star recruit, he signed with Nebraska over Wisconsin and started the past two seasons at nose tackle. After the 2023 football season, he dropped 45 pounds, joined the Huskers' wrestling team and qualiﬁed for the NCAA wrestling championships. Nicknamed "The Polar Bear," Hutmacher translates several of his wrestling techniques to the football ﬁeld, keying on leverage and hand placement to break down blocks. He is tight through his hips and rushes like he is wearing skates because of balance issues, which hinder the way he can affect the backﬁeld. Overall, Hutmacher is a compact, sawed-off plugger with limitations, but stands out because of his power and competitive energy — which could earn him a reserve role.

Tavareon "Bam" Martin-Scott picked up his nickname because of the ﬁreworks celebration he typically receives to celebrate his birthday. He grew up playing pee wee football in Fort Wayne, Ind., but developed late and was mostly a part-time player until his senior year at Snider High (alma mater of Jessie Bates). He posted 87 tackles and 6.0 sacks as a senior in 2018, but it wasn't enough to put him on the recruiting radar. A no-star recruit, he played two seasons with Dodge City (Kan.) Community College and then received several SEC offers. His playing time and production gradually increased each season for the Gamecocks, and he put intriguing ﬂashes on ﬁlm. Martin-Scott is a good-sized athlete, with pursuit speed to match races to the perimeter. He competes with a banger mentality to pinball off blocks and stay determined on his path to the ball. Overall, Martin-Scott freelances a tad too much with inconsistent steps in coverage, but he is a classic run-and-hit linebacker who likes to play loose and chase plays — necessary ingredients for NFL special teams.

Graham Mertz grew up outside of Kansas City, Kan., with his parents (Ron and Amy). His father played for John Gutekunst (father of Packers GM Brian Gutekunst) on the offensive line at Minnesota (1989-92). His older sisters (Lauren and Mya) played college basketball at Kansas State and Drake, respectively. Mertz grew up playing quarterback and started training with private coach Justin Hoover in sixth grade. After starting at Bishop Miege High, he transferred as a junior and led Blue Valley North to the 2017 Class 6A state title (3,684 yards passing and 49 touchdowns). A four-star recruit, Mertz had Wisconsin ties and connected with former head coach Paul Chryst, becoming the highest-ranked quarterback to ever sign with the Badgers. After a rocky four seasons in Madison (19-13 as a starter), he entered the transfer portal and landed at Florida, where he started 16 games over the past two seasons (7-9 record) but missed nine because of injuries. A good-sized athlete, Mertz is efficient on play action with enough mobility (in and out of the pocket) to buy time. He is quick to scan, and his internal clock has upgraded over the years, although his accuracy drops off with his secondary reads. Overall, Mertz struggled to stay healthy in Gainesville, but he played with improved conﬁdence and better decision-making than what he showed at Wisconsin. He will get his chance to compete for an NFL roster spot, once he's healthy.

Payton Page grew up in Greensboro, N.C., with his parents (Eric and Felicia). His father played football at North Carolina A&T. Page considered himself a basketball player growing up until he was convinced to switch to football at Dudley High (former Dudley quarterback Hendon Hooker helped sway him). Page collected 191 tackles and 55 tackles for loss over his ﬁrst three years (his senior year was canceled because of the COVID-19 pandemic). A four-star recruit, Page picked Clemson over North Carolina and Tennessee, then waited his turn to become a starter for the Tigers as a senior. After enrolling at Clemson weighing 395 pounds, Page became serious about nutrition — he has lost more than 100 pounds. He gets off the snap with bouncy quickness and the hand strength to force his way through a blocker's shoulder. However, his pad level lowers his chances for quick sheds or counters, and he needs to ﬁnd more ways to impact the pocket. Overall, Page spent most of college buried on the depth chart, but he ﬂashed the type of potential on his senior tape that suggests there is more in his game than his production suggests.

Dalton Cooper grew up in central Oklahoma, with his parents (John and Stefanie). At Prague High, he played both ways as a right tackle and defensive lineman (147 combined tackles his ﬁnal two seasons), earning all-state honors in 2018. A three-star recruit, he received just two FBS offers and started out his college career at Texas State. After three seasons as the starting left tackle, he entered the transfer portal and jumped at the chance to move closer to home. He started 21 games over the last two seasons at Oklahoma State, primarily at left tackle. Cooper is quick out of his stance to close space on defenders in the run game or cut off edge speed in pass protection. He gives up initial ground to power rushers, especially when his initial strike placement is off, but he works hard to center his block and sit down, relying on snatch techniques. Overall, Cooper is a cerebral, coordinated blocker, with the spatial awareness and play strength to get the job done. NFL scouts believe he can play tackle or guard.

Sean Martin, one of seven children, grew up with his parents (David Leggett and Torie Martin). He was an all-state basketball player and all-state defensive end at Blueﬁeld High, and he did battle against Zach Frazier when Blueﬁeld faced rival Fairmont. A three-star recruit, Martin initially committed to North Carolina but later ﬂipped to his home state West Virginia, partially because of Frazier's inﬂuence. He ﬁlled out his frame over the last ﬁve years and was used across the defensive line, which showed his versatility, but I don't think he found a true "home" position. His lackluster production reﬂects his overall impact, but he has the frame and movement traits that ﬂash against both pass and run — he just needs to translate the talent into more consistency. Overall, Martin is a durable player (played every game the past four seasons), with above-average length and body twitch. It won't be a surprise if he becomes a better pro than college player, likely in a 4i-/ﬁve-technique role.

A part-time starter at South Carolina, Jules was a rotational defensive tackle in defensive coordinator Clayton White's four-man front, lining up primarily as a three-technique. A late bloomer who didn't become a starter until his ﬁfth season of college football, he joined the Gamecocks for his ﬁnal year but struggled to stand out on a deep defensive line, even before his midseason knee injury. Jules aces the eye test. He has the size and lower-body quickness to factor into the play when he gets off the ball and puts himself in the right positions. However, he is often late to react to the blocking scheme and doesn't show enough urgency in his stack and shed. Overall, Jules doesn't have a proven track record of impacting the quarterback, but he is big, long and physical — and the NFL values big, long and physical players in the trenches. He is worth a late-round developmental ﬂier and would be a candidate for a practice squad.

beast_summary: Olatunbosun "Tommy" Akingbesote (ah-KING-bah-so-tay) grew up in District Heights, Md., with his parents (Odun and Arinola). He saw himself as a basketball player before making the switch to football as a junior at Charles Herbert Flowers High, because that was his best chance at a college scholarship. A four-star recruit, Akingbesote received offers from Oklahoma, Texas A&M and others, but he was locked on nearby Maryland because of the coaching staff. He was the second-ranked defensive lineman in Mike Locksley's 2021 class, behind Chop Robinson. Akingbesote carries most of his weight in his upper half, and he can dent the depth of the pocket with initial quickness off the snap. He made gradual improvements each season and has yet to play his best football, although he is still connecting the dots — and things won't slow down in the NFL. Overall, Akingbesote has unquestionable talent, especially for his size, but he was more of a cog in the machine than a difference-maker that jumped off the tape or the stat sheet.

Carrington Beaux Collins, the youngest of three children, grew up with his parents (D'Andre and April). His father played linebacker at New Mexico State and later became a coach. Collins prepped at St. John Bosco and had a standout junior season with 41 catches for 1,008 yards (24.6 average) and 14 touchdowns, leading the team to a 13-1 record and state title. A four-star recruit, he was the third-ranked receiver in California (behind Troy Franklin and Xavier Worthy) and followed his high school quarterback (DJ Uiagalelei) to Clemson. After three years, he transferred to Notre Dame for his senior year and helped the Irish to the national title game. A loose, limber athlete, Collins can alter his pacing mid-route and ﬂashes a second gear to run under the deep ball. However, while the separation tools are there, the execution is lacking. He has the body control to make back-shoulder grabs look routine, but focus drops were an issue. Overall, Collins doesn't have the tape or production of a playmaker, but he has draftable traits — that might be enough for a team to believe in his potential.

Caleb Etienne (E-tee-en) was born and raised in New Orleans, with his mother (Leslie). He met his ﬁancee (Sataizha Buckner-White) at Butler (Kan.) Community College in 2020 and the couple has a 3-year-old son (Caleb Etienne Jr.). After playing right tackle as a high school junior, he started at left tackle as a senior at Warren Easton High in 2018. Etienne was forced to go the junior college route out of high school and became a three-star juco recruit, signing with Oklahoma State. He became the starting left tackle in 2022 but decided to transfer the following spring (Mike Gundy: "He felt he got beat out, so he left."). He transferred to BYU before the 2023 season and struggled at right tackle. But he then replaced Kingsley Suamataia at left tackle in 2024 and played at a high level, putting himself on the NFL radar. Etienne is a large human who works hard to reach his landmarks and shield defenders with base angles. Though his long arms are a selling point, his hands often land wide and late in pass protection, negating his length advantage. He is a high-cut blocker — pad-level issues frequently pop up for him in both the run game and as a pass blocker. Overall, Etienne doesn't play with the reaction quickness to answer NFL talent, but he is a mountain of a human with intriguing tools that can be cultivated.

A two-year starter at Ole Miss, Prieskorn was a ﬂex tight end in offensive coordinator Charlie Weis Jr.'s spread scheme (44.1 percent of snaps in the slot, 34.3 percent inline/wing, 11.9 percent wide). An older prospect who is married with two young children, he has taken a long journey to this point — quarterback in high school and at Fork Union Military Academy, walk-on (with a position switch) at Memphis, ﬁnal stop of his college career at Ole Miss. Prieskorn doesn't have the speed to easily separate (before or after the catch), but he can be more physical than defenders at the top of routes and displays outstanding hand-eye coordination (caught 11 of 13 contested targets with the Rebels). He can cover up defenders as a blocker in the run game, too, but doesn't have the lateral agility or power to re-establish the line of scrimmage. Overall, Prieskorn is a vacuum-handed, dependable pass catcher who can be a chain-mover, but he isn't an explosive threat and has limitations to how he can impact the game. He is an easy player to like but has a low ceiling as a pro.

beast_summary: Luke Newman grew up in Bloomﬁeld Hills, Mich., with his parents (John and Tinney). He prepped at Brother Rice High, an all-boys Catholic school, and earned all-league honors at left tackle and defensive tackle. Weighing just 250 pounds, he received only FCS recruiting interest and committed to Holy Cross over Lafayette. He earned the starting left tackle job in his second season and ripped off 37 straight starts. After the 2023 season, he considered going pro but instead jumped into the portal and transferred back home (his parents are both Michigan State alums). Looking to showcase his versatility, he moved to left guard and started every game there in 2024. THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 243 Newman is quick in his pass sets to shuffle, slide and mirror while also tracking blitzers. He has the upper-body torque to dump rushers but doesn't show the same power as a drive blocker to displace in the run game. Overall, Newman will have a tough time controlling the point of attack against long-armed defensive linemen, but his movement skills, demeanor and durability should give him a chance to stand out in an NFL training camp.

Robbie Ouzts (OOTS) grew up playing sports in Rock Hill, S.C., and developed a love for football, because of the physicality. His favorite player growing up was fullback Brad Hoover (which is why Ouzts wears No. 45). He was a fullback/tight end at Rock Hill High and posted 465 receiving yards as a senior. A three-star recruit, Ouzts committed to Alabama over other SEC programs and played a variety of roles, from aligning in the I-formation under Bill O'Brien to the "H" tight end position in Kalen DeBoer's scheme. With his trademark mustache, he has always been wired to be the hammer and not the nail — he plays with immense pride in laying out his body on every play and ﬁnishing his block by whatever means necessary. He saw just 21 career targets but showed good hands and body control when he got chances (also played 537 snaps on special teams). Overall, Ouzts is a throwback player with a gladiator mentality. He would have more opportunities in NFL offenses of 30 years ago, but he has a chance to make a roster as an H-back "sniffer" and goal line tight end.

Brant Kuithe (keeth-ee), whose twin brother (Blake) also played at Utah, grew up outside of Houston with his parents (Dennis and Debbie). He started playing football in grade school (on the offensive line) and grew into a do-everything weapon (including punting) at Cinco Ranch High. As a senior, he rushed for more than 1,000 yards in seven games and was named district MVP. THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 176 A three-star recruit, Kuithe made an immediate impact for the Utes as a hybrid tight end and received draftable grades from NFL scouts. But he suffered a torn ACL (Sept. 2022), which required multiple surgeries — the setbacks kept him sidelined for 2023, as well. He returned in 2024, only to suffer another season-ending injury. When healthy, Kuithe is an NFL-caliber athlete and a matchup weapon out of the slot. He stems and creates separation, especially on in-breakers, which also gives him a chance to show off his YAC talent. He is a more physical blocker than one might expect, but he will always be limited by his size. Overall, Kuithe has draftable talent with the athletic versatility and pass-catching ability to help an offense and play special teams. His durability, though, is the chief concern.

A part-time starter at North Carolina, Nesbit was a "joker" tight end in former offensive coordinator Chip Lindsey's spread pro scheme (80.1 percent of his 2024 snaps came in the slot). He didn't start playing football until his junior year of high school but quickly put himself on the NFL map while catching passes from Drake Maye, before injuries disrupted his ﬁnal two seasons. Nesbit has functional athletic traits in his routes and at the catch point, but his NFL paycheck will depend on his receiving impact — he needs to play stronger through contact and button up his catch-point focus. Though he ﬂashed promise as a move blocker in college, he consistently punches below his weight class with below-average sustain/ﬁnish strength. Overall, Nesbit has silky adjustment skills and is more of a large-framed wide receiver than traditional tight end. He doesn't have much to offer as a blocker, however, and might have a tough time convincing an NFL coaching staff that his receiving upside is enough to compensate. His best chance at the next level might be as a big slot.

beast_summary: Charles "Chaz" Chambliss (cham-bliss) grew up with his parents (Cliff and Angela) and started playing football at age 5. His father, who spent two decades as a U.S. Army drill sergeant, died of a stroke at age 53 (March 2020). At Carrollton High, Chambliss combined for a career 251 tackles and 31.5 sacks. A four-star recruit, he committed to Georgia and bounced between inside linebacker and the Jack outside linebacker position. He saved his best for last, posting career-best numbers as a senior in 2024, including a team-high 6.5 sacks. Compactly built, Chambliss has tweener size and length, but he plays with the physicality in the run game to control the point of attack and string out runs. He makes himself a small target for blockers and uses his ﬂexibility to maneuver his body around the trees. His chase speed stands out, he doesn't miss tackles and his teammates say he's the toughest guy on the team. Overall, Chambliss is a sawed-off edge defender who can provide depth as an outside linebacker in a 3-4, but his ticket to an NFL roster spot will be as a special teams ace.

A one-year starter at South Carolina, Simpkins settled in at right guard in former offensive coordinator Dowell Loggains' zone-based scheme. Over his ﬁrst three seasons at North Carolina Central, he developed into one of the best offensive linemen in the FCS (primarily at center), then adapted quickly at right guard against SEC competition in 2024. Simpkins is a strong, assignment-oriented blocker who always keeps busy and looks to ﬁnish in close quarters or out in space. Though he plays with urgency, he often plays rushed, which leads to excessive leaning and shaky technique. He got away with those hiccups in the FCS, but it became more of a challenge while at South Carolina. Overall, Simpkins needs to continue maturing his sloppy habits, but his heavy latch hands and physical brand of football help him execute as both a run and pass blocker. His durability and experience — at center and guard — haven't gone unnoticed by NFL teams.

beast_summary: Justin Barron grew up in central Connecticut, with his parents. His father (Jason) played football at UConn; his mother (Sara) played college soccer at Hartwick. Barron was a wide receiver and safety at Suffield Academy and posted 525 receiving yards and two interceptions as a senior, leading the team to the 2019 Class A New England Championship. A three-star recruit, Barron committed to Syracuse over UConn and others, and he made the switch from receiver to safety in 2020. Over the last few seasons, he played all over the back seven — linebacker, safety, big nickel — and reached at least 90 tackles in each of his ﬁnal two seasons. Barron is an impressive size-speed athlete, and there are zero concerns about his competitive toughness or football-playing temperament. Though his burst to close jumps off the tape, his coverage movements are inconsistent and missed tackles made for a nagging issue on his 2024 tape. Overall, Barron needs better consistency to ﬁnd a full-time role on defense, but he can provide versatile depth. His special teams experience (949 snaps in college) will pay immediate dividends.

A three-year starter at Syracuse, Clark was an interchangeable safety in defensive coordinator Elijah Robinson's scheme, splitting time evenly between nickel, ﬁeld and boundary roles. After one year at Rutgers, he jumped to Syracuse, where he posted consistent production each season. Clark's speed, explosiveness and physical proﬁle are more good than great, but he likes to play with urgency when driving on plays and arriving with pop. Though the hunger to make plays is there, he doesn't put himself in position to get his hands on the football often enough. Overall, Clark has the versatile skill set and toughness to compete for a nickel role at the next level, but his college tape leaves you wanting more from a playmaking standpoint. His upside on special teams will help his chances of sticking in the NFL.

beast_summary: Rokafewlloa "Roc" Taylor, the youngest of four, grew up in Oxford, Ala., with his mother (Christina). He started playing football at age 4 and was an all-state receiver as a junior at Oxford High (1,291 receiving yards). A three-star recruit, Taylor was committed to Tennessee for more than 18 months, but the school rescinded his offer days before signing day after a coaching change. Taylor landed at Memphis instead and combined for 2,033 receiving yards over his junior and senior seasons. Taylor has the look of an NFL receiver with his long, muscled-up frame — and the way he extends outside that frame to snatch the football. His hand-eye coordination shows in crowded environments, although it also shines a light on his struggles to set up defenders and easily separate at the tops of routes. Overall, Taylor will struggle to escape press and tight coverage over the ﬁrst two levels, but his competitiveness and ability to adjust to the football will be his tickets to success at the next level, especially in the red zone.

A one-year starter at Baylor, Linton was a wide edge rusher in head coach Dave Aranda's four-man front, lining up mostly in a two-point stance. After playing a 4i-technique at Syracuse, he moved to a more natural seven-/nine-technique role at Texas Tech in 2023 and Baylor in 2024, ﬂashing disruptive ability as a sub-package defender (averaged 33.2 defensive snaps per game over the past three seasons). Linton is long-limbed and quickly attacks the arc, but he is overly reliant on his speed and doesn't have a deep toolbox as a pass rusher, despite being a sixth-year prospect. Although he can occasionally use his length to stay detached in the run game, his strength breaks down at the point of attack and teams know they can ﬁnd success running to his side of the ﬁeld. Overall, Linton is one-dimensional and hasn't proven himself beyond being a ﬂash pass rusher, but his ﬁrst-step explosion and body length will earn him extended looks. He projects as a designated rusher on sub-downs (if he can stay healthy), in the mold of Arden Key.

beast_summary: Keondre Jackson, one of 14 children, was born and raised in Freeport, Ill. He started at receiver and safety for two years at Freeport High, plus qualiﬁed for state in wrestling. A no-star recruit, Jackson signed with Nebraska-Kearney but entered the portal in his ﬁrst semester and transferred to Illinois State, which is closer to home. A three-year starter, his production improved each season, and he generated some buzz after his performance during Senior Bowl week. Jackson is a heavy downhill striker, and his energy pops on tape (defense and special teams). He runs the alley with conviction, using loose feet to make abrupt changes to adjust with shifty ball carriers. His coverage reads and angles tend to be inconsistent from the post, although he keys quickly in underneath zone coverage. Overall, Jackson's average burst and speed aren't ideal, but he is physically imposing as a tackler and projects best near the line of scrimmage where he can man cover tight ends.

Drew Moss grew up in North Texas with his parents (Douglas and Regina), both of whom were college athletes at Rice. Drew Moss was a three-year starter on varsity at Richardson High, playing both tackle and guard, and earned all-state honors as a senior (also earned all-district honors for the shot put and discus). A no-star recruit, Moss received mostly Division III offers until FCS Lamar offered late in his senior season. He started all 22 games at right tackle in two seasons at Lamar before entering the transfer portal and landing at Colorado State. After staying at right tackle in 2023, he moved inside to right guard in 2024 and had his best season. Moss is an efficient mover with an assignment-sound mindset to understand his responsibilities. He has a smooth-muscled body with shorter arms and can be troubled by point-of-attack power (ﬂagged 17 times in two seasons at Colorado State). When his technique stays on schedule and he doesn't get overextended, he can show off his ﬁnishing grit. Overall, Moss might be a center-only option because of his measurables, but he has the tools and intangibles to develop into a potential reserve.

Jahvaree Ritzie grew up with his mother (Kindra), a heptathlete at SUNY Brockport, and younger brother (Jahnaul), who competes in the shot put and discus at Charlotte. Jahvaree Ritzie was also a standout in track at Glenn High (personal best of 57 feet in the shot put), but his calling was on the football ﬁeld — he had 18.5 tackles for loss as a junior. A four-star recruit, Ritzie stayed close to home, choosing North Carolina over LSU, Texas A&M and other SEC programs. After not starting as a junior, he posted career bests in backﬁeld production in 2024. Ritzie is a unique athlete, because of his smooth movements and foot speed (ran relays in high school), which showed on an 84-yard pick six in 2024. But he stays hung up in the wash too long and struggles to disengage single blocks, often conceding ground to power-based run blockers. Overall, Ritzie ﬂashes explosive power and short-area quickness, but he hasn't learned how to translate his talent to consistent production and impact, which could change with NFL coaching.

Nikko Reed was born in San Francisco and raised by his mother (Maria Napitan). His older brother (Khalil Hudson) played wide receiver at Southern Oregon. Reed played wide receiver and corner at Moreau Catholic High and collected 2,199 career all-purpose yards and 13 interceptions (three returned for touchdowns). An undersized (155 pounds) three-star recruit, he committed to Colorado, his lone then-Power 5 offer. After starting in 2022, he was part of the program's max exodus that came after Deion Sanders took the head-coaching job and ﬂipped the roster. Reed transferred to Oregon and became arguably the Ducks' most consistent starter in 2024. He is light-footed with balanced movement skills and recovery speed. His pattern recognition has shown steady improvements, although you'd like to see him better anticipate break points to be more disruptive. Overall, Reed lacks ideal size and explosiveness, but he plays ﬂuid and natural in reverse and is quick to support the run. He's a candidate for a nickel role.

Rivaldo Fairweather grew up playing different sports, but his "ﬁrst love" was basketball. He gave football a chance as a junior at Boyd Anderson High, starting out as the punter. He moved to a pass-catching role as a senior and exploded with 812 receiving yards and 15 touchdowns (also lettered in basketball, soccer and track). A three-star recruit, he was late to enter the recruiting process, but Florida International took a chance on his senior-year ﬂashes. After three productive seasons with the Panthers, he joined Auburn for his ﬁnal two college seasons. Still a relatively unpolished player, Fairweather does a nice job with blocking angles to shield defensive ends from the ball, but he needs to be more consistent executing second-level blocks. He was very effective blocking for a two count before releasing as a target, showing his natural body control to easily adjust to errant throws. Overall, Fairweather doesn't create as much as I was hoping after the catch, but he is athletic at the catch point and has upside as a blocker that will interest NFL teams.

Joshua "Josh" Kelly, who has an older brother (Chris), grew up in California with his parents (Chris and De'Andra). He moved to wide receiver in high school at Bullard High before transferring to San Joaquin Memorial for his senior year, posting 1,127 receiving yards in 2018. A three-star recruit, he stayed close to home and played at Fresno State, catching passes from Jake Haener. After an injury-riddled 2022 season, Kelly transferred to Washington State in 2023, then to Texas Tech for his ﬁnal season — he posted career-best numbers out of the slot in 2024. Kelly isn't the most detailed or explosive route runner, but his stem breaks are sharp because of his quick, urgent feet. Despite a relatively lean frame, he owns large, conﬁdent hands and works well with bodies around him to ﬁnish in traffic. Overall, Kelly ﬂashes elusiveness before and after the catch, but his lack of desired speed (on tape and the stopwatch) is a high hurdle that will be tough to clear versus NFL coverage.

Jordan Williams grew up in Gainesville, Ga., and played on both the offensive and defensive lines at Gainesville High. While starting at right tackle as a senior, he earned class 6A all-state honors and helped his team to the 2019 state playoffs. A three-star recruit, he passed on NC State, South Carolina and others to stay close to home at Georgia Tech (same recruiting class as Jahmyr Gibbs). Lining up primarily at right tackle, he set the school record for career starts (53) and was part of a program turnaround, including his best season as a super senior in 2024. Williams is quick into blocks to reach and engage defenders. Although his range is mediocre, he understands angles to ﬁt up linebackers away from his starting square. He isn't underpowered, but you'd like to see better drive mechanics from him so he could better move defenders in the run game. Overall, Williams can get off schedule when his balance drifts, but he has solid size, length and strain through contact. His experience and tackle-guard versatility work in his favor.

Power Echols (named after actor Powers Boothe) grew up in an athletic family — his father (Brian Echols) was a defensive back at Michigan State and had short stints with the 49ers and Jets; his mother (Astarlove Robinson) played basketball at Western Michigan. After growing up in Arizona, Echols moved with his family to Charlotte at age 12. At Chambers High (formerly Vance High), he was a four-year varsity starter on varsity and compiled nearly 400 career tackles, plus led the team to a 2020 state title as an all-state senior. A four-star recruit, Echols committed to North Carolina over Clemson, Penn State and Tennessee and started every game in the 2022-24 seasons (39 straight starts). He is quick to read the play and ﬂow, and he isn't afraid to stick his nose in the blender to pull down the running back. He reaches landmarks in coverage and has shown improved recognition, although he will struggle to man up with NFL tight ends and backs. Overall, Echols is durable and trusts his instincts (for better or worse) to go get the football, although inconsistent take-on and leverage angles need to be addressed. Overall, Echols is durable and trusts his instincts (for better or worse) to go get the football, although inconsistent take-on and leverage angles need to be addressed.

Elijah "Eli" Alston grew up in the Chesapeake, Va., area and started playing football at age 5. He was a four-year letterman as a defensive end at Oscar Smith High, helping the team to three straight state title games. A three-star recruit, he received his ﬁrst offer from James Madison but ultimately chose Marshall, because his mother (La Juan Stepney) encouraged him to leave the state to experience something new. He became a starter at Marshall, then entered the transfer portal after the 2023 season and committed to Miami over Texas A&M and others (Miami's defensive coordinator in 2024 was Lance Guidry, Marshall's defensive coordinator in 2021-22). Playing mostly as a Jack edge rusher, Alston was asked to rush, drop and ﬂatten to make plays down the line. He has enough strength in his frame to set an edge and constrict run lanes. I like his effort on defense and special teams, although I don't think he has the speed for special teams coverages in the NFL. Overall, Alston is only an average athlete, but he plays with energy to make plays against both pass and run, which can earn him a practice squad spot.

A four-year starter at Kentucky, Weaver was primarily a stand-up edge rusher in defensive coordinator Brad White's 3-4 base scheme. Possessing one of the more unique backgrounds in this class (has 11 ﬁngers, off-ﬁeld work, etc.), he didn't quite live up to the promise he showed on the ﬁeld as an underclassman, but he was a steady contributor for the Wildcats. Weaver is a worker-bee defender who works to get off blocks and make plays. Despite being an older player, there is still some upside there, if he improves some of the technical parts of his game, including improved leverage points as a rusher to fully access his power. Overall, Weaver has athletic and physical tools to work with at the next level, but his below-average contact balance and rush instincts will be tough to overcome against NFL competition.

beast_summary: Gus Hartwig, who has two younger brothers, grew up north of Indianapolis with his parents (Myles and Amy). His father played offensive tackle at Ball State. Hartwig became an All-American guard and center at Zionsville High (also a standout in the shot put). A four-star recruit, he received a host of Big Ten and MAC offers and committed to nearby Purdue. Aside from a season-ending knee injury in 2022 (which held him out to start the 2023 season), he was a model of consistency for the Boilermakers, earning honorable mention All-Big Ten honors each of his ﬁve college seasons. With his ﬂexible base and knee bend, Hartwig is quick off the snap and works his feet into position to seal off and control blockers in the run game. His ability to replace his hands and reﬁt improved on his 2024 tape, helping him drop anchor against power. Overall, Hartwig isn't a mauler and blocking NFL bull rushers will be a tough ask, but he plays with the functional size, athleticism and experienced know-how to keep defenders occupied.

Shamari (shuh-MAR-ee) Simmons grew up in Alabama with his parents (Madelin Durrell and Stanford Simmons). His father was a defensive back at Auburn (1999-2001). Shamari Simmons was an all-state athlete in basketball and football at Central High, leading the football team to the 2018 Class 5A state championship as a safety and wide receiver. He started out at Hutchinson (Kan.) Community College before two THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 509 productive seasons at Austin Peay, then two more at Arizona State. While playing a hybrid nickel role, Simmons did some of his best work near the line of scrimmage, using his burst and physicality to be a disruptive run defender (his run blitz forced a safety in Arizona State's playoff game versus Texas). His motor runs hot, and he explodes with force through the ball carrier as a tackler (has a knack for knocking the ball free). Overall, Simmons brings it every day as a competitor, plays bigger than he looks and has adequate range and ball skills in coverage.

Garmon Randolph grew up down the road from Athens, Ga., with his parents (Joseph and Monja). His older brother (Joseph) played defensive line at The Citadel (2016-19). Randolph was known more at Jefferson High for what he could do at tight end (14 catches for 205 yards and ﬁve touchdowns as a senior), but he also played defensive end (34 tackles, one sack and one interception, which he returned for a touchdown). A three-star recruit, he committed to Baylor and then-coach Matt Rhule over offers from Alabama, Michigan and others. Randolph moved to defense full time and played a variety of front-seven roles over the past six years for the Bears, primarily as a stand-up edge rusher. He has an explosive ﬁrst step as a rusher and smooth movement skills when dropping into space. A taller player, he gets upright when setting the edge, but his length and hand strength help him win battles. His motor also jumps out, although his hard-charging style leads to too many missed tackles. Overall, Randolph is still learning how to fully weaponize his size and athleticism, but it feels like there is untapped talent ready to be developed.

Zemaiah (zuh-my-uh) Vaughn, one of eight children, grew up in southeast Texas, with his parents (Chris and Zipporah). Following in one of his older brother's footsteps, he grew up playing quarterback and earned ﬁrst-team all-district honors in 2019 as a senior at United High (1,049 rushing yards and 854 passing yards). A no-star recruit, he was overlooked until Utah and defensive coordinator Morgan Scalley gave him a walk-on opportunity as a defensive back. Despite having no experience in the secondary, he joined the Utes and made the positional transition, eventually starting 31 straight games at left cornerback to ﬁnish his career. Although leaner than is ideal, Vaughn has an elite mix of height, length and straight-line speed. He is leggy in his movements — some of that stiffness hinders his ability to stay attached with quick-twitch route runners. He entered the 2024 season with high expectations, but offenses found too much success throwing at his side of the ﬁeld. Overall, Vaughn allows too much separation in man, but he is long and fast and has upside as a corner in Cover 3, where he could read and react.

Jordan Clark, who has two sisters, grew up in Baton Rouge, La., with his parents (Ryan and Yonka). His father put together a 13-year NFL career (2002-14) at defensive back, mostly with the Pittsburgh Steelers, despite going undrafted out of LSU (Ryan Clark is now an NFL analyst for ESPN). Jordan Clark developed a love for football and told his father in eighth grade that he eventually wanted to play college ball. He became an All-America defensive back at University Lab School in Baton Rouge. A four-star recruit, he committed to Arizona State, where he lined up primarily as a nickel over ﬁve years in Tempe. Clark transferred to Notre Dame for his ﬁnal season and was part of the nickel rotation in Al Golden's scheme, helping the Irish reach the national title game. He is very smooth in his movements and doesn't look out of his depth with man-coverage duties. He shows hip snap as a tackler, although his technique can be buttoned up to help him be a more consistent ﬁnisher. Overall, Clark is a ﬂuid athlete with a nose for the football. NFL teams speak highly about his interviews and intangibles.

A part-time player at Ole Miss, Bentley was a complementary back in offensive coordinator Charlie Weis Jr.'s balanced run scheme. After producing at SMU, he transferred to the SEC, but his impact for the Rebels was more sporadic than steady — he didn't command consistent playing time as part of the game plan. A gliding athlete, Bentley can put his foot in the ground, drop his weight and make strong cuts to break off long runs (one of only four SEC players with multiple carries of 50 yards or more in 2024). However, he isn't built to run between the tackles and is too reliant on ﬁnding outside tracks as both a runner and receiver. Overall, Bentley's ﬂashes in college teased the explosive-play creation that will give him a chance to stick in the league, but he is undersized and will have a very deﬁned role. His experience as a kick returner should boost his chances.

beast_summary: Mason Richman grew up outside of Kansas City, Kan., with his parents (John and Kathryn Richman Wallace). His younger brother (Maguire) signed with Kansas State in the 2025 recruiting class at linebacker. Mason Richman moved up to varsity as a sophomore defensive lineman at Blue Valley High and earned all-state honors as a senior, playing both ways as a defensive end and tight end. A three-star recruit, Richman was a 250-pound offensive tackle projection and committed to Iowa over Kansas (he added 60 pounds during his ﬁrst two years in the program). He earned the starting left tackle job in 2021 and ripped off 52 starts the last four seasons (most by an offensive lineman in the Kirk Ferentz era). Richman positions himself well to sustain in pass pro and shows good lateral quickness off the snap to reach, seal or cut off speed, although he overshoots his landmarks at times. Though he needs to show better control in space, he gets low in the run game and washes on down blocks. Overall, Richman graded as an NFL camp body last summer, but he worked himself into the conversation as a draftable prospect with his play in 2024 and offers valuable experience for the next level.

Donte Kent grew up in Harrisburg, Pa., with his parents (Ronald and Kathy). He was a two-way star (wide receiver and cornerback) at Harrisburg High and combined for 10 interceptions over his junior and senior seasons. A three-star recruit, he received mostly MAC offers and committed to Central Michigan. He compiled almost as many passes defended (47) as starts (48) over the past ﬁve seasons. As a senior, he added punt return duties to his resume and averaged 13.6 yards per return, including a 68-yard touchdown. Playing a lot of Cover 2, Kent skillfully uses his eyes to pick up on route clues and drive on throws. His aggressiveness can get him in trouble at times, but he shows the make-up speed on tape to recover. Despite getting his hands on a lot of footballs, he was able to convert only two passes into turnovers. Overall, Kent is an above-average tackler for the position (at least 50 tackles each of the past four years) with NFL-quality speed, processing and special teams value.

Dymere (die-meer) Miller grew up outside of Philadelphia, with his mother (Chaquita). After a car accident sidelined him for a stretch at Coatesville High, he attended Salisbury for a post-graduate year in 2019 and put himself on the radar of several FCS schools. He signed with Monmouth and set single-season school records for catches and receiving yards. For his ﬁnal season, he jumped into the portal and committed to Rutgers over Memphis, Pitt and Texas Tech. He led Rutgers in receiving in 2024. Miller is both quick and fast to pace his routes, cross up corners and create passing windows for the quarterback, which is necessary since he is a smaller target. Despite his movement skills, he wasn't very elusive on his 2024 tape and got himself in trouble by taking his eyes off the ball too quickly, leading to drops. Overall, Miller needs to be more reliable putting catches away, but the athletic talent is NFL-worthy in the slot and gives him upside on special teams coverages.

A four-year starter at Wake Forest, Davis was an edge defender in former defensive coordinator Brad Lambert's versatile fronts, lining up as a 4i-/seven-technique. The prize of the Demon Deacons' 2020 recruiting class, he led the team in sacks and tackles for loss each of the past three seasons and ﬁnished his career No. 2 in school history in tackles for loss (51) and No. 3 in sacks (25.5). Davis generates impressive force once he gets rolling downhill, ﬂashing the strong hands and contact balance to work off blockers. According to Wake Forest defensive line coach Dave Cohen, his energetic play style and motor compares to that of Kobie Turner as the best he has ever coached. Overall, Davis can get tied up too much in the run game, but his powerful hands/limbs and obsessive effort lead to production, especially as a pass rusher. He can offer an NFL defensive line immediate depth.

beast_summary: Dontae Manning grew up in the Kansas City, Mo., area and was a standout basketball, football and track athlete at Raytown High. He played on all three phases for the football team and earned ﬁrst-team all-state honors as a senior with 970 rushing yards, 97 tackles and 24 total touchdowns. He also set school track records of 10.67 seconds in the 100 meters and 22.27 in the 200. A ﬁve-star recruit, he was a consensus top-ﬁve corner in his class and originally committed to Oklahoma before ﬂipping to Oregon. He struggled to separate himself as a full-time starter and spent most of his career as a nickel/dime outside corner (22.8 defensive snaps per game in 2024). He was able to make an impact as a senior as a core-four special-teamer (216 special teams snaps in 2024). Manning has electric speed but lacks fundamental transition ability to stay attached to routes. His anticipation and feel for concepts are still in the development phase. Overall, Manning doesn't have draftable tape on defense, but he offers a combination of rare length, athletic gifts and special teams experience that makes him worth bringing to training camp.

Jack Henderson grew up outside of New Orleans with his parents (Paige and Steve). An all-around athlete at Mandeville High, he was one of the top lacrosse players in the area and earned all-district honors as a running back and defensive back. A no-star recruit, he received an offer from SE Louisiana and ﬂourished as a three-year starter. He entered the portal after the 2022 season and committed to Minnesota over Louisiana Tech and Louisiana Monroe. Henderson started for two seasons as a hybrid nickel while establishing himself as a core special-teamer. Despite sporting a slender frame, Henderson plays with a contact-driven mentality, but he must be more consistent with his ﬁnishing technique as a tackler. He shows some tightness when making sudden transitions but feels routes coming and ﬂashes ball instincts when he has opportunities. THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 508 Overall, Henderson is a competitive and energetic athlete who has proven himself in a variety of roles and alignments, but special teams could be his ticket to an NFL roster spot.

Aiden Williams, the oldest of three children, grew up in Alaska, with his parents (Travis and Sarah). He started playing football in third grade. He was a defensive end and tight end at Anchorage East High and earned all-state honors as a 225-pound senior (also played all four seasons on the basketball team). A no-star recruit, he became the ﬁrst Alaska native to sign with Division II Minnesota-Duluth. He arrived as a tight end and played the position his ﬁrst three years before the coaches asked him to shift to left tackle going into the 2022 season. He added more than 50 pounds that offseason and continued ﬁlling out his frame. Williams is quick-footed and agile in his pass sets to cut off rush angles, although his pad level and timing need to be developed to have any chance at slowing down interior power. He missed most of Shrine Bowl practices (and the game) because of a minor toe injury, but he held his own during the ﬁrst practice. Overall, Williams faces a steep learning curve, but he offers the athleticism and mindset to be a moldable ball of clay for a team willing to develop him. A college tight end and left tackle, he will move inside to guard or center in the NFL.

Zion Childress, one of three children, was born and raised in Houston with his parents (Cynthia and Deric). Originally a wide receiver at New Caney High, he moved to quarterback and combined for 3,505 passing yards, 2,901 rushing yards and 68 touchdowns over his junior and senior seasons. A three-star recruit, he signed with Texas State as a defensive back and played for two seasons as a nickel. Looking to play at a higher level, he entered the transfer portal and committed to Kentucky (over TCU and Washington). He was a two-time captain for the Wildcats and started 25 straight games as a nickel safety. Although he is undersized, Childress is quick to read and drive to inﬂuence the play. He made a number of plays on the 2024 Georgia tape early in the season but struggled to build off that performance the rest of his ﬁnal year. Overall, Childress is easy to appreciate because he plays fast, physical and decisive, but his missed tackles and lackluster ball production make it tough to fully buy in. His special teams mentality certainly will help.

Seth Coleman grew up on Florida's Atlantic coast and started playing football in ﬁrst grade, although basketball was his focus through childhood. He played both sports at Holy Trinity Episcopal Academy and received several basketball offers, but a big senior year on the football ﬁeld (101 tackles, 13 sacks) changed his outlook. A four-star recruit, he committed to Illinois (over Utah and others), initially lining up as a defensive end before moving to a stand-up edge role, from which he posted steady backﬁeld production the past four seasons. Coleman plays with effort and energy to aggressively attack the pocket, although his hands, feet and dip often feel disconnected when attempting different moves. Though his motor also translates to the run game, he has only average strength at the point of attack and can be late unwinding from blocks. Overall, Coleman doesn't bring much deception to his pass rush, but he offers length and burst to wrap the edge and affect the quarterback.

Micah (muh-ky) Bernard grew up in Southern California and started playing football at age 5. He lettered in basketball, football and track at Gahr High, where he combined for 3,127 rushing yards over his ﬁnal two seasons. A three-star recruit, he received offers from Oregon and USC, but Utah entered the mix and received Bernard's commitment. After backing up Zach Moss in 2019, Bernard was part of a committee the next few years, including playing both ways (corner and running back) in the Rose Bowl vs. Ohio State. After missing most of the 2023 season because of injury, he returned as a senior in 2024 and had a career year. An upright slasher, Bernard can be a power back when he wants, but he also can put his foot in the ground and cut back across pursuit. Despite some stiffness in his hips, he does a nice job keeping his feet beneath him. He also looks comfortable catching the football out of the backﬁeld. Overall, Bernard isn't consistently patient or creative, but he is quick both to and through the hole, with the run balance and subtle cuts mid-stride to gash the defense.

Tresean "Tre" Stewart was born and raised in Winston-Salem, N.C., with his parents (Lashonda Stewart and Angelo Terry). While lettering in basketball, football and track at Winston-Salem Prep Academy, he had a record-breaking junior season (2,045 rushing yards, 1,493 receiving yards and 46 total touchdowns, scored ﬁve different ways). A no-star recruit, he signed with Division II Limestone (S.C.) University and led the team in rushing as a sophomore and junior. He entered the transfer portal for his ﬁnal season and committed to Jacksonville State over several FCS offers (Indiana State, Mercer, Samford). He ﬂourished in Rich Rodriguez's offense in 2024, joining Ashton Jeanty as the only two FBS running backs with at least 1,600 yards rushing and 25 rushing touchdowns. THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 74 Although his movement patterns aren't always efficient, Stewart is able to pick, slide and string together multiple moves with his abrupt run style. He runs upright, with below-average run strength that leaves him easily turned at contact. Overall, Stewart has his limitations, but he was a fun study because of his lively run style and ability to create in the passing game.

A part-time starter at LSU, Williams was a complementary back in offensive coordinator Joe Sloan's inside-outside zone scheme. He went from a scout team walk-on in 2019 to emerging as the most well-rounded back on LSU's roster the past few seasons, despite his lackluster career production. Though he can get what is blocked for him, Williams isn't a power back and his short-area movements won't threaten defenses. Never the star of the LSU backﬁeld, he didn't bring electricity to the ﬁeld, but he was Mr. Dependable with his ball security, pass catching and blocking. Overall, Williams is a speciﬁc type of running back who doesn't have the juice most teams covet at the position, but he is a potential ﬁt for an offense that values reliability in a third-down role.
